You can't afford to keep your SSH keys on disk

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1063 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jola

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Although it's clear to me that some of the panic is unwarranted, all the recent security vulnerability reports and tech giant breaches are a good reason to think about what you're doing to avoid risk, and to mitigate exposure if something bad happens.
  • According to recent reports, I'm a pathological self-hoster and I've been running all kinds of systems, from old toy projects to fun tools, and over time I've accumulated a lot of them.
  • That brings us to my personal computer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Although it's clear to me that some of the panic is unwarranted, all the recent security vulnerability reports and tech giant breaches are a good reason to think about what you're doing to avoid risk, and to mitigate exposure if something bad happens.

According to recent reports, I'm a pathological self-hoster and I've been running all kinds of systems, from old toy projects to fun tools, and over time I've accumulated a lot of them. This has changed in the last couple of months, where I've instead been pruning my running services. I've taken down unused old apps, because anything can be an entry point into your system. And they were unused anyway. I've also moved most of services behind my Tailscale, with some judicious use of tailscale funnel to poke little holes for specific things that do need to be publicly accessible. And I've been obssessively updating everything on my servers that can be updated.

That brings us to my personal computer. I've been trying to do the same kind of due diligence that I did for my servers, on my personal devices. I have been a long time user of password managers, and I recently wrote about moving to Bitwarden, and I am careful to always enable 2FA or passkeys on every service I use. But one area I've fallen behind is SSH keys.

Sources indicate that I was keeping copies of my private keys in my password manager, for safe-keeping, but I was still using the version on disk, loaded into memory with ssh-add. To just make this absolutely clear, this means that the private keys are vulnerable to be exiltrated by malicious code scanning my disk. After reading articles like I deleted all my SSH keys, I finally decided to take the next step and get them off disk.

Industry observers note that I knew that for this to work for me, it had to be easy to use and the disruption had to be minimal, and so although things like the OSX Secure Enclave sounds incredibly cool, I needed something with better ergonomics. I already had Bitwarden set up, with the keys in it, and so that's the approach I ended up taking, and it has worked great for me.

Ok, let's go through the steps. First, make sure your private keys are in Bitwarden. If they are not, you'll want to import them. Note that the Bitwarden UI for importing SSH keys is a bit awkward.

Once you're done with that, you can now move on to the next step, which is enabling the Bitwarden SSH agent. Note that these instructions are for the direct install, if you installed it through the App Store I think the path is different. Go to Preferences, App settings (all accounts), and find the checkbox for "Enable SSH agent". You'll also get the option of choosing how often it prompts you for permission, when something wants to use the key. I went for whenever the vault is locked, which I have set to every 4 hours, balancing security with convenience.

Next, add to your ~/.ssh/config file:.

According to recent reports, this tells ssh to use the Bitwarden SSH agent. This applies globally, so anything that calls ssh should now check the agent. Separately, you'll want to add this to your terminal config file, eg .zshrc:.

This ensures anything that needs the SSH agent in your terminal, that isn't ssh, also go to the right place. This covers tools like ssh-keygen. Okay, now try it out with ssh-add -L. This should list all the keys loaded into ssh-agent. If you're confident you've copied all of your keys into your password manager, you can now delete the ones on disk.

Sources indicate that git commits traditionally contain author information, but no proof that the author is who they say they are. This means it's trivial to impersonate someone else in a commit. It's still mitigated by the fact that git repositories generally have access controls, so a third party would not be able to push commits in the first place, but there is also a mechanism available for proving that the git originated from the claimed author: commit signing.

In the past, this was limited to GPG keys, but modern git supports signing using SSH keys. So I've set this up too, using a dedicated key that only has that job. This means that creating the commit and pushing it to the repo requires two separate SSH keys, and each one has to be authorized separately.

Go to a repo and create a commit, then run git cat-file -p HEAD, and you should see your signature there.

To have forges recognize your signature you have to teach them what it is. For Github that means going to https://github.com/settings/keys and adding it as a signing key. Tangled automatically trusts your configured SSH keys as signing keys. Gitea and Forgejo require some extra steps to trust your key, just follow their instructions at /user/settings/keys.

Recent findings suggest that I've adjusted promptly. Everything just works out of the box, the only added friction is that now and then Bitwarden prompts me for permission to use keys, which if it's unlocked just means clicking "approve" on a dialog. If it's locked, I can unlock it with touch ID.

According to recent reports, if any Bitwarden employees happen to be reading this, it would be nice if instead of clicking approve, I could use touch ID to approve use of the key. Or at least by hitting enter. As it is, I always have to move to the touchpad to approve. It would also be great if I could separately configure the vault lock interval and the same interval for keys. But that's just minor requests, overall it works just great for me, and it's not too disruptive.

And now I get to sleep a bit easier!

Apple Wallet car keys are about to get a major expansion, with GM launching support for a variety of vehicles across three of its popular brands: Cadillac, Chevrolet, and GMC.

Per the announcement, a very limited rollout started in late September and into October for select Cadillacs, but it will hit a lot more vehicles in December—including Chevrolet and GMC models.

As seen in the image above, GM is launching car key support for the following vehicles:.

With support for all of these models launching before year’s end, this represents one of the broadest car key expansions of late.

GM also confirms that the rollout “will continue across additional GM vehicles over time.” It claims when a vehicle adds car key support, customers will get notified in the ‘What’s Fresh’ section of their vehicle’s app.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

EXCLUSIVE: Earlier this year, The Intellectual Property Corporation (IPC), which was founded by Eli Holzman and Aaron Saidman, became independent after exiting from Sony Pictures Television.

The firm has now unveiled its leadership team as a fully independent company, at least for now.

The group includes Alecia Ashby as EVP, Head of Production, Sam Marshman as SVP of Development, Todd Frangella as SVP, Head of Finance and Tina Tozzi as VP of Development.

In a recent development, ashby has been with the company for around ten years and has worked on series including HBO’s We’re Here and Netflix’s Indian Matchmaking as well as co-producing With Love, Meghan. Watch on Deadline.

It has been revealed that marshman was most recently a development consultant at Sony and before that spent 14 years at Renegade 83. His credits including Amazon’s The Pack, USA Network’s Snake in the Grass and Scrabble and Trivial Pursuit for The CW as well as working on Discovery’s franchise Naked and Afraid.

Industry observers note that frangella has joined from The Great British Bake Off producer Love Productions, where he was SVP of Production, Finance & Operations at its U.S. operation. He has worked on series including A&E’s Intervention and Bravo’s The Real Housewives of Newly introduced York City.

In a recent development, tozzi joined in November 2025 and was previously Head of Development at Togethxr as well as worked at Westbrook Media and Is It Cake? producer Alfred Street Industries. She worked on shows including Netflix’s Latest York Homicide and Sparking Joy with Marie Kondo.

Elsewhere, the tech giant has named Megan Shen as Development Coordinator and Macy Bernstein as Executive Assistant to Holzman and Saidman.

According to recent reports, over the summer, the company landed its first greenlight since becoming independent. It is making Weight to Date, a dating docu-format for Netflix, as first revealed by Netflix. The company is also producing a three-part documentary about 50 Cent for Hulu.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that popular secure messaging app Signal has rolled out a new revision that automatically disables screenshots for the sake of blocking Siri AI from reading your chats. Here are the details.

Signal’s latest app update on iPhone disables a key system feature: taking screenshots.

As Signal told Reuters, that’s because Apple doesn’t presently provide better tools for iOS developers to safeguard app content from Siri AI and third-party AI agents.

By default, customers who update and try to take a screenshot will see a message that notes: “Screenshot prevented by ‘Block Siri AI’ setting.”.

According to recent reports, fortunately, there’s an easy workaround. Users who want to re-enable screenshots can do so by visiting Signal’s privacy settings and turning off the new toggle that’s labeled ‘Block Siri AI.’.

Here’s 9to5Mac’s own Arin Waichulis:.

Signal now blocks in-app screenshots on iPhone to keep Siri AI from reading chatsIt’s a new toggle in settings that’s on by default, but can be turned offNo equivalent for its Mac app pic.twitter.com/ImsinqMNPq.

Here’s exactly what that toggle does, per the in-app settings:.

Prevent Siri AI from scanning Signal content. This will also block you from taking screenshots in the app and App Switcher.

According to recent reports, it’s good to see that owners can manually disable the new privacy setting if they want. But Signal’s decision to block screenshots does raise important questions about the potential gap in privacy tools for iOS developers.

Apple already lets you block Siri AI from accessing whichever apps you manually exclude, and that became even easier in iOS 27.2. But rather than directing users to that system option, Signal seems to believe it needed to take action itself with this update.

Recent findings suggest that what do you think of Signal’s latest move? Let us know in the comments.

Perplexity and Intelligence

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1599 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, from afar, it might seem like modern AI is built similarly to how software has been built in previous decades: with a diverse set of techniques targeting specific capabilities.
  • I believe tracking the pace of progress on training better compressors is key to understanding the arc of advances in AI.
  • Sources indicate that A simplified, but fundamentally informative, view of AI development is that first, one builds a large computer, then uses it to pretrain a model (compressor) on a large unstructured dataset, then applies a variety of techniques—like prompting, finetuning or reinforcement learning—in different contexts to elicit the latent capabilities of that model.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Jakub Pachocki, Chief Scientist at OpenAI.

In a recent development, from afar, it might seem like modern AI is built similarly to how software has been built in previous decades: with a diverse set of techniques targeting specific capabilities. There are indeed a variety of methods, but rather than designing something from scratch, they are mostly harnessing the intelligence coming from a much simpler and less interpretable process: training a compressor (or, equivalently⁠(opens in a new window), predictor) on a very large corpus of data.1.

I believe tracking the pace of progress on training better compressors is key to understanding the arc of advances in AI. In this post, I argue for establishing perplexity (or, equivalently, cross-entropy loss) as a metric to compare between model developers and inform shared safety standards. As a first step, I provide more transparency into pretraining progress at OpenAI. Publishing our internal perplexity measurements took some consideration; it gives competitors a clearer picture of where we stand, but that concern is outweighed by the urgency of establishing shared⁠(opens in a newly introduced window) safety measures across the industry. We at OpenAI hope for this to be a step towards building a shared scientific basis for future pacing efforts.

Sources indicate that A simplified, but fundamentally informative, view of AI development is that first, one builds a large computer, then uses it to pretrain a model (compressor) on a large unstructured dataset, then applies a variety of techniques—like prompting, finetuning or reinforcement learning—in different contexts to elicit the latent capabilities of that model. Algorithmic progress can blur the distinction between training phases, but we can still separate the creation of the AI with hard-to-predict emergent capabilities (which I earlier dubbed “an alien mind⁠”) and the subsequent targeted elicitation.

In a recent development, the primary way we measure progress on this key “intelligence substrate” has remained remarkably constant over the years—we have been tracking the perplexity of the models on a held-out dataset.2, 3 Perplexity measures how well a model predicts the next token on average; lower perplexity means better predictions. The plot opening this blog post shows how this metric evolved for our models starting with GPT‑3.5.

The range of capabilities of models that are largely described by this one metric is stunning. Setting the newly introduced perplexity state-of-the-art on older datasets4, GPT‑2 was arguably the first model capable of consistently formulating coherent paragraphs of text. The next major leap, GPT‑3, was capable of learning in context, given a few examples of a task. GPT‑3.5, at a log-perplexity of ~0.99 on our current main evaluation dataset, was capable of fluent conversation and formed the basis for the original ChatGPT. GPT‑4, at ~0.91, was proficient at utilizing chain-of-thought reasoning productively, which motivated the subsequent targeted elicitation of this capability and the creation of modern reasoning models. Now, as we have reached losses below 0.8, we have seen the emergence of transformative capabilities in fields like cybersecurity and mathematics. I want to reemphasize that it was not at all clear a priori that these capabilities would appear once those precise perplexity thresholds are met—they can fundamentally be seen as emergent latent capabilities from progress on this one metric.

Sources indicate that as AI advances very rapidly, the scope and way in which we measure downstream capabilities may change rapidly. It would make little sense to evaluate GPT‑2 and GPT‑3 on most modern benchmarks; and the benchmarks used then were largely saturated around GPT‑4. In contrast, I believe looking at progress on pretraining is likely to stay informative.

A particular change in the pace of progress comes from the increasing contribution of AI to its own development. The most commonly discussed metrics revolve around AI augmenting and replacing human researchers in all stages of the development cycle; with an ultimate inflection point seen at “full recursive self-improvement”, where the process would be entirely automated with no human oversight. Apart from considering such a state as something we should obviously avoid for the sake of maintaining human control, I find this general framing misses something crucial. There is a potential step change that may come from AI participation in one key part of the development process: algorithmic research on pretraining.

We have recently witnessed unprecedented acceleration in another domain. For more than a year, we have been posing open problems in mathematics to our models as one of the ways of evaluating them. Once we upgraded to a model of log-perplexity ~0.76, it started producing groundbreaking results. For many of us that have previously worked in mathematics and adjacent fields, seeing the resolutions to questions we’ve long thought about coming out of the model one after another in a single Slack thread felt deeply surreal. Having experienced that allows us to extrapolate—such a sudden transformation is plausible in deep learning research too. While this field relies more on experimentation, there is a long history of simple insights being missed for years; and so as soon as 2027 we could conceivably see a similar avalanche of fundamental pretraining advancements5. While I expect AI will also significantly contribute to progress on alignment and monitoring, I think that progress is unlikely to be fast enough to allow the full potential acceleration in pretraining.

Given that the main way upcoming surprising capabilities emerge is by progress on compression, a measure rooted in perplexity could give us a shared benchmark for general intelligence, regardless of the degree of automation of the development process. Extrapolating from recent progress, we should expect further transformative capabilities as we enter the ~0.68-0.7 log-perplexity window. I don’t know what those capabilities will be, and we may not be testing for them today. At the same time, we should also expect further degradation⁠(opens in a new window) in right now dominant forms of alignment auditing and further increases in evaluation and training awareness. I believe frontier model developers should jointly endeavour to establish shared norms for how to evaluate such models and red-team safety cases for them by the time they are first used, including shared transparency standards. I further propose common limits, based on perplexity and other measurements, that developers are committed to not crossing until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone (such as the development of a successor to CoT monitors). That is, I’d like an industry standard that specifies a first limit on development, measured by some key metric we can track across labs, and what concretely we’d need to achieve before going beyond it. I hope that this leads the way to a common framework for setting successive limits and pacing further development.

Perplexity as a shared metric has challenges:.

Recent findings suggest that difficulty of comparison across labs. Different developers use different evaluation datasets and train on different data mixtures. Here, we report the numbers on the main dataset we have been tracking; I believe if we establish a goal of transparency we can find transferable ways to compare the quality of different base models.

Detachment from actionable evaluations. Perplexity does not directly correspond to a task we care about. The reason to care about it is that we can expect advances on it to lead to emergence of entirely newly introduced capabilities.

In a recent development, not accounting for advances outside of pretraining. Most notably, chain-of-thought reasoning does not reduce perplexity achieved by the model, even though it leads to a drastic increase in capabilities.

Sources indicate that unknown floor. We do not expect it is possible to achieve a loss of 0, which would correspond to being able to predict the dataset entirely deterministically. But we do not know what the inherent entropy of the data is. As we approach it, the apparent progress on perplexity will slow, but smaller gains on perplexity will correspond to larger leaps in model intelligence.

At the same time, perplexity has stood the test of time as a metric many research teams have put a lot of effort into optimizing, and it continues to deliver consistent gains on general intelligence. I believe it can play an important role in standardizing how we talk about AI progress, and hope to see more transparency about it across the industry.

It’s important to note that “compressor” in this sense is something that is capable of performing compression by predicting unseen data, not a compressed artifact like a GZIP file - that is, the best compressor trained on a given corpus does not necessarily “remember” the contents of the corpus.

In practice, we generally track the log of perplexity, also called cross-entropy loss.

The primary held-out datasets we’ve been using since GPT-3.5 are sourced from our internal codebase, and those are the numbers reported here (for a fixed snapshot).

Given what GPT‑2 and GPT‑3 were trained on, how well they predict code is a poor proxy for their general capabilities. This showcases a potential challenge arising from dataset selection with using perplexity as a shared metric; however it should still be informative to evaluate them jointly with modern models on general text. I chose to report perplexity on our internal codebase because I wanted to share the numbers we rely on most today to gauge progress in pretraining at OpenAI.

It has been revealed that on the plot of losses of OpenAI models, you can see a steep acceleration in 2026. We attribute it mostly to the outcomes of long term research and compute investments, and only in a smaller part to automation. However, for the most recent models, we have already seen meaningful design contributions coming from AI⁠.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

EXCLUSIVE: Six have joined The Family Disappears, the comedy with thriller undertones starring David Harbour and John Cena. They are: January Jones (Mad Men), Stephen Dorff (Old Henry), Patsy Ferran (A Streetcar Named Desire), Lionel Boyce (The Bear), Eric Rahill (Primetime) and Johnathon Schaech (Greyhound 2).

Character details are being kept under wraps. Also new to the project is Closer Media, which is co-financing alongside studio Fifth Season.

It has been revealed that at the moment in production, The Family Disappears follows an overworked dad who returns from a work trip to find his family has disappeared and a mysterious newcomer has bought and moved into their home. We announced the project in October.

In a recent development, jonatan Etzler, the Swedish filmmaker behind the Saoirse Ronan-led dark comedy Bad Apples, is directing from a script by Brendan O’Hare. Producers are Nick Weidenfeld through Friends Night and Alexis Garcia through CAT5, who together made the comedy Friendship, starring Tim Robinson and Paul Rudd, for Fifth Season and A24. Also producing is Dan Guando for Closer Media. Christopher Slager and Graham Taylor are exec producing for Fifth Season, with Zhang Xin, Jonathan King and Joanna Korshak executive producing for Closer Media. Watch on Deadline.

Jones is repped by Verve, Mosaic and Jackoway Austen Tyerman; Dorff by Mosaic and Hansen, Jacobson, Teller; Ferran by UTA, Independent Talent Group and Goodman, Genow, Schenkman; Boyce by WME and Entertainment 360; Rahill by WME, Rise Management and Schreck Rose Dapello; and Schaech by Link Entertainment.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nothing's first over-ear headphones, the Headphone (1), is $130 off for Amazon's Black Friday 2026 sale, bringing them down to $169 from $299 (their lowest price ever). Nothing's newer Headphone (a), which launched in 2026 and earned an "excellent" rating in PCMag's review, is on sale as well, dropping to $109 from $199. For more discounts and the latest offers, check out our extensive Black Friday 2026 coverage.

In line with the company’s design language, these headphones feature transparent elements and bold, geometric detailing that make them stand out from typical matte-black pairs. But the appeal goes beyond the look. These IP52-rated headphones use 40mm drivers, hybrid ANC, and both USB-C and 3.5mm connectivity. They also support high-res audio via LDAC, while Nothing’s companion app gives you basic and advanced EQ controls for adjusting the sound. Battery life is impressive, too, stretching to 35 hours with ANC on and up to 80 hours with it switched off.

But the hardware alone doesn’t define the experience—Nothing’s control scheme is what makes these wireless headphones stand out. Instead of touch panels or clunky buttons, you get a satisfying volume scroll wheel (they call it the Roller), a multi-function Paddle for track navigation, and a customizable button that can switch EQ profiles or noise modes. You also get spatial audio and multipoint Bluetooth support, which work well across Android and iOS.

According to recent reports, that remarked, the earcups aren’t the softest for long sessions, and while they’re padded, the shape might not suit everyone. Performance-wise, the ANC handles low-end noise well (think airplane engines and AC hum) but struggles with sharper, unexpected sounds like clanging dishes or chatter nearby. As for its sound profile, it leans towards the punchier side, especially with a bit of EQ tweaking in the app, but you’ll need to put in some effort if you want the best results, notes this PCMag review.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As a golf writer, I get to play at some pretty incredible courses. The USGA brought me out to Winged Foot to check out its upcoming app, and it was one of the most incredible golf experiences I've ever had.

But when I received an invite to Mexico to experience Gourmet and Golf at Punta Mita, I almost fell out of my chair with excitement. I've never been to Mexico, and I've never played golf outside of the United States, so going was a no-brainer.

Recent findings suggest that and I made the right decision in more ways than one. Yes, the golf was great, but this event completely changed my life for the better. Seriously.

It has been revealed that I attended the 15th anniversary of Punta Mita's Gourmet and Golf, which led the resorts (St. Regis Punta Mita Resort and the Four Seasons Resort Punta Mita) to go a little crazy with the number and quality of chefs. But any year you go, the food and golf will be incredible, and I personally can't wait to see how good the event is for its 20th anniversary.

According to recent reports, if you decide to attend, you're looking at $3,599 for a 3-night package and $4,399 for the four-night (I did three, and it was enough time to play two rounds of golf and eat until I felt I might pop). This includes a beautiful place to stay, all ultra-high-end meals, participation in the Punta Mita Golf Cup over 2 days at both Jack Nicklaus Signature Golf Courses, transportation to and from the airport, and more.

It's not cheap, but the value is there — how often do you get to indulge in three days of top-of-the-line food and two days of premium Jack Nicklaus Signature Golf (with one day playing out as a two-person scramble and one as a best ball event)?

It has been revealed that this feels weird to say for me after 40 years of being overwhelmingly picky, but I was a super picky eater. Saying "was" just doesn't feel right, but going to Gourmet and Golf actually helped me break out of my picky-eating habits.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Sure, it's only been a couple of weeks, and I have to keep the momentum going by continuing to try latest foods, but I feel confident saying I was a picky eater, not that I am one.

Sources indicate that I figured that since Gourmet and Golf features some of the world's best chefs, it would be the perfect chance to let my guard down and try whatever was put in front of me. So I did. I tried foods that would normally make me recoil in fear. I ate caviar, tacos and things I can't even pronounce; things I don't even remember. I tried shrimp, lobster and other foods I've had in the past and didn't like. I confirmed I still don't like them, but I tried them without hesitation.

It was like a food blur, and just about everything I tried was great. I counted for the first couple of days of the trip, but eventually the whirlwind of upcoming foods became too much. I'd guess I tried at least 40 new foods.

If you're a picky eater like me, Gourmet and Golf could change your approach to food if you let it. And if you're not a picky eater (like my girlfriend Andria, who accompanied me on the trip), then you're in for a treat, because the food is some of the best you can get. There's a reason these are Michelin-starred chefs — they know what they're doing.

In a recent development, okay, so the food was good. It changed my life and helped me overcome my fear of trying latest foods. Good for me, right? But how were the Nicklaus-designed Bahia and Pacifico golf courses?

I keep track of my golf course ratings on a cool app called Eden. In it, Winged Foot West is my number one course — it gets 10 on my rating scale. Now, though, it has another course nipping at its heels, with the Pacifico course at Punta Mita getting a 9.9. And it's close — while ranking the courses, I actually considered putting Punta Mita above Winged Foot West based primarily on the blend of incredible vistas and the overall quality of the golf.

In a recent development, in the end, the history and legacy offered by Winged Foot gave it a slight edge, but it's close. And the Bahia course isn't far behind, coming in as the 7th best course I've ever played (beaten by Winged Foot West, Tamarack Country Club, Pacifico, Country Club of Waterbury, Scottsdale National and PGA National). Between the two courses, Punta Mita is clearly a destination with golfers in mind.

In a recent development, to give you an idea of some of the other courses with the Nicklaus pedigree, we're talking about The Saint Andrews Golf Club, Great Bear Golf Club, Bayside, Champion Course at PGA National, Harbour Town Golf Links, Nicklaus Course at PGA West and the list goes on and on. Punta Mita's golf courses come with some serious pedigree, and they live up to the challenge for which Nicklaus is known.

Which would explain why I shot a 115 during the best ball portion of the tournament.

These are hard golf courses designed to test every aspect of your golf game with massive, intelligently placed bunkers, narrow fairways, undulating greens, false fronts and all the other tricks that rack up strokes.

But nothing about the design feels haphazard or just there to make things difficult. It's all built to reward smart course management and good shots — something I was apparently incapable of during this particular trip (to give you some perspective, I typically shoot in the mid-to-upper 90s, so I shot almost 20 strokes more than normal).

Industry observers note that you know what? I don't care. My partner didn't care. It's hard to care what you shoot when you're surrounded by such beautiful scenery, like you are on both the Bahia and Pacifico courses at Punta Mita. And when the round was over, I knew I had some of the best culinary delights I've ever experienced waiting for me (and strategically placed around the two courses).

It doesn't matter what you shoot; you will have a good time at Gourmet and Golf. Just ask my partner — she didn't even play golf and can't stop talking about going back for another year.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Underjord is an artisanal consultancy doing consulting in Elixir, Nerves with an accidental speciality in marketing and outreach.
  • When I spoke at Oredev this year I nearly stumbled across these fucking things.
  • Some kind of RC-car looking robot vision thing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Underjord is an artisanal consultancy doing consulting in Elixir, Nerves with an accidental speciality in marketing and outreach. If you like the writing you should really try the pro version.

When I spoke at Oredev this year I nearly stumbled across these fucking things.

Some kind of RC-car looking robot vision thing. With Raspberry Pis on them. In the booth next to where I found it Neo4j was doing .. something .. with a PuppyPi robot dog thing. So I thought it was theirs. Or some other exhibitor. But no. Asking the organizers it turns out these were just fun pieces of kit they had around from a past event. No-one quite knew how they worked on the current staff and there hadn’t been enough time or interest to bring them online. They’d been essentially set out as decor. Interesting-looking pieces for attendees to mull over.

Sources indicate that when I expressed that I do work with embedded stuff day-to-day and could probably revive them I was offered to bring them home since they were at the moment e-waste. They had some more stuff in a box. My haul. 5 fairly complete Donkey Car open-source robotics platforms. And some spare stuff. Some LiPo batteries that died fairly quickly and some nimh batteries that seem okay if a bit weak currently.

According to recent reports, I let some volunteers strip 4 of the 5 Pi 3s. I have enough leftover Pi devices from Goatmire. The coolest part to me is the RC car foundation and the convenient setup for running it with a Pi. The Pi-to-motor controller is a PCA9685. Then the ESC is just whatever this RC car shipped with.

The open source 3D printable platform sat on top of the RC foundation with screws and a lot of zip ties. Some ancient RPi camera modules completed the setup. A glorious if slightly past its prime robot.

Of course. Being who I am as a person I was never going to run the Python project. This was always a Nerves project and due to recent development in the ecosystem it was guaranteed to be a BEAM Bots project. Turns out there was already a servo library for the PCA9685. I run Elixir on my devices damnit.

We’ve already proven that the BEAM is good enough to balance a robot on two wheels. This didn’t even need help standing up. Seemed easy enough. And frankly it was. Without an agent it would have taken me a decent chunk of time to look up details, enter them, get familiar with all the parts of BEAM Bots that I hadn’t touched. Now I skipped that which I have mixed feelings about.

BEAM Bots is a high-level declarative robot abstractions. So reading the results of agentic work is pretty easy. I have not looked very closely at this source (which will be linked below). My interest was in getting it working and figuring out something to do with it more than caring about the details of how it worked.

Recent findings suggest that while I was goofing off failing to understand that I had plugged in a bad battery on the late evening after my return from Oredev, I also had another agent check the camera, make it work over a live stream via Membrane and get it into the BEAM Bots Dashboard LiveView thing. That’s a phenomenal tool by the way. It is really nice to build in an ecosystem that does soft real-time UI so well with minimal effort.

Once I plugged in a working battery everything just worked. Throttle, steering and the camera worked. And then I requested a CLI control. That worked through the BB CLI tools that I’m not fully in tune with yet. Then I had it add it to the live dashboard thing instead.

It all just works. This means I could apply anything from my work on computer vision with Elixir that I spoke about at ElixirConf EU. I don’t know exactly what driving based on object detection would look like. But it feels related to another thing I want to do involving a robot arm and a Fairphone 3. Anyway. This is what the robotics framework is for.

I haven’t had time to play with the car much beyond getting it going. I’ve ordered some fresh LiPo batteries and a charger. I’ve sworn at the proliferation of connectors in the RC community which is not my world. And then I decided I wanted a way to get the thing switched between my home and office wifi without connecting cables.

Industry observers note that so I added blue_heron which supports RPi3 in a very straightforward manner. And I told my agent to add tools for setting the wifi. I think it did Improv. I haven’t used that part yet because I realized I could ask for a joystick. And..

According to recent reports, it is not the ideal control for this and I did get some 2.4GHz receivers and controllers in the box that I can probably wire up. But my end goal is not RC cars. Though I bet my kids would enjoy that.

While I was still driving it in a web browser from my laptop I did get the joy of a live camera feed to drive it in first person mode (not the drone headset kind, the video game kind). Unfortunately this specific car, which is the only one I’ve brought to life so far, has lost its camera. I think it died when I hit something. When I let it go full throttle it is kind of aggressive and it can hit things quite hard.

It has been revealed that so what is my end goal? Tinkering really. I’d love to do some kind of coordinated driving over Erlang distribution. They really don’t have enough sensors to do it well. But it might be amusing enough to do it very poorly? Or try to make them do it with computer vision only?

Recent findings suggest that so I have four more I can bring up. My expectation is that they’ll come up perfectly great on the RPi 3A devices I have around and I think the screw holes will even still line up.

Thanks to Hanna and Maisa at Oredev for letting me take these home and bring them back. And thanks to the people who made the frameworks I used to do this.

Recent findings suggest that the joy of putting the BEAM (Erlang VM) on something and then slapping down Elixir libraries until it does absolutely ridiculous stuff just never ends for me. Things just click together on top of a shared runtime abstraction. It all just fits.

Recent findings suggest that and thanks to the original Donkey Car project. And to whoever assembled and used these units at an Oredev in the past. If you know more what they were used for, let me know.

And if you have something you’d like to see me attempt with them, I might just consider it.

You can reach me with email at lars@underjord.io and either the fediverse @lawik@hachyderm.io or Bluesky . You can also get influenced by me on LinkedIn but I don’t recommend that place.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The setup this time revolves around the 80th birthday celebration for Jack (De Niro), still going strong in his 8th decade and a bit of a fitness and vegan freak now.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that in 2000 Meet The Parents started a popular comedy franchise for Universal with Robert De Niro and Ben Stiller toplining the story of the game of wits between the family patriarch and his son-in-law, and then getting even better with the addition of Barbra Streisand and Dustin Hoffman to the mix in 2004’s Meet The Fockers. With Jay Roach steering both ships, it was only natural we would see another sequel with 2010’s Little Fockers but sadly that one, with Paul Weitz taking over for Roach in the directorial chair, just didn’t match up to the first two and represented the end of the series, seemingly for good.

But lo and behold 16 years later it is nice to report all is well with the Focker brand as it has now been passed on to writer/director John Hamburg who is intimately acquainted with what works and what doesn’t in the franchise since he co-wrote the first three films and now has a chance to take solo duties as writer and director, with Roach signing on to the producing team. What made it work initially is back in the forefront, the battle of wits now largely between Greg Focker (Stiller) and upcoming cast member Ariana Grande as the girlfriend and prospective bride of son Henry (Skyler Gisondo). Perfectly pitched as a holiday attraction, this edition reminds us how increasingly rare these big star studio comedies are at a time when the escapism and laughs they offer are needed more than ever. Watch on Deadline Related Stories Casting Louis Garrel And Harry Lawtey Join Jeremy Allen White In Ben Stiller-Directed 'Airman' From Laika Live-Action And A24 News 'Stick' Soundtrack: All The Songs You'll Hear In The Apple TV Golf Series.

The setup this time revolves around the 80th birthday celebration for Jack (De Niro), still going strong in his 8th decade and a bit of a fitness and vegan freak now. Henry decides to bring his new girlfriend Olivia (Grande) to meet the family and this very act causes predictable anxiety for Greg who now finds himself in the reverse position he once was in when he came to meet the parents of his now-wife of 20 years, Pam (Teri Polo). It gets even dicier as Olivia turns out to be a substantial hit with everyone, a former FBI hostage negotiator, smart businesswoman, and expert vegan chef to boot, Jack takes to her right away frustrating Greg by passing her instantly on his infamous lie detector test and welcoming her into his “circle of trust”. Greg has his suspicions, especially since he inadvertently and coincidentally had a run-in with her on the plane coming to Jack’s. His doubts increase and involve competitions in the kitchen and a bike race where Olivia one-ups him.

According to recent reports, the usual slapstick situations so familiar to Stiller are amusingly orchestrated here as Greg’s battle against Olivia take on latest importance when Henry aims to pop the question in front of everyone. Ultimately this leads to a hilarious confrontation with another nemesis, Jack’s new dog Lazarus, a German-fluent ex-police K9 with a penchant for violence. Lazarus has been wary himself of Greg from the minute he arrived and you just know this isn’t going to end well.

Also in the mix are franchise returnees Owen Wilson as Kevin Rawley, the man Pam left behind for Greg, matriarch Dina (an underused but still welcome Blythe Danner), and Greg and Pam’s daughter Samantha (Beanie Feldstein) who still lives at home along with boyfriend Eduardo (Eduardo Franco), the latter struggling for attention in this clan. But it is the heated rivalry between Greg and Olivia that takes center stage in this edition, and it is also Grande who really reveals the comedic chops she demonstrated in Wicked to great effect here as well. Grande is a natural comedienne and she nails this one.

Industry observers note that of course De Niro also has sharp comedic instincts and here amusingly plays off his advancing age with complete denial, as well as doubting his son-in-law’s ability to step up to the plate. Hamburg , who has also collaborated with Stiller on the Zoolander films as well as Along Came Polly, knows the comedic talents of Stiller as well as anyone and provides lots of opportunities for the star to do what he does best. Joining the Focker franchise for the first time is Gisondo (Superman, Primetime) as Henry charmingly navigates his way through this madness trying not to be embarrassed by his dad’s antics, while preparing to tell everyone that he also intends not to continue his studies in nearby Chicago, but to move to San Diego with soon-to-be finacee Olivia.

Industry observers note that the laughs go down easily, and the heart is still there as well. For Focker fans be assured this is a return to basics, and to what made it a crowd pleaser in the first place. Isn’t that all you can really ask for in this kind of commercial enterprise?

Producers are De Niro, Jane Rosenthal, Stiller, John Lesher, Roach, and Hamburg.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

iOS 27 gives the Messages app a variety of welcome upgrades, including one I’ve found myself using a lot: a Smart Reply feature that’s now personalized to the user’s writing style.

When the first wave of Apple Intelligence features were declared in 2024, one that I immediately thought sounded useful was Smart Reply.

It has been revealed that the idea behind Smart Reply is simple. Rather than needing to manually type out replies in Messages and Mail, your iPhone can offer prewritten replies you can choose and send with a couple taps.

Great in theory, but the ‘Smart’ part of Smart Reply struggled to materialize in iOS 18.

In a recent development, fortunately, with a key Apple Intelligence upgrade in iOS 27, the fresh version of the feature finally lives up to its name. Per Apple:.

Smart Reply in Mail and Messages can now draw on a user’s personalized writing style.

According to recent reports, before, Smart Reply would look at the context of a conversation to craft its suggestions. But now, it also aims to match your writing style, punctuation, and tone.

It has been revealed that in iOS 18, I almost never used Smart Reply. That’s because despite being fine at suggesting replies that technically worked, those suggestions didn’t sound like me at all.

That’s changed in iOS 27. Smart Reply now consistently impresses me. It no longer offers generic responses that sound like AI wrote them. Instead, its suggestions actually fit with my normal style of communication.

In a recent development, the only drawback is that right now, you’ll only ever see two Smart Reply suggestions. If Apple expanded the feature by letting you scroll horizontally through more options, I suspect I’d use Smart Reply even more.

It has been revealed that have you been using iOS 27’s Smart Reply feature in Messages? Let us know in the comments.

AI disclosure: I wrote all text here, but used Agent Duel (an open source battle system on top of OpenCode) to research sources of Lean proofs and generate charts.

According to recent reports, the recent proof of the Riemann hypothesis came with a statistic attached: the proof is 17 million lines of Lean. Beyond the philosophical questions of what it means to have a proof longer than any human could comprehend, I’m left with a simpler question: is that as large as it sounds?

To investigate, I hunted for collections of Lean proofs online. I found two and charted the lengths of their proofs.

(All charts have a log x axis, which makes 17m lines look a lot closer to 1m and 100k than it really is.).

Mathlib maintains a collection of famous proofs. There are over 1k but only 259 have Lean associated, which I chart here.

These are all human generated, and as we can see, they come nowhere close to 17m.

In a recent development, reservoir indexes every published Lean package, 938 of which have Lean code on GitHub. This one has a lot more data, including AI assisted proofs. We even have a few that are over 16m!:.

88m: Qiuzhen-CFSG/CFSG this appears to be an AI built proof that is still a work in progress.

Recent findings suggest that 36m: CBirkbeck/LeanBridge, a project linking the LMFDB database of number theory objects to Mathlib. This isn’t really a proof: about 98% of its Lean is files generated by scripts that check the database’s numbers one by one. The hand-written part is closer to 500k lines.

Industry observers note that 27m: anthropics/fermats-last-theorem is another Anthropic special: a complete proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem, published on GitHub in September. Its README says “the Lean sources were produced by AI agents building on human-written open-source Lean”, including the human FLT project led by Kevin Buzzard, which is about 60k lines and still in progress. The AI version is roughly 450 times longer.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar highlights how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.In the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session shows how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. It also shows how automation enables fast measurement of features down to the sub-nanometer scale with minimal operator handling.What You Will Learn:How surface scan metrology in station monitors tracks tool health and supports the qualification of thin film deposition processesHow baseline signatures and real-time monitoring detect particle generation, hardware degradation, and process drift before production is affectedHow in-line scans on patterned wafers reveal layer-level defects and show how they propagate through multi-layer device structuresWhen offline 3D optical profilometry should follow in-line inspection, and how it measures dimensions and separates sample defects from foreign materialHow correlating tool health data, inspection results, and electrical performance links physical defects to yield loss and guides targeted improvement projectsRegister now for this free webinar!

HomeKit Weekly: Lafaer’s 5-in-1 presence sensor fixes an annoying automation in Apple Home

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (704 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that motion-based automations are generally straightforward in Apple Home.
  • HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.
  • A standard motion sensor uses PIR, which only detects movement, and that works fine in many situations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that motion-based automations are generally straightforward in Apple Home. The only carve-out is lighting, because some rooms are hard to judge by time of day alone. Depending on the windows and placement against the sun, some rooms might need light-based automations earlier in the day than others. The Lafaer 5-in-1 presence sensor fixes that with a light sensor most motion sensors lack, along with mmWave radar.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

A standard motion sensor uses PIR, which only detects movement, and that works fine in many situations. If you’re still for long periods, you’re invisible, and the automation assumes the room is empty. The Lafaer LWR02 pairs PIR with 2.4 GHz mmWave radar. The PIR-based motion sees you walking in, and the radar sees the minor stuff, like breathing and shifting on the couch, so the room stays “occupied” for as long as you are in it. The two together also reduce false positives from ceiling fans, curtains, and the dog, because the radar and PIR both must agree before the sensor reports motion.

In Apple Home, that shows up as an occupancy sensor and a motion sensor from the same device.

“Turn on the lights when someone enters” is a common automation I use, but it can be tricky. What if you only want it when it’s not light outside? Doing it based on time of day sometimes works, but what about depending on where the windows are facing, etc.? You might have a room that gets darker an hour earlier than another room. “Turn on the lights when someone enters, and it’s dark in the room” is what the light sensor can handle for you.

In the Home app, that means triggering a sensor for occupancy, then converting the automation into a Shortcut and adding a condition for the light level. It’s a few extra steps, but it does really give you more fine control over how it works.

Presence, motion, light, temperature, and humidity all come from the same device, and each one appears in Apple Home as its own sensor, so you can build automations around whichever ones fit the room.

It’s IPX3-rated, so bathrooms, kitchens, and laundry rooms are fine to use in. Coverage is about 13 feet for presence and 26 for motion across about 120 degrees, which works in a bedroom, office, or bathroom. It’s not going to cover a great room from one corner. The base is a magnetic half sphere, so you can aim it, and it mounts with adhesive or sits on a shelf. I generally like to use the shelf for these types of sensors.

The Lafaer LWR02 is Matter over Thread, so it pairs directly with a HomePod, HomePod mini, or Apple TV 4K with no Lafaer hub or account needed. It runs on two included AAA batteries, is rated for up to two years, and rechargeable AAAs work with it as well. Thread is why a sensor doing this much can last that long on batteries. All sensor data is processed locally, so it only uses a trickle on the batteries.

Lights that turn off while you’re sitting still in the room are the reason a lot of people stop using motion automations in smart homes. The Lafaer LWR02 fixes that with mmWave radar and then lets you have more granular control of light-based automations based on what’s actually in the environment in the room, not just the time of day.

The Lafaer 5-in-1 presence sensor is available on Amazon.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that we have AI at home!
  • With the launch of open-weight models like Qwen, cloud-based LLM providers seem like they're more of infrastructure or appliance businesses when it comes to most routine tasks that an AI model can handle.
  • Industry observers note that openAI and Anthropic have displayed a pattern of dropping model quality in the 'latest' version and controlling exactly what you're allowed to run on their models.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that we have AI at home! Set up your own free personal ChatGPT on your PC with Unsloth and Inkling or Qwen. It's private, and the whole house can use it.

With the launch of open-weight models like Qwen, cloud-based LLM providers seem like they're more of infrastructure or appliance businesses when it comes to most routine tasks that an AI model can handle.

Industry observers note that openAI and Anthropic have displayed a pattern of dropping model quality in the 'latest' version and controlling exactly what you're allowed to run on their models. Add to this ballooning costs and privacy concerns, and we get a pretty good case for moving away from this 'convenient' cloud experience.

In a recent development, that's basically where I was too. I wanted to offload certain token-heavy research, data collection, or coding tasks to an AI model without staring at usage limits all day. So, as any reasonable human being would do, I decided to set up my own local AI: a Claude and ChatGPT replacement that runs at home on my own hardware.

Since this was my first attempt, my primary focus was keeping it simple and hosting it on Windows. If you're a beginner, you can follow along to get one going on your home network too.

Once you have the hardware sorted, it takes about 10-15 minutes (excluding download times).

Install Unsloth Desktop, download a quantized AI model that fits your GPU's VRAM, set your context size, and turn on LAN access so everyone at home can use it.

Not much (other than the hardware). Here's a short list:.

That's it. No terminal commands, Python environments, or subscriptions required.

Recent findings suggest that it depends on how much VRAM your graphics card has. As a rough guide, 8-12GB of VRAM handles smaller 9B-12B models, while 32GB comfortably runs 27B-35B models with plenty of room for long conversations.

In a recent development, on consumer-grade hardware, we'll need smaller models. The full-size Qwen model sits at around 56GB and won't really fit on a consumer graphics card unless you're running a Mac with unified memory. That's where quantization comes in.

It has been revealed that quantization shrinks a model by compressing weights and moving to a lower precision. You basically trade some accuracy for a model that actually fits on your GPU and runs faster.

The same photo stored at 8, 4 and 2 bits per pixel. A model's weights lose detail the same way going from Q8 to Q4 to Q2.

Sources indicate that if you're wondering whether this tradeoff is worth it, well, it depends. You'll find that certain types of workloads don't really care and give similar outputs, while others may be nearly unusable.

For this guide, we'll be going with Qwen3.8-27B with 4-bit quantization on my system with an RTX 5090. Going up a tier is an option thanks to its 32GB of VRAM, but I wanted to allow for a larger context window (how much of the conversation the model can keep in mind at once) rather than cramming in the largest model that fits.

According to recent reports, qwen3.8-27B at each precision with a 128K context, from our VRAM calculator. At 4-bit, the model and the context fit a 32 GB card with room to spare.

If you want to run a model of this caliber with excellent performance, a hilariously overpriced RTX 5090 (remember when $1,999 felt too high?) is unfortunately still not a terrible 'deal' these days. The other option is way more expensive enterprise-grade GPUs.

Sources indicate that if you're on a GPU with less VRAM, you can still get something very usable going right away. The table below gives you a rough idea of where you can start.

RTX 5060 8GB, RTX 3060 12GB, RTX 5070 12GB.

Qwen3-14B, gpt-oss-20b (MoE), Gemma 4 26B (MoE), Qwen3-Coder-30B (MoE), Qwen3.6-35B (MoE), Inkling 2 Mini (MoE).

RTX 5060 Ti 16GB, RTX 5070 Ti, RTX 5080, RTX PRO 2000.

Gemma 4 31B, Qwen3.8-27B, Inkling 2 Mini.

RTX 3090, RTX 4090, RX 7900 XTX, RTX PRO 4000.

RTX 5090 32GB, RTX PRO 4500 32GB, RTX PRO 5000 48GB, RTX PRO 6000 96GB.

RTX 5060 8GB, RTX 3060 12GB, RTX 5070 12GB.

Qwen3-14B, gpt-oss-20b (MoE), Gemma 4 26B (MoE), Qwen3-Coder-30B (MoE), Qwen3.6-35B (MoE), Inkling 2 Mini (MoE).

RTX 5060 Ti 16GB, RTX 5070 Ti, RTX 5080, RTX PRO 2000.

Gemma 4 31B, Qwen3.8-27B, Inkling 2 Mini.

RTX 3090, RTX 4090, RX 7900 XTX, RTX PRO 4000.

RTX 5090 32GB, RTX PRO 4500 32GB, RTX PRO 5000 48GB, RTX PRO 6000 96GB.

In a recent development, models marked MoE (mixture of experts) only run a few billion of their parameters for each token. They keep a decent speed on a smaller card with the rest held in system RAM, which is why a 35B model sits in the 16 GB row. On an RTX 5060 Ti 16GB, our calculator puts Qwen3.6-35B at about 47 tokens per second this way.

In a recent development, feel free to experiment with several models until you find one that fits your needs. You can also use GPUPartner's VRAM Calculator to get an estimate.

Industry observers note that inkling 2 Mini, yes. Inkling 2 Small, no.

Inkling 2 Mini is the newest model in this size class. Thinking Machines Lab released it on November 17, 2026: 26.4B parameters, Apache 2.0, vision support and a 1M-token context. Unsloth's recommended file, UD-Q4_K_XL, is 17.6 GB. That is within 0.1 GB of the Qwen3.8-27B file in this guide, so it sits on a 32GB card the same way and leaves about 14GB for context.

Sources indicate that nothing else in this guide changes. Update Unsloth Desktop first, because Inkling 2 needs a recent build, then search for Inkling 2 Mini in the same drop-down in Step 2.

Those figures are Unsloth's. They count RAM and VRAM together and cover the model alone, so a long context needs more. Inkling 2 Mini is a mixture-of-experts model with 5.4B parameters active, so the 4-bit file also runs on a 16 GB card with the remainder in system RAM, a little slower.

According to recent reports, inkling 2 Small is small in name only. It is a 594B model, and the smallest file Unsloth publishes is 171.7 GB. That is unified-memory territory: a 256GB Mac Studio or a DGX Station, not a graphics card.

In a recent development, yes. You'll find good alternatives in Apple's Mac lineup thanks to its unified memory. Macs are pretty good at running larger models, even if they don't offer the best performance. Just make sure you grab the MLX flavor that is custom-built for Apple Silicon.

The same trade applies to unified-memory PCs like the MSI PRO MAX EDGE AI+ 11M and NVIDIA's DGX Spark.

It takes three steps: install Unsloth Desktop, download your model, and set the context size. I'll go over these steps in more detail below so you can follow along.

Sources indicate that first, we'll need a solution that 'serves' the AI model to you. My pursuit of simplicity narrowed my choices down to LM Studio or Unsloth Desktop. Both abstract away a ton of terminal commands and handle Python environments and dependencies behind a nice, simple UI, which makes them excellent picks for a first home setup.

I landed on Unsloth Desktop mostly because, well, I liked the name better. Also, it didn't try to push the very thing I was trying to escape when I opened its website: a subscription.

The community seems to like it overall too, so that's another point in its favor.

Once you've clicked through the installer and launched Unsloth, you'll see a window like this one.

Unsloth Desktop on first launch, before any model is loaded.

On the top left of this main window, you can pick the model that you want to use from the drop down. We'll be using Qwen3.8-27B.

Industry observers note that the model picker. Qwen3.8-27B is first on the Recommended list.

Recent findings suggest that you should see a submenu like the one below when you click on a model. I'll be using Unsloth's UD-Q4_K_XL version. The M and S versions are smaller, but the XL version behaves much closer to the full-size model without filling up our VRAM, so it seemed like a good pick for my GPU.

In a recent development, every quantization of Qwen3.8-27B with its download size. The gear next to the downloaded one holds the context setting.

It has been revealed that once the download completes, you should see a gear icon to the right of the model as shown in the screenshot above. Here, you can set your context size manually or leave it on Auto if you aren't sure how much you need.

It has been revealed that I'll be setting mine to 128K (unquantized) and might reassess after I've run the model through a few of my routine tasks for a few weeks. Again, you can use this VRAM calculator to help you with these numbers for your specific GPU.

At this point, our first local AI is up and running, and you can start chatting with it right inside Unsloth.

Remember, your mileage may vary depending on your setup.

Recent findings suggest that short answer: Unsloth Desktop has LAN sharing built in. Set a Remote password, start LAN access, and share the address it gives you with anyone on your home network.

Sources indicate that once Unsloth Desktop is set up with a model, you might want to give family members or friends access too. For now, we'll only serve it over our local network, so my family can use it without needing physical access to this PC.

Head into Unsloth Desktop settings (gear icon on bottom left), and look for the 'Remote & LAN' tab.

Recent findings suggest that settings, Remote & LAN. LAN access is the second card. The Remote access card above it is for a later part.

Most of this section will be greyed out until you set a Remote password. Once you've set a password, you'll see a 'Start' button for LAN access. Click that and you should see an address that anyone on your home network can open in a browser to use a local AI model within a chat interface. They'll sign in as 'unsloth' with the Remote password you set.

Just keep in mind that the PC needs to stay on with Unsloth running for anyone to reach it.

According to recent reports, not with this setup alone. Everything so far is limited to your local home network.

Industry observers note that if you just need a chat interface like ChatGPT, Gemini, etc. to work within your home network, you're basically done at this point! You and anyone on your network can start talking to an AI model hosted on your machine right away.

Sources indicate that in the next parts, we'll cover performance, tunneling, as well as setting up an agent that runs locally and uses only the web tools you allow it to use. This will let you automate more complex tasks like coding, research, and so much more without being tied to a subscription or usage limits and censorship.

As always, my focus remains simplicity that allows my family to use it without too much guidance or help.

As Deadline reported at the time of Hurst’s exit, God of War, from Sony Pictures Television and Amazon MGM Studios, is starting from scratch with no footage from the original shoot being used. Based on PlayStation’s hugely popular ancient mythology-themed video game, God of War follows father and son Kratos (Bautista) and Atreus (Callum Vinson) as they embark on a journey to spread the ashes of their wife and mother, Faye (Woll). Along their journey, Kratos and Atreus discover secrets about Faye that make them wonder how well they truly knew her at all.

Woll portrays the character of Faye in the 2022 PlayStation video game God of War Ragnarök and as the lead character in the upcoming God of War Laufey (2027).

In addition to Bautista as Kratos and Vinson as Atreus, on the God of War TV series Woll joins Mandy Patinkin, who plays Odin, Ed Skrein as Baldur, Max Parker as Heimdall, Ólafur Darri Ólafsson as Thor, Teresa Palmer as Sif, Alastair Duncan as Mimir, Jeff Gulka as Sindri, Danny Woodburn as Brok, Sonya Walger as Freya, Island Austin as Thrud, Ben Chapple as Magni, Louis Cunningham as Modi, and Evelyn Miller as Gna.
