  • Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar.
  • At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.
  • It has been revealed that I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar.

At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.

It has been revealed that I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell, the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die.

It has been revealed that the patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies, the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke.

It has been revealed that “We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell says. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded Remedy Robotics, based in San Francisco. With a team of engineers, he developed this robotic catheter and its related software to help ischemic stroke patients in remote and rural places, who lose crucial hours while being transferred away from hospitals incapable of providing care. According to 2025 data, at least 5 million people around the world suffer ischemic strokes every year. In the United States, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death.

When Remedy Robotics cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell initially met, they matched each other’s energy right away.Christie Hemm Klok.

Sources indicate that the screen highlights my catheter at a fork in the narrowing road, and I decide to take a sharp right; I think I can make it. This device feels easier to drive than a typical robotic instrument that I controlled on a hospital tour the summer prior. I say to Bell that here my movements are smoother, more precise—exactly the talking point you’d expect to hear from a surgical robotics company. Never mind that, Bell corrects me: “Smoothness and precision are not clinical outcomes. Neither is a surgeon’s ergonomics.”.

For Bell, the outcome that matters is whether the robot can get stroke treatment to patients who otherwise wouldn’t receive it in time. Today, only about 1 in 10 patients eligible for thrombectomy receive one. That’s where the long-unrealized promise of telesurgery is meeting an urgent problem: providing access to thrombectomies before life-threatening damage takes hold.

But can putting a robot in one hospital and a surgeon somewhere else actually close that gap? Remedy has already taken a first step, remotely testing its system on a small group of patients. “The remote stroke need is well known,” says Jake Sganga, who cofounded Remedy with Bell and leads the technology side. “It’s just a hard problem to take on.” Making telesurgery a practical part of stroke care will require more than a capable robot: It will depend on communications infrastructure, hospital resources and workflows, and ultimately, evidence that patients actually benefit.

As recently as the early ’90s, physicians who treated stroke struggled with “therapeutic nihilism.” A 1991 editorial by two lamenting neurologists expressed hope that a successful drug therapy for stroke would emerge that would “reverse the trend of nihilism.” Five years later, clot-busting drugs revolutionized stroke treatment, followed about a decade later by mechanical thrombectomy, in which a blood clot is physically removed from an artery.

In a standard thrombectomy a surgeon snakes a flexible wire through a small opening in the patient’s groin. This guide wire sets the route for a fine hollow tube around it, the catheter, to travel through the blood vessels to the brain, where instruments remove the clot. Suddenly a stroke was no longer a sentence of profound disability or death but a treatable event.

Recent findings suggest that yet decades later, thrombectomies remain inherently blind expeditions. The surgeon stands beside the patient, physically pushing these lines up, inch by inch. The only view comes from a live X-ray, which can’t see soft tissues like blood vessels. The surgeon shoots brief puffs of contrast dye through the catheter to illuminate the path ahead. A nimble operator can avoid scraping or piercing artery walls while bending the guide wire’s rounded tip around corners. But even these left or right turns are not intuitive. The guide wire can twist inside the body, and because the surgeon sees only a flat silhouette, steering it left may actually rotate the guidewire to the right.

The N1 robot feeds the catheter along a rail lined with seven modules, using a thin wire that allows precise control through a patient’s vascular system, even from kilometers away. Christie Hemm Klok.

If all goes as planned, the doctor reaches the brain and pushes instruments through the catheter to dislodge the clot, then carefully pulls everything back out. Bell remembers how thrombectomies felt when he performed them. “I’m one and a half meters away from my catheter tip. I’m not in control of it. I can’t see where the blood vessels are. I thought, what is the ideal way to do these procedures? It’s certainly not what I’m doing now.”.

Sganga and Bell want their robots to do two things: see what surgeons can’t see and be where surgeons can’t be. When I visited Remedy’s office in January, the team indicated me their robotic arm and instruments that snap onto it. Motorized cartridges live on the robotic arm, one containing several actuators that use small gears to grip the threadlike instruments to move them in and out of a body. The instruments include a stent, an expandable wire-mesh tube used to pierce, grab, and yank a clot back out. It’s all typical stroke operation equipment—except for the catheter.

Remedy’s catheter is steerable, so it doesn’t need a guide wire to pave its path. Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream. As I maneuver the catheter with the Xbox controller, Bell and Sganga tell me they made wayfinding a priority. Sganga toggles on a CT scan to overlay on the X-ray feed. Suddenly I see the bright three-dimensional routes of blood vessels along a path that had been invisible on X-ray.

In a recent development, I noticed a pattern of small markings on the catheter. Sganga tells me they’re not for the surgeon, but for a computer-vision algorithm that tracks the catheter’s rotation inside the body. If an operator wants to steer right, Remedy’s software automatically translates that intention into the correct action. Instead of squinting at a 2D silhouette on an X-ray and mentally compensating for every twist in the catheter, the surgeon simply toggles to the right on the X-ray image, the Remedy system adjusts, and the catheter moves in the correct direction.

Recent findings suggest that this system grew out of ideas that Bell and Sganga were pursuing when they met at Stanford in 2019. Already a physician, Bell was completing an MBA and enrolled in a robotics class in hopes of meeting an engineer who might share his interest in creating a medical robot. The professor connected him to Sganga, a bioengineering doctoral student who was developing pathfinding algorithms for an FDA-approved robotic bronchoscope to navigate the lungs.

Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream.

Recent findings suggest that sganga’s engineering work had exposed him to surgical robotics companies that failed because they hadn’t chosen a valuable enough problem to solve. He sought a medical problem where a robot could prove its worth well before human trials, and stroke stood out. “It’s an already verified clinical need,” Sganga says, “Time.” When he and Bell met for coffee, they matched each other’s energy right away: “It was like ‘Hey how you doing?’ and then we were looking at medical images of blood vessels together off of his phone,” Sganga says.

Sources indicate that about a year after they both left Stanford, Bell and Sganga rented a two-car garage in Southern California and X-ray-proofed it with lead lining. “We called it the bunker because it had exposed lead on all sides, including the ceiling,” Sganga claims. “It was just big enough to fit a bed and this rickety old C-arm [X-ray].” There they test-drove a prototype of their steerable catheter through silicone arteries—first controlling the robot on-site from another room, and then from a laptop hundreds of kilometers away. “We were trying to get an initial sign of life,” Sganga says. “And it was that moment that we realized that this could work.”.

Dreams of remote surgery predate modern stroke care. In the 1980s and 1990s, the companies Computer Motion and Intuitive developed bedside robots to assist surgeons. Then, in 2001, French surgeon Jacques Marescaux and Canadian surgeon Michel Gagner removed a patient’s gallbladder from more than 6,000 km away. In New York City, Marescaux used a computer connected via high-speed fiber optics to control a Computer Motion robot in Strasbourg, France. The milestone, known as the Lindbergh Operation, was completed safely with no complications.

In a recent development, but telesurgery did not take off after Lindbergh. Instead, companies invested in robots operated by surgeons in the same room. Computer Motion and Intuitive merged in 2003, more companies sprang up, and robotic surgery steadily entered the mainstream. Today thousands of surgical robots operate in hospitals around the country, assisting in roughly 22 percent of surgeries. In 2023 alone, more than 2 million surgeries were performed with da Vinci, Intuitive’s flagship platform.

Recent findings suggest that remedy mechanical engineer Chris Hapstack [left] and software engineer Campbell Crowley adjust the N1 robot. Christie Hemm Klok.

In the summer of 2025, telesurgery appeared to regain momentum when surgeons near Orlando, Fla., removed the prostate from a man 11,000 km away in Luanda, Angola. Around the same time, Intuitive demonstrated what it called “telecollaboration,” in which two surgeons on different continents operated together on a tissue model. Meanwhile, India-based SS Innovations has been testing cardiac telesurgery; in Panama, the Texas-based medical robotics company XCath has tested a steerable guide wire for thrombectomies. These companies are building on advances in computer vision and machine learning, yet remote robotics is hardly a sure bet.

It has been revealed that “The first procedures are going to be those procedures where time is critical,” indicates Brad Nelson, who develops surgical robots at ETH Zurich and is not affiliated with Remedy. Last year, Nelson coauthored a report in Science Robotics arguing that telesurgery’s future success hinges on finding emergency operations where patients can’t always reach specialists in time, including stroke, heart attack, and fetal operations.

Sources indicate that surgeries that occur within blood vessels seem an attractive proving ground for teleoperation in emergencies. “If you have a hiccup, the nice thing about vascular procedures is nothing bad can happen other than the thing stops moving,” Nelson states. There’s neither a large open cavity to tend to, nor the urgent choreography one might need in organ transplants. If the surgeon loses connection to the robot while the catheter is inside a blood vessel, the operation can pause in place without damage.

It has been revealed that nelson’s lab is also working on a stroke solution. He has partnered with the Mayo Clinic in Arizona to build microscopic robots—the size of a coffee grain—steered with magnets to dissolve a clot.

After preliminary success in the garage, Sganga and Bell turned their focus to the environment where the Remedy N1 would live. Doctors and nurses advised them to improve the live audio-video feed, as any surgery is a coordinated team effort requiring constant communication. They were told to improve setup time, maintenance, cleaning, and began a series of conversations about secure communication and cybersecurity.

In a recent development, in 2021, CEO David Bell naps next to Remedy’s first X-ray machine in a lead-lined garage in Venice, Calif. Remedy Robotics.

Recent findings suggest that absent a cyberattack, the elephant in the room for any telesurgery hopeful is latency. Experts speak about latency, or lag, in terms of how many thousandths of a second it takes for a small packet of data to reach a destination then ping back to its original source. In a major city with strong 5G or fiber-optic internet, latency might measure in the tens of milliseconds. In rural areas, even in the United States, lag can drag above 100.

Recent findings suggest that noticeable lag may not be a dealbreaker. When researchers in Japan analyzed five years of surgical simulations and demonstrations, they reported surgeons adapting to the connection speed. They paused. They moved more slowly. Remedy has noticed similar behavior in test runs. “We’ve actually found that operators are quite resilient to latency,” Sganga notes.

It has been revealed that still, Remedy targets a round-trip latency of no more than 150 milliseconds, below the average human reaction time of 200 milliseconds. Whenever latency sneaks above that threshold, the system pauses all surgical action. Bell and Sganga say they’ve tailored their system to work with the slower internet speeds common in rural areas that would benefit from better access to stroke care, claiming they recently operated their system from across the Pacific using a mobile hotspot.

But sorting out the engineering details raises more questions about how telesurgery might change surgical practice. Bell told me he worries about what a telesurgical future could bring. What if surgeons’ skills erode? What if trainees become dependent on specific platforms? What if two patients need care from the same remote surgeon at the same time? “Is the person suffering a stroke in America necessarily more important than the person suffering a stroke in India? No,” Bell says. “So how do you figure that out? That’s something I think about a lot.”.

During a stroke, a blockage in the brain triggers symptoms within seconds or minutes. The following hour is the so-called golden period for saving the brain before the risk of permanent damage grows. “Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die,” indicates neurologist Archit Bhatt of Providence Medical Group in Portland, Oregon. “You really need to act fast.” Yet decades after the advent of thrombectomies, one in five Americans lives more than an hour from a hospital that offers the procedure.

Recent findings suggest that medium and small hospitals often lack the 24-hour surgical team, experience, or equipment for thrombectomies, so they must transfer stroke patients to large hospitals. As a result, standard stroke care is concentrated in urban areas. For example, Alaska’s only two thrombectomy centers serving the 739,000 people who live or work in the state are both in Anchorage, leaving more than half of residents out of range.

Industry observers note that but the places most in need of telesurgery may also be the hardest places to deploy it. For starters, they may not have the high-quality network connections that remote surgery requires. Last June, experts from five major robotic corporations coauthored a list of technical standards for what they called “surgical-grade networks.” Mike Teodorescu, an information systems researcher with the University of Washington, says experts usually consider 100 milliseconds a safe threshold, but his team recently reported that many rural communities—and even most countries—struggle to meet it.

Neuroradiologist Hal Rice of the Australian Stroke Alliance remotely operates Remedy’s N1 System.Remedy Robotics.

And connectivity is only part of the problem. The smallest and most remote hospitals may lack other support needed for thrombectomy, including neurologists, catheterization teams, CT scanners, and specialized intensive care units. “It’s an infrastructure problem,” Teodorescu says.

It has been revealed that medium-size regional hospitals may be a better target. Although they rarely offer thrombectomies, many already have the right support, experience, and patient volume. “There is a window for a thrombectomy center in a reasonably sized town where there is a stable economy,” says neurologist Bhatt.

“Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die.”–neurologist Archit Bhatt.

Sources indicate that telesurgery could do more than bring a distant specialist into the operating room. Jasdeep Bahra, an emergency medicine physician and lecturer in Kilifi, Kenya, worries that telerobotics could concentrate expertise in cities—widening the skill gap between rich cities and poor towns. The thrombectomy access problem is real, Bahra says, but lower income communities might benefit more if a system like Remedy’s could both treat patients and help train clinicians on-site. Sganga says Bahra’s idea fits Remedy’s mission.

In a recent development, “Digital operating rooms where you have surgeons that are over your shoulder as a mentor,” Bahra claims. “If that’s what we’re talking about in telesurgery, that is the future for me.”.

If smoothness and precision aren’t clinical outcomes, as Bell told me, what would count as success? One target is safety. In more than 1 percent of thrombectomy operations, surgeons unintentionally slice open a blood vessel, a feared and sometimes fatal occurrence that Bell believes robots can prevent.

According to recent reports, in September 2025, Bell flew to Toronto for Remedy’s first test in human patients. Ten patients had consented to nonemergency procedures with Remedy’s robot. A neurosurgeon with a laptop would operate on six patients in an adjoining room; two elsewhere in the hospital; and two at an entirely different hospital across town. The Remedy team had experimented for years on silicone models, like the one I test-drove. Tests on lab animals suggested that, compared with a human, their robot collided less often with blood vessels and finished procedures faster.

According to recent reports, neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira pilots the N1 system in 2024 for its first in-person robotic procedure, in Toronto. Remedy Robotics.

Recent findings suggest that in the run-up to the Toronto procedures, the team measured internet latencies meticulously. Now they could only hope that their results would translate to human patients. “You’re never sure of how that leap is going to look, and it’s actually really hard to test,” Bell says. The night before the first operation, Bell barely slept.

Industry observers note that the procedures—recording images called angiograms from within patients’ blood vessels—were a success, and were completed nearly twice as quickly as the current standard. “I cannot explain the relief,” Bell notes. Remedy considers speed one measure of success because it can allow doctors to treat more people.

In 2025, neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira and his team at Unity Health Toronto perform the first fully remote robotic neurointerventional procedures. Remedy Robotics.

A few months after my visit, Remedy revealed US $62 million in latest funding to support upcoming clinical trials. A portion of that investment came from the University of California system, which will host the clinical studies within a year, according to Bell. Remedy’s first trials will be on-site elective procedures, such as treating unruptured aneurysms, before expanding to remote surgeries in Australia or within the University of California system, near the end of 2027.

Sganga emphasizes that the on-site trials are not just a stepping stone. He’s come to believe that Remedy’s success depends on improving operations even when the surgeon is in the room. “The remote solution—it’s very flashy, it’s very obvious what that patient need is—but in order to get there, we believe you have to solve a meaningful problem on-premise,” he says. “Otherwise, doctors simply won’t use the system, and if they don’t use the system, they’re not going to gain the expertise required to operate remotely.”.

The steerable catheter and computer-vision algorithm are two features he claims will improve thrombectomies, remote or not. And as trials ramp up, Sganga says they will look at factors beyond safety and surgical speed. “How promptly are doctors picking up on this fresh technique? How smoothly are the bedside interactions going? How quickly are folks able to set up the draping and interact with the tools?” he says. Bell has wondered whether to add a photo or video of the patient’s face to the surgeon’s display to preserve the emotional stakes of surgery.

Recent findings suggest that these ambitions draw Bell and Sganga’s 25-person organization into uncharted waters. Beyond one-time demonstrations, no robotics company has earned full regulatory approval for telesurgery, and no patient has been operated on remotely in the United States. Remedy hopes to change that. Decades after stroke research conquered the “therapeutic nihilism” that once defined the field, Remedy hopes telesurgery can bring thrombectomy to everyone who needs it, no matter where they might be.

AirPods 5 vs AirPods Pro 3: Which should you buy this holiday season?

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the holiday shopping season is here, and Apple’s AirPods are sure to be one of the most popular gifts.
  • AirPods 5 were introduced in September and come in two different versions.
  • According to recent reports, the case for the higher-end AirPods 5 ($149) supports wireless charging and Find My.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the holiday shopping season is here, and Apple’s AirPods are sure to be one of the most popular gifts. If you’re shopping for AirPods, Apple sells three different models: AirPods 5, AirPods Pro 3, and AirPods Max 2. Here’s how they compare.

AirPods 5 were introduced in September and come in two different versions. Unlike their predecessors, both versions of AirPods 5 offer Active Noise Cancellation. They differ in the charging case, battery life, and volume control. The base model AirPods 5 ($129) come with a case that can only charge via USB-C.

According to recent reports, the case for the higher-end AirPods 5 ($149) supports wireless charging and Find My. You also get one extra hour of battery life. The higher-end model also adds on-stem volume control, so you can adjust the volume just by swiping up or down on one of the earbud stems.

Here’s a full comparison between both AirPods 5 models:.

In a recent development, the key thing about AirPods 5 is their open-ear design, unlike the in-ear design of the AirPods Pro 3 (more on those later). Even with that open-ear design, AirPods 5 offer incredible Active Noise Cancellation capabilities.

If you are shopping for AirPods 5, I do recommend spending the extra $20 to get the higher-end model. The better charging case alone is worth the extra money. With Find My integration and a built-in speaker, you can track your AirPods and play a sound from the case if you lose them.

If the person you’re shopping for doesn’t like in-ear earbuds, AirPods 5 are an excellent choice.

For most people, though, AirPods Pro 3 are probably the better choice ….

AirPods Pro 3 are Apple’s most capable earbuds, even with the introduction of AirPods 5 this year. They offer an in-ear fit and come with five foam-infused silicone ear tip sizes. With that in-ear design, AirPods Pro 3 can offer up to 3x stronger noise cancellation than AirPods 5. In my testing, this difference is notable.

AirPods Pro 3 also offer several other features you won’t find on AirPods 5, including a heart rate sensor for workouts, plus Hearing Test, Hearing Aid, and Hearing Protection features.

I still think AirPods Pro 3 are one of the best products in Apple’s lineup today. I wear mine for multiple hours every single day and can’t imagine life without them. I love the in-ear fit, and the ANC still impresses me, whether I’m at home or somewhere like a coffee shop.

Industry observers note that if you know the person you’re shopping for (whether it’s yourself or someone else) likes the in-ear earbud design, I think AirPods Pro 3 are the best option. This is especially true when AirPods Pro 3 are on sale, like they are right now at $149. The price difference between AirPods 5 and AirPods Pro 3 is very small, and you’re getting a much better product.

Finally, we have AirPods Max. These are Apple’s only option for people who want AirPods in an over-ear headphone form factor. Last year, they were pretty hard to recommend since they’d gone five years without a real upgrade.

This year, however, Apple officially introduced AirPods Max 2, bringing modern features to Apple’s high-end headphones. This includes features like Adaptive Audio, Conversation Awareness, Personalized Volume, and more.

In a recent development, airPods Max 2 are a far more compelling option than AirPods Max were at this time last year. They’re still pricey, but I love the aesthetics and find them very comfortable. There’s something about the premium aluminum design with an elegant Digital Crown that really stands out.

In a recent development, if you’re looking to splurge this holiday season, AirPods Max 2 are a great choice. For more realistic budgets, I think AirPods Pro 3 are the best option.

Are you planning to buy anyone AirPods this holiday season? Are they on your wishlist? Let us know down in the comments.

Breaking: Building a wireless network adapter for the Super Nintendo

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1765 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Boland

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Building a wireless network adapter for the Super Nintendo.
  • I always come back to the Super Nintendo (SNES).
  • I dropped out of my final years of high school to study hands-on electronics at college, and continued on to university.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Building a wireless network adapter for the Super Nintendo.

By Danny Boland · November 2026 · Source.

I always come back to the Super Nintendo (SNES). It was my first console and it’s still my most potent source of nostalgia. It inspired my early interest in electronics as a teenager, designing circuits for mods and flash carts that I hoped to build one day. I followed the launch of Hackaday, Adafruit, and the progress of bunnie Huang’s Chumby and knew exactly what I wanted to do.

I dropped out of my final years of high school to study hands-on electronics at college, and continued on to university. Then, finally equipped with those skills I’d aspired to, I went off-track and spent the next fifteen years working in data, ML and software. A lot has changed in that time but I’m back now, picking up exactly where I left off.

The Super Network Adapter is an exercise in ‘16-bit futurism’, it aims to be a faithful peripheral to the original SNES hardware and what we imagined the future might be back then: a wireless link to the net, sync’ing saves across devices and an uplink to AI.

In a recent development, the SNES never had a dedicated network port. The closest it came was the Satellaview, a modem peripheral connected to a hidden expansion port that could receive game broadcasts via satellite. There was also the XBAND, a modem that plugged into the cartridge slot and supported pass-through patching of specific games for online play. Reproducing the hardware of either of these today would be challenging, however most peripherals for the SNES took a much simpler route, they used one of the controller ports.

Sources indicate that the SNES controller ports are small synchronous serial buses that a game can control, setting and reading individual lines and driving the clock. These ports have seven lines but in a typical controller cable, only five tend to be present, with the wires for D1 and IOBit left out. To make sourcing parts for this project easier, my design also only relies on the remaining five wires.

According to recent reports, first I needed a protocol for talking over this serial link, which I iterated with Mesen and a virtual network adapter written in Lua simulating the controller port link. This protocol has the SNES writing to the Latch line and reading from the adapter on D0, one bit at a time (‘bit-banging’). Even with some optimisation (unrolling loops and ignoring mid-stream replies) this approach tops out at about 30 KB/s, but that’s enough for the ’90s.

The first physical prototype was built using a Pico 2 W dev board. The additional circuitry needed was very simple, just some pull-up resistors for CLK and Latch. The board’s RP2350A can handle the console’s 5v logic on its pins directly, and it has two cores: one can maintain the console link, while the other maintains the Wi-Fi network link, without juggling interrupts.

The prototype runs from USB, with the console’s 5v only feeding the pull-ups. I did not connect the SNES 5v to the Pico’s VBUS or VSYS while USB is plugged in. The Pico was powered on before the console so the RP2350’s pins were ready to handle 5v. The PCB design later can run on either supply.

It has been revealed that adding Cloud Save or ‘Save Sync’ seemed the most practical use for a Wi-Fi connection. I often go back to the SNES and start a latest game, but if I could continue playing that save file in RetroArch on my phone and then back to the SNES, it would fit into my life much more easily.

Recent findings suggest that game save data is stored in battery-backed SRAM and in order for a game to send that through my adapter, I needed some of my own code to run. I already have a programmable flash cart for the SNES, so I wrote a utility to patch ROMs and inject this ‘save sync’ code into the reset vector. At power-on and whenever the console is reset, it syncs the save data through the adapter to a WebDAV server as saves//.srm (the same path RetroArch uses) so the console save can be continued on the phone, and vice versa.

Recent findings suggest that first though, the adapter needs to join the local Wi-Fi network. I wanted an era-appropriate UI that can be run from a setup ROM (fig.2), which has you pick a network and type its password with an on-screen keyboard, one letter at a time. That felt most ‘authentic’ but I also made a second iteration that shows the typical QR code on the TV for setup via mobile phone.

The second version has the adapter set up a temporary network. Scanning the QR code with a phone joins the network and it then does the usual captive portal flow to open the adapter’s setup page, where the network and WebDAV auth details can be input in a much more user-friendly way.

An vital detail to get right was checking whether the save on the cartridge was newest, or whether to download a newer one from WebDAV. RetroArch keeps a manifest file with a hash of every save, so the adapter updates that too, comparing hashes to decide whether the cartridge or the server has the newest save. If both sides have changed, nothing is overwritten and the cartridge’s save goes to a conflicts folder to play it safe.

SRAM saves are small but this sync still has to run whenever a game starts, potentially introducing a delay. To avoid this, the save is split into chunks that each have their own checksum, so only the chunks that have changed are sent over the controller port. In practice this makes the save sync delay imperceptible, and only when an existing save is pulled by the SNES for the first time is there a 1-2s load screen.

Naturally in 2026, an internet connection also means a connection to LLMs. The dialogue in SNES-era games tends to be fixed and unresponsive. In A Link to the Past, the villagers don’t react when you smash their pots (unlike in subsequent Zelda games). With the network adapter though, we can hook the game’s dialogue text renderer to swap out the original text for an in-character line generated by an LLM.

In a recent development, in order to prompt for dialogue, the LLM needs to be passed the game context, such as the character being interacted with and recent events. Since Link to the Past has been fully disassembled, it was possible to patch it to accumulate this state in RAM and push it out over the controller serial to the adapter and on to an LLM (via a proxy I ran on a local machine that holds the API key).

In a recent development, I tried a few different models and settled on Claude Opus 5.5, as cheaper models would break character or leak spoilers despite being prompted not to. I used LLM as a Judge evals to measure the proportion of responses that fit the context - Haiku scored 66%, Sonnet 90% and Opus 98%. The challenge was the time to first token of the LLM, for Haiku it was about 0.8 s but for Opus it averaged 2.2 s.

Sources indicate that to avoid game-breaking delays from the LLM response times, I switched to speculatively generating the dialogue when Link approaches an NPC, storing the responses in a cache and invalidating them as the context updates. The delay from using a larger model was hidden and most NPC interactions had the response ready. This is a great way to burn tokens so probably not something to do for the full game duration!

When designing the PCB version of the adapter (fig.0) I replicated the same architecture as the prototype, an RP2350A microcontroller that handles the 5v lines and maintains the serial link, with an ESP32-C3 Wi-Fi coprocessor that handles the Wi-Fi connection. These communicate with each other over UART, allowing each link to be maintained by a dedicated core.

It has been revealed that A PIO state machine on the RP2350 watches clock and latch, queueing the data and filtering out glitches shorter than 100 ns. This frees up the cores to prepare data to be sent over D0 while also talking to the C3.

The USB socket was included not just for flashing the board but also to support debugging it while it is powered from the SNES. This means the board needs to safely support taking a 5v supply from either the controller port or USB, and avoid backfeeding if both are connected. This is done with a LM66200 dual ideal diode. Supply can be taken from either source and we avoid the voltage drop that would come with using actual diodes. I’d seen some brownouts in tests on the breadboard, so designed the PCB with plenty of headroom for the LDO regulator even if the supply rail sags on a Wi-Fi burst.

While prototyping I also had issues when using series resistors on the link lines. This may be related to erratum RP2350-E9 in the A2 revision (stepping) of the RP2350A on my Pico 2 W. In the assembled PCB order I switched these to 0 Ω links, as they’re just for protection and I wasn’t sure which stepping the PCB would be assembled with. The boards turned out to have the fixed A4 stepping, so real resistors can go in next time.

The case is just a tray and a lid that sandwich the PCB, though I did want it to nod toward an era-appropriate design language. It was generated in code (build123d) using the PCB’s STEP files from KiCad, so that the design could be tested within a single 3D model.

The two halves join around the cable and the USB socket, and there are M2 pillars that align with the drilled holes in the PCB to hold everything together.

Since the PCB has a status LED, this design has a light pipe that channels that light up to become the dot of the etched Wi-Fi icon. It’s not the prettiest of designs, but I thought that was cute.

I’ve ordered a batch of these enclosures to be 3D printed and will upgrade with actual photos once they arrive and the adapter is fully assembled. I’m also considering how to fabricate a single assembly that can insert directly into the controller port. Reach out at [email protected] if you’re interested!

#142599. Industry News: I spent the weekend playing GTA 6 in AR glasses — and there’s no better way to keep your time in Vice City private while being fully immersed

Industry News: I spent the weekend playing GTA 6 in AR glasses — and there’s no better way to keep your time in Vice City private while being fully immersed

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2207 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomsguide

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After 13 long years, the wait is finally over, and like many of you, I couldn’t wait to load up GTA 6 for the first time this weekend.
  • With a game this massive and this anticipated, the last thing you want is to be interrupted — or worse, unable to play because someone else in your household claimed the TV first.
  • For those of us with a significant other or kids at home, though, carving out the necessary time to finally play GTA 6 hasn’t been that easy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After 13 long years, the wait is finally over, and like many of you, I couldn’t wait to load up GTA 6 for the first time this weekend. However, instead of playing on the largest screen in my house, I decided that a pair of AR glasses might be the best way to experience this upcoming and improved Vice City. Let me explain.

With a game this massive and this anticipated, the last thing you want is to be interrupted — or worse, unable to play because someone else in your household claimed the TV first. Now, if you’re an adult who lives by yourself and got to play GTA 6 sprawled out on your couch with one of the best OLED TVs, more power to you.

For those of us with a significant other or kids at home, though, carving out the necessary time to finally play GTA 6 hasn’t been that easy. Fortunately for me, I knew there was another way instead of trying to sneak in a late-night play session in front of the TV.

Industry observers note that you see, over the summer on a trip to Taiwan for Computex, I spent almost my entire 17-hour flight playing Red Dead Redemption on the Switch 2 in AR glasses. That got me thinking: what if I tried playing GTA 6 the same way? Well, that’s exactly what I did, and I don’t think I’d be nearly as far in the game right now if I hadn’t.

Here’s why you, too, might want to consider donning a pair of AR glasses—or more accurately, display glasses — to take in the sights, sounds, and excitement that Vice City has to offer in GTA 6.

In a recent development, this bundle has everything you need to start playing your game consoles in AR. You get a pair of Viture Pro 2 XR glasses and the Viture Pro Mobile Dock. This way you can plug your Switch 2 in directly over USB-C or consoles like the PS5 or Xbox Series X in over HDMI and the included dock brings big-screen console gaming right to your glasses. Alternatively, if you only initiative on playing your Switch 2 this way, you can pick up the Viture Pro 2 Mini Dock Pack for $375 (down from 428) right now.

Recent findings suggest that with a gaming PC or even a handheld like the Steam Deck, playing with AR glasses is as simple as plugging them in. On a console, though, it’s not that easy. Fortunately, Viture makes a few accessories to help.

Sources indicate that for instance, there’s the Viture Pro Mobile Dock and the latest Viture Mobile Dock Mini. While I played RDR using the latter, when I tried playing my Switch 2 in AR glasses back at launch, I used the former. Don’t get me wrong, the new mini dock is super compact and easier to bring with you, but for playing on any console besides the Nintendo Switch, it’s missing one very notable port: HDMI.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Now with the Pro Mobile Dock, in addition to USB-C out ports for two pairs of glasses — and a USB-C input for devices like the Switch 2 — you also get a full-sized HDMI port. Admittedly, I didn’t have a use for it before as I’ve mainly played games in AR glasses while traveling or on vacation, but with my PS5 Pro fired up with GTA 6 installed and ready to go, it was time to put it to the test.

According to recent reports, I ran a long HDMI cable from the back of my console, plugged it into the dock along with a pair of the Viture Pro 2 AR glasses, powered it on, and I was good to go. GTA 6 appeared almost instantly on the Micro-OLED displays in the glasses, and since they have built-in speakers, that was all I needed.

Although I love their more affordable $299 price, Viture did have to cut one of my favorite features from its other glasses. Unlike the firm’s other models — and this is true with the Xreal XBX A01 glasses, too — there isn’t any built-in electrochromic dimming. Instead, you get a lens shade in the box.

Now, if you’ve never worn a pair of AR glasses before, electrochromic dimming lets you go from a clear display where you can see the world around you (in addition to the content from your game console, phone, or tablet) to a dimmed one without ambient light seeping through, all with the push of a button.

In a recent development, the Viture Pro 2 glasses do have one feature going for them that made my GTA 6 play sessions a whole lot more comfortable, though. They’re extremely lightweight at just 63 grams.

Playing GTA 6 with AR glasses felt just like making my way through the Wild West as John Marston in RDR. I was able to take in all of Leonida without bothering anyone else in my house, and since the game runs at 30 fps, I didn’t lose anything when it came to visual quality. Now, if I were playing on PC, that would be a different story, since the Pro 2s come equipped with a 120Hz refresh rate — making them just as good for fast-paced games as they are for slower ones.

According to recent reports, if you want to try something similar, you’ll get the best experience using the Pro Mobile Dock — or better yet, Viture’s new HDMI to USB-C adapter cable. Mine is still in the mail, though, so I made do with the Pro Mobile Dock, and for now, everything worked exceptionally well. However, that isn’t the only way to play GTA 6 in AR glasses.

Sources indicate that besides using Viture’s AR glasses with one of its docks, I’ve also spent a fair amount of time playing on a smartphone, too. If you have a newer iPhone, Samsung phone, or any smartphone with DisplayPort Alt Mode over USB-C, you just plug your glasses in and you’re good to go. With that kind of setup, you can load up a remote play app like PXPlay (for PlayStation) or XBXPlay (for Xbox) and use a wireless controller.

Industry observers note that that does leave your phone just lying there, which is why Viture teamed up with 8BitDo a while back to create a variant of the 8BitDo Ultimate Mobile Gaming Controller with a full-featured USB-C port. On most mobile game controllers, the USB-C ports are just used for passthrough charging. With this one, though, you can plug in a pair of AR glasses and actually get video out.

According to recent reports, just like I did during my second long-haul flight to Taiwan a few years back, I popped my Samsung Galaxy S24 FE into the controller and plugged in my AR glasses. After getting PXPlay set up on that phone, I was able to use remote play on my PS5 Pro to play GTA 6 in bed.

As I was fixing up Jason’s house, though, I noticed that it was slightly difficult to see and read the button prompts on the edges of the screen. Since this was my first time playing GTA 6, I had no idea which button to press when using a nail gun to hang drywall or to fix the shingles on my roof. So I put the Pro 2s down and switched to the Viture Luma Pro glasses instead.

In a recent development, with the simple mission of giving you the best bang for your buck in AR glasses, Viture knocked it out the park with Luma Pro. These have the best color science of any glasses on this list, and there’s versatility in the Spacewalker software to turn any space into a giant 152-inch panoramic workspace with 3DoF tracking that keeps it anchored.

In a recent development, with their higher-resolution lenses (from 1080p per eye to 1200p), wider field of view (from 46 to 52 degrees), and redesigned optical stack, what was blurry on the Pro 2s became instantly clear on the Luma Pros. Now, if you’re on a tight budget and already know the controls, you can still definitely play GTA 6 with the Pro 2s. However, since I was fresh to the controls and had both pairs of glasses handy, making the switch was easy and absolutely worthwhile.

One feature that you’ll find on both pairs of glasses — and pretty much the rest of the AR glasses in Viture’s lineup — are myopia dials. With these, you can turn the dials to go from a blurry to a clear picture if, like me, you wear glasses or contacts. Most of the time I wear contacts, and I make it a point to have them in when wearing AR glasses. However, since I wanted to play in bed, I decided this was finally the time to try them out.

Now, I had to fully light the room in the pictures above, but on Friday and Saturday — and hopefully on Sunday evening once I’m done writing this — I cozied up in bed with that special 8BitDo controller and my AR glasses and played more GTA 6 than I’d like to admit. And frankly, it was awesome.

At first, I was a bit worried about the remote play experience with such a complex game, but with one of the best mesh Wi-Fi systems equipped with Wi-Fi 7 and a fast internet connection, it worked really well.

Now, I did have my PS5 Pro plugged into my router with an Ethernet cable during those play sessions. However, when I took the pics above, I had it unplugged, and that tanked the game’s performance. So if you want to play GTA 6 remotely — with or without AR glasses — I strongly recommend connecting your console over Ethernet for a smoother and more stable remote play experience.

Industry observers note that as I’m also at the moment testing out the Viture Pro Neckband, I decided to put it on and go play outside for a bit of fun. While the device around my neck might look like a wearable fan, it’s actually a wearable Android tablet, if you can believe it.

Now, what I like about this setup compared to using the Pro Mobile Dock or a smartphone is that my hands weren’t weighed down and I wasn’t tethered to my console. Likewise, if you’re using a third-party app like PXPlay, you can use whatever controller you want and aren’t limited to just using a wired DualSense (like you are on PC).

Now, I must say that playing GTA 6 wasn’t nearly as good on the Pro Neckband as it was on a smartphone. Still, with my Eero Outdoor 7 mesh node on the fence behind me and seated in The Foldable Gaming Chair, it was quite comfy and still very playable. If only the weather had been Vice City sunny instead of overcast.

In a recent development, with a pair of AR glasses and the right dock — or even a capable smartphone — the possibilities are really endless. You’re not just limited to sitting in front of your TV or, if you have kids like I do, playing at your desk. On that second point, I haven’t seen anything too spicy — except for Mandy in a bikini — just yet, but given this is Grand Theft Auto after all, I know it’s coming. I wouldn’t want my son or my wife walking in on something inappropriate on my TV, and by playing with AR glasses on, I don’t have to worry about it.

Now, I know AR glasses, or display glasses, aren’t a must-have gadget like a smartphone, but they make for a very useful accessory. While they’re amazing on planes — and trust me, I’ve put in quite a lot of hours gaming or even watching movies with them aboard an aircraft — they’re just as useful and convenient at home.

As for me, it’s time to get back to Vice City and enjoy the quiet, slow-paced life of Chapter 1 before I eventually have to go pick up Lucia from prison.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple's AirPods Pro 3 are some of the best noise cancelling earbuds you can buy, but they're definitely not cheap. Thankfully, big sales events like Black Friday are the perfect time to pick up a pair at a much more palatable price. They're still not "cheap", but they have dropped to their lowest ever price.

You can pick up the AirPods Pro 3 for $149 in Amazon's Black Friday sale, which is $100 off the usual price tag. That makes now the perfect time to pick up a pair for your own iPhone, and enjoy all the advanced features Apple has to offer for less.

Apple's best wireless earbuds have dropped to their lowest ever price, knocking $100 off the usual price tag. For your money you're getting improved audio and active noise cancelation, extended battery life and a newly introduced, more comfortable design that should offer a secure fit.

Industry observers note that one of the things I like about Apple's AirPods is that they're a lot harder to lose than the dirt-cheap wireless earbuds some of you may be drawn to. My wife was in that situation, and three lost pairs of earbuds later, it was clear that something needed to be done to stop them from going missing. Enter the AirPods Pro 3, and the built-in Find My support.

Industry observers note that apple's earbuds all have a direct connection to the Find My network, which lets you track down any lost earbuds from your iPhone — even if they're not with the case. On top of that, Precision finding in the AirPods Pro 3 means you can track down their exact location more easily, rather than being given a fairly broad area to search through. It isn't foolproof, but it is a much better system than cheap non-Apple buds tend to offer.

It has been revealed that but there's more to the AirPods Pro 3 than being harder to lose. Apple has ramped up the noise cancellation, and the latest iOS patch gives you a sliding scale to choose ANC, transparency mode, or a middle ground between the two modes. Apple's also upped the battery life, offering 8 hours with ANC switched on, and the charging case extending the grand total to 24 hours.

Other notable features include live translation powered by Apple Intelligence, heart rate monitoring, IP67 water and dust resistance and the ability to recharge via both an Apple Charger and MagSafe wireless charger. There's even latest XXS ear tips, for those of you that have struggled with the larger sizes on past AirPods models.

Recent findings suggest that just make sure to take advantage of this deal while you can. Discounted AirPods tend to sell pretty swiftly, and the last thing you need is to miss out on this all-time low price because someone else got to them first. By which I mean, don't wait for Black Friday in the hopes that they might drop to a lower price — that isn't likely to happen.

This Note-Taking Pebble Ring Is so Simple, and I Love It

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Pebble’s $75 ring, the Index 01, has one job: It lets you record voice memos.
  • In this era where every tech product is trying to also be every other tech product, I appreciate the Index’s simplicity.
  • According to recent reports, to buy the Index 01 ring, you get yourself a sizing kit (either buy one for $10 or 3D print it yourself), order the ring, and pair it with the Pebble app on your phone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pebble’s $75 ring, the Index 01, has one job: It lets you record voice memos. That seems like it would be underwhelming, and the idea was ridiculed by some of Pebble’s fans when the product was first unveiled. But I’ve been wearing it for a few weeks, and folks: I love it.

In this era where every tech product is trying to also be every other tech product, I appreciate the Index’s simplicity. This is a ring with no heart rate sensors or even charging pins, just a microphone, a button to activate it, and a light to let you know that it’s working. The audio is processed on your device; no need to send anything to the cloud.

According to recent reports, to buy the Index 01 ring, you get yourself a sizing kit (either buy one for $10 or 3D print it yourself), order the ring, and pair it with the Pebble app on your phone. I use an iPhone rather than an Android, which means I can’t use certain features like setting timed reminders or connecting to Beeper, but it’s still an incredibly useful little device. The Index has no charger, since it uses a disposable battery that Pebble estimates will last about two years.

In a recent development, the simplest way to use the Index is to wear it on your index finger (hence the name, get it?) and press the button with your thumb. Speak a quick note while holding the button in, and the ring will flash to let you know it got the message. A moment later, you’ll get a notification saying that it added (whatever you said) to your “Notes to self” note.

Sources indicate that to take this further, you can create different notes and ask the ring to add what you say to a specific note. You can also double-click the button to ask a question. The answer will appear in the notification you get on your phone or watch a moment later. (The ring does not speak to you.).

It has been revealed that all the notes you leave yourself appear as plain text in the Pebble app, fully editable. If you tap on each one, you can see a timestamp from when you left the note, and you can replay the voice recording if the transcription doesn’t make sense. (Why is there a “pencil sharp pepper” on my packing list? Ohh, that’s a pencil sharpener.) You can also add notes by typing them, which I find useful when starting a to-do list or a packing list.

It’s incredible how useful a simple timestamped note can be. I used to do something similar with my “notes to self” chat in Signal, but the Index makes it even easier since I won’t get distracted by opening my phone. For example, I make a note on the Index whenever I take a medication, so that tomorrow morning I will be able to check whether I already took, say, a long-acting allergy pill. (You do not want to accidentally double up on those.).

There’s one thing that, for years, I wished for a simple tool to help me do. It’s trivial, which makes it extra frustrating that I have not been able to find a good solution. I would simply like to note when I leave for a road trip, and when I start and end each stop. This way I can tell how long the driving took as a portion of the whole trip, and how long my stops tend to be so I can initiative them better next time.

You’d think this would be easy, but every existing tool drove me nuts in a different way. Stopwatches only store a single number, so I can’t break down how long each stop was—and if I miss a button press, I’m screwed. Sending myself a Signal text is probably my best option, but if I’ve just parked my car after three hours of driving, the second I pick up my phone I’m going to see all the notifications that arrived while I was on the road, and I’ll forget to actually send that text.

Industry observers note that but this is exactly what the Index does well. I don’t even need to open my phone or look at my watch. Pressing the button with my thumb means I can do this one-handed without having a microphone always listening. (It’s also a great way to jot down the random things I think of while driving.).

Sources indicate that the Index worked perfectly for my travel log, and I even used it for a workout after I got to my hotel room that night. I’d do 10 pushups, then tell the ring “add 10 pushups to my workout.” I’d do 20 crunches, and add that as well. I left the workout note open on my phone and could glance over and see what I had already done, since my messages got added to the note as I went.

I didn’t need a workout app for any of this, or a special-purpose travel app. I can just leave myself a dang note, and the note-taking app can remember when I left the note and, if I choose, play back exactly how I said it. It’s gloriously simple. Good job, Pebble.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, cellular IoT has extended low-power connectivity to many remote places. Even so, about four-fifths of the earth’s surface remains outside the range of a base station. Non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by adding satellite access to the 5G standard. One modem can then connect through a satellite when no terrestrial cell is available.

It has been revealed that this shift changes how devices are designed. Satellites are in motion. Signals therefore face long propagation delays and changing Doppler shift. Link budgets are tight and device antennas are small. A device can pass static conformance tests and still fail on a real satellite link.

This White Paper explains these challenges. It also outlines the test conditions and measurements needed to evaluate synchronization, signaling, receiver performance, and link reliability.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Elixir HLS makes FPGA circuits from functions written in Elixir: high-level synthesis (HLS).
  • FPGA circuits are usually written in a hardware description language such as Verilog or VHDL, register by register: which value goes into which register at which clock.
  • In a recent development, in Elixir HLS that language is Elixir.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Elixir HLS makes FPGA circuits from functions written in Elixir: high-level synthesis (HLS).

FPGA circuits are usually written in a hardware description language such as Verilog or VHDL, register by register: which value goes into which register at which clock. This is called RTL (register transfer level). High-level synthesis generates that RTL from code in a software language: the author indicates what to compute, and the tool decides the clocks and the registers.

In a recent development, in Elixir HLS that language is Elixir. A function defined with defhls stays an ordinary Elixir function that runs on the CPU, and also becomes an FPGA circuit. Each circuit is simulated against its Elixir function and used only if the results match, so the Elixir function is the circuit's specification. Why it is built this way: vision.

Industry observers note that elixir HLS 0.1.0 is its first release, an early one: it synthesizes integer functions, with state, tables, memories and fixed loops, and instances joining them with streams, levels and events, in the FPGA or on the CPU; its first target is the Sipeed Tang Primer 25K with AtomVM, and its working example the FM radio (atomvm-fm-radio), whose whole demodulator runs in the FPGA. Not there yet, among others: division, floats, recursion, and of Elixir's streams what needs the whole collection.

Sources indicate that stream_kernel takes a 32-bit value, compares its low and high 16 bits as signed numbers and computes its result depending on which is larger. Given an integer, it computes on the CPU, as an Elixir function. How the same function runs as a circuit in the FPGA: On a board.

According to recent reports, A type such as u32 (unsigned, 32 bits) is the circuit's bit width. A circuit spends wiring and logic on every bit, so narrower widths make it smaller and faster. On the CPU the values are cut to the same widths, so the CPU and the circuit compute the same results.

mix ehls.compile turns each defhls function of the files into a SystemVerilog circuit and then simulates every circuit against its function; it stops at a circuit that does not match.

In a recent development, what can be written with defhls (a function, which runs both on the CPU and as a circuit) and definstance (an instance: functions placed as circuits), beside Elixir. ✗: not in Elixir HLS. Details: How Elixir HLS works, EHLS.defhls/2, EHLS.Pipeline, EHLS.Stream.

Shared state and events (definstance).

definstance places functions as circuits (or, without an FPGA, as processes on the CPU), and gives an application new things to call:.

A defhls function runs in the FPGA where a definstance places it. The simplest instance takes a value and gives a value, called like a function from the CPU; an instance can also take a stream, values one after another, and run on its own, with the data flowing from devices through the kernels without the CPU.

What comes next (what needs no board, the steps on a board): Getting started.

mix docs builds these documents and the modules' documentation (the modules above, the backends and the mix tasks) as HTML in doc/, as on HexDocs.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that that might not immediately seem like the most obvious fit, turning your research notes into a mass of HTML code.
  • Website building is rolling out now for Gemini Notebook's web app for all people, and is "coming soon" to the mobile app.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gemini Notebook, Google's AI tool for study and research, already lets you do a lot with your notes: You can turn them into flashcard quizzes, interactive podcasts, video explainers, mind maps, and infographics, as well as interrogating the sources you've collected through AI-powered prompts and responses. Now there's something upcoming. You can also build interactive websites from your notebooks.

It has been revealed that that might not immediately seem like the most obvious fit, turning your research notes into a mass of HTML code. But it gives you another way to look at your material and to get insights from it. Here's how it works, what you could potentially do with it, and how impressively it worked when I put it to the test on some early 20th-century Irish literature.

Website building is rolling out now for Gemini Notebook's web app for all people, and is "coming soon" to the mobile app. You won't see a website option in the Studio panel alongside Audio Overview, Reports, Quiz, and the rest; instead, you type something along the lines of "make me a website" in the prompt box.

Recent findings suggest that to make a website, you need sources, so I set Gemini Notebook to collect information about James Joyce's 1914 collection of short stories, Dubliners. As I studied Dubliners many years ago (I highly recommend it), I was hoping I'd spot any AI errors and hallucinations, and be able to properly assess the quality of Gemini Notebook's analysis.

Recent findings suggest that with a suitable amount of information absorbed into the AI brain, I got Gemini Notebook to make me a website. Google doesn't give too much official guidance here, but states you should add "a description of what you want to build for work or study," so if you have a particular style or angle in mind, include it.

Industry observers note that here was my prompt: "Build a website using all the sources and information collected so far. Make it an interactive guide to the individual stories in Dubliners, as well as the overarching themes and context. I want to use it as a study aid to explore different aspects of the story collection.".

According to recent reports, the finished website pops up in the Studio panel, and in my case it took around five minutes to put something together from 26 different sources. Click on the website, and it opens in a fresh window—you can use it from there, open it in a separate tab, or download the code to your computer.

According to recent reports, I was honestly impressed by how much Gemini Notebook managed to pack into a single website: I got plot summaries, analysis, critical context, and some of the main themes and motifs outlined. There was an interactive quiz at the bottom of the page to test my knowledge, and even a graphic I could click through to reveal different elements of how the stories fit together.

It has been revealed that everything was well laid out and functional, albeit with the standard "sheen" you get from anything made by AI (which tends to always pick the same colors and fonts). I wouldn't have necessarily thought that I needed a website if I was still studying Dubliners today, but I can definitely see how it would have helped.

According to recent reports, for something like my project, a website really works well as a study aid, since it offers a different way of interrogating the information. You can already do that in the main chat, and with tools such as the audio and video overviews, but this is different. It's a bit like having a mini-Wikipedia focused just on whatever you're researching.

The interactive elements that are included—so in my example, I could click from story to story, and theme to theme, within the same page—make a site more engaging than a standard report document and a static wall of text, and should help the information stick if you're trying to study it.

According to recent reports, I can also see how this might be useful for sharing data with others. Maybe you need to analyze monthly report figures, or you want to chart how your organization has developed a product over time—perhaps an interactive website will relay that information in a more compelling way than a slide deck or PDF.

Recent findings suggest that maybe you have a notebook stuffed with details of a big family vacation. Putting together a website through Gemini Notebook would give your family a hub that they could use to easily check up on the details of the trip—where you're going and when, what you'll see there, what they need to pack, and so on. Another idea might be a family tree, if you have ancestry data and sources packed together in a notebook. Putting together a website would be a great way to visualize it, and, again, it's something you could share with relatives. If there were updates to the data you've collected, you could generate a new website.

Bear in mind that you can do a lot with your prompt. My website turned out the way it did because that's what I asked for, and if you need more interactivity or specific types of sections, then you can ask. Based on my follow-up prompts, you can also specify colors and certain layout choices, though it's not quite a full-scale website builder.

According to recent reports, it looks like these sites are single-page creations, though they do have interactive elements and sections that change as you click around. It might be better to think of them as mini apps rather than sites. As of yet, there's no built-in option for publishing a site online or sharing it with others, so you need to download the HTML and do that manually.

If you want a gaming chair that tries to do literally everything, allow me to introduce you to the DXRacer Martian Pro. It’ll massage you, heat your butt, and even cool your you-know-whats thanks to a built-in fan (which I’ve affectionately labelled “the junk wafter”).

It has adjustable lumbar support, adjustable arm rests, an adjustable head rest, and loads of control over positioning thanks to its electronic controls. It’s built well and moderately comfortable… for a gaming chair (spoiler: that’s foreshadowing).

However, despite its many positives, the chair isn’t perfect. It’s very expensive at $899, and obviously all those goodies up there need juice, which means cables. It’s also a gaming chair, meaning it’s about as comfortable as most gaming chairs — so not very.

But could this still be the best gaming chair for you? Find out in my full DXRacer Martian Pro review.

Sources indicate that the Martian Pro packs lots of features, plenty of adjustment and a heavy, sturdy design. It’s also fairly comfortable as far as gaming chairs go.

The best thing about the Martian Pro is its wide array of cool features. Unlike the base DXRacer Martian, the Pro has a built-in back massager, like those chairs at airports. There are loads of different modes, and the massaging is genuinely pretty good. I found myself oof-ing on quite a few occasions as the massage balls dug into tight spots on my back. The massage only lasts for 10 minutes if you don’t press the cycle button, so you have to either cycle through constantly or restart regularly. This is a little annoying, but not a huge deal — I’d rather it turned itself off than keep running — and you’ll swiftly get used to where your favorite massage setting is in the cycle order. I like massage setting two, which made things fairly easy.

The base of the chair has a heating element, so you can warm up your butt during colder seasons. But there’s also a cooling fan for when your junk gets a little hot. As I mentioned up top, I’ve christened it “the junk wafter”. It really works, providing a strong cooling breeze. Now, given not everyone is as hygienic as I am (and I’m sure you are, dear reader), I can think of obvious downsides related to blowing air up and over the ol’ undercarriage. But hey, as long as you’re on your own at your gaming desk, who am I to judge you for cooling down your best bits?

Industry observers note that you can’t heat, cool or massage without electricity, so it figures that DXRacer gave the Martian Pro electronic adjustment. The chair back is adjusted using a toggle on the left base, while the two-part lumbar pad is adjusted on the right.

Un-electronically, there’s a seat height paddle, and four-axis armrests that offer an impressive amount of adjustment (and can have their tops replaced when worn out). This lets you fine tune the chair’s shape and support.

According to recent reports, the DXRacer Martian Pro is built pretty well. I’m not so keen on all the red accents, as I think they look a little childish and more than a little tacky, so initially I had my doubts about whether the chair would feel sturdy. But it does, for the most part.

Industry observers note that as soon as you try and get this behemoth out the box, you’ll notice it’s extremely large and very heavy, which is reassuring. The leather feels premium, there’s nice spongy padding on the armrests, and all the buttons and electronics work as they should. It never feels like it’s going to break on you.

It has been revealed that my only gripe is that the plastic side trims that cover the pivot mechanism look cheap and feel all scratchy, as a result of cheap plastic. On a nearly-$900 chair, I’d expect better.

Now, there’s a monumental caveat here: I’ll cover it in more detail later on, but in short, gaming chairs are all about show — they almost all use an inherently uncomfortable flat-backed design.

In a recent development, that said, as gaming chairs go, this one is alright. That’s primarily thanks to the adjustable lumbar pad, which provides support for your back. It’s nowhere near as big, pronounced and supportive as the large (necessarily so) lumbar supports on the best office chairs, but better than nothing — i.e. better than the Razer Soma Chroma I tested recently. There’s also lots of padding on the arm rests and an included neck cushion (although I found this a little too large).

If you want a gaming chair that’s as comfortable as they come, check out the Razer Iskur V2 NewGen, which has a much larger lumbar pad and a decidedly ergonomic design.

Sources indicate that alas, if you want proper support and comfort, this chair isn’t for you. It needs to be charged regularly and is quite complicated to build. And there’s no way I’d recommend paying $900.

As I mentioned above, gaming chairs are almost all inherently uncomfortable. Flat backs and necks, padded rather than mesh bases, small lumbar cushions, etc. This makes their very existence weird and kinda meta: they only exist because streamers and YouTubers use them (as they look "gamer-y), which makes the general public want them too. Certain brands therefore supply the aforementioned streamers and influencers with them, which keeps the public buying them. Ah, the circle of modern life.

Recent findings suggest that what I’m trying to say here is, if you want a comfortable time, do not get a gaming chair. There’s absolutely no reason why you can’t game in a luxurious office chair, and if you ask me, that’s what you should do. For the same or less money, you can get a much more comfortable and supportive chair. It's just that you won't look like a streamer.

The Martian Pro has lumbar support, yes, but even at its greatest extent it’s just a small mound. The Boulies EP460, Boulies EP500, Autonomous ErgoChair Pro and Sihoo Doro C300 Pro V2 all have huge mesh lumbar pads, which is what you actually need to properly support your back.

It has been revealed that I found the Martian Pro’s neck cushion ridiculously oversized, and extremely firm, meaning no give. The result was that my head and neck were pushed forward — as if I were doing Jim Carrey’s trademark bird-like head thrust.

Recent findings suggest that worst of all is the seat pad. I have a type of immuno-arthritis that affects my legs and lower back, so it’s key my seat pads are comfortable. Let me tell you now: there is nothing quite like mesh for butt and coccyx comfort (and natural cooling as a secondary benefit). The Martian Pro uses a basic cushion, which is fairly thick, but still puts too much compression on my lower back. I had to use a coccyx cushion to stay comfortable.

As I already mentioned, all those electronics above need power, which means the Martian Pro needs a cable. Now, to its credit, there’s a battery inside (and a fairly major 5,000mAh one at that). After a full charge, the chair lasted me a few hours of massaging while gaming.

Sources indicate that you need to charge it regularly, though, which I found annoying. What’s worse is that when you’ve run out of charge, you can’t adjust the recline or lumbar support as both are done electronically.

In a recent development, it’s just too complicated for me. Again, I’d prefer the natural cooling and better analog lumbar support of a decent mesh office chair.

In a recent development, thanks to all those electronics, the Martian Pro is somewhat tricky to build. While each step is fairly easy, there are just lots of them and the chair is extremely heavy — I’d recommend having two people and a lot of space before building it. You’ve also got to make sure everything is wired in properly, which can be a little confusing. I didn’t quite hide one wire properly so had to backtrack and redo my steps at one point.

Recent findings suggest that the Martian Pro took me 42 minutes to build alone, and I was drenched in sweat afterwards. I’ve built a lot of chairs in my time as reviews editor here at Tom’s Guide, so I’m an experienced builder — I once put together the Boulies OP180 in just 10 minutes! 42 minutes is a long time for me.

There’s absolutely no way on Earth this chair should cost $899 / £649. Sure, it has some nifty features and is built well, but it looks pretty cheap and tacky with the red accents — it’s like a five-year-old’s fever dream. To be fair, you can buy it in a plain black model, which I’d recommend. But as I mentioned above, some of the plastics used are scratchy and cheap, too.

In a recent development, if you want to look like your favorite streamer, and be just as uncomfortable, you can pick up the SecretLab Titan Evo for $569, which looks much more premium. Even the Razer Iskur V2 NewGen — the gold standard of gaming chairs from a comfort perspective — costs only $649 from new, which pretty well puts things into perspective: the Martian Pro is overpriced.

The DXRacer Martian Pro is unfortunately a mixed bag. It packs lots of features and is fairly comfortable for a gaming chair. It offers lots of adjustment and a sturdy build. But I can’t give this chair one of our higher scores and my outright recommendation. It’s not truly comfortable in the same way as an office chair. It’s complicated to build and needs a cable to function, and for $900 I’d expect near perfection, not to mention a premium-looking design. Maybe this one’s better suited for Mars.

Industry observers note that peter is a Senior Editor at Tom's Guide, heading up the site's Reviews team and Cameras section. As a writer, he covers topics including tech, photography, gaming, hardware, motoring and food & drink. Outside of work, he's an avid photographer, specialising in architectural and portrait photography. When he's not snapping away on his beloved Fujifilm camera, he can usually be found telling everyone about his greyhounds, riding his motorcycle, squeezing as many FPS as possible out of PC games, and perfecting his espresso shots.
