Breaking: Amazon buys Decart’s AI tech and its founders in a deal worth about $7.5bn

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (372 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Decart co-founders Moshe Shalev, Dean Leitersdorf and Orian Leitersdorf (left to right).
  • Amazon has agreed to buy the technology behind Decart’s AI optimisation software and to bring the Israeli startup’s three co-founders and their team into the company.
  • According to recent reports, amazon will pay about $7.5bn for the assets, a person familiar with the matter told Matt Day of Bloomberg.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Decart co-founders Moshe Shalev, Dean Leitersdorf and Orian Leitersdorf (left to right).

Amazon has agreed to buy the technology behind Decart’s AI optimisation software and to bring the Israeli startup’s three co-founders and their team into the company. Amazon confirmed the deal on Monday without giving a price.

According to recent reports, amazon will pay about $7.5bn for the assets, a person familiar with the matter told Matt Day of Bloomberg. It is not buying Decart’s AI models, the person said. News of their talks first emerged in October.

According to recent reports, the deal covers the Decart Optimization Stack, software that helps AI models run faster and more cheaply across different chips. The co-founders, Dean Leitersdorf, Moshe Shalev and Orian Leitersdorf, will join Amazon with their researchers and engineers. The deal still needs regulatory clearance.

“Every leap forward in AI starts with getting more out of every chip,” mentioned Peter DeSantis, Amazon’s senior vice president for foundational AI models, custom silicon and quantum computing.

It has been revealed that decart has worked with Amazon since 2025, including on its Trainium chips, which Amazon pitches as a rival to Nvidia’s GPUs. Amazon said the technology will help it get more out of both its AI inference and its custom chips.

“Joining Amazon gives our team the scale, the customers, and the infrastructure to pursue that mission faster than we could on our own,” said Dean Leitersdorf, Decart’s co-founder and chief executive.

According to recent reports, amazon is making the deal through Annapurna Labs, its chip development arm, Israeli business daily Globes reported. The payment is in shares and depends on meeting targets over five years, according to Globes. The three founders have committed to stay at Amazon for that long.

Recent findings suggest that the founders hold about 64% of Decart and stand to share $4.8bn, Globes reported. The bulk of that money comes in the later years of the deal.

Anthropic had held talks to buy Decart for about $6bn before it walked away in September.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Netflix's newest streaming hit, The Body, is drawing in millions of viewers, great reviews, and a gaggle of protests from people who didn't much care for the trailer. But if your lesbian-forward supernatural horror series isn't drawing cries of "blasphemy!"...what are you even doing? In that spirit, we'll conjure up some other shows dealing with the (extremely) dark side of high school.

This time-hopping survival drama is about a group of teenage girls who are stranded in the wilderness in 1996 and do terrible things to survive—the extent of which we only learn about via flashbacks from the present day, where the events of 19 months spent in the wild continue to resonate. There are ambiguous teases of the supernatural here (much more ambiguous than in The Body), but there's plenty of human-level horror as well. The show explores the nasty things we get up to when in survival mode (whether trapped in the wilds, stuck with other teenagers—or god forbid both at once), while also cynically (but accurately) positing that there's a huge difference between the version of the past we talk about and the one that really happened. Stream Yellowjackets on Paramount+.

Sources indicate that situated between flashbacks and flash-forwards (not entirely unlike Yellowjackets), mystery/thriller The Wilds sees an airplane full of teenage girls crash on the way to an empowerment program in Hawaii. It quickly becomes clear that the accident was engineered and that the whole thing is some sort of social experiment, and the survivors are forced to compete against each other if they want to live. The show understands the ways in which young women are exploited and expected to compete against each other in the real world, and the ways in which we'll do just about anything when survival is on the line. Stream The Wilds on Prime Video.

According to recent reports, when pretty, popular girl Kate Wallis (Olivia Holt) goes missing without a trace in 1993, awkward Jeanette Turner (Chiara Aurelia) steps in to fill the gap, modeling herself after Kate by working her way into the missing girl's social circle and getting close with her boyfriend. That's all going great until Kate reappears two years later, accusing Jeanette of having witnessed the events around her disappearance and keeping quiet. Whoops. There's even more going on, as the show shifts back and forth between 1993, 1994, and 1995 to slowly reveal the missing pieces. Season two takes on a different story set in 1999 and 2000, and the forthcoming (surprise) third season will shake things up again. The emphasis here is on mystery, but it's a show about the aftereffects of trauma and of the dark secrets that can tear families and communities apart. Stream Cruel Summer on Hulu.

Juicy import Elite follows a group of working-class friends who earn scholarships to Las Encinas, a fictional private school that is, in the show’s universe, the most exclusive in Spain. What they find there is snobbery, mystery, murder, and lots and lots of sex (between and among characters of various sexual orientations and numerical groupings). The smart, wonderfully trashy show ran for a shocking (in our modern streaming era) eight seasons, with a couple of regional remakes. There's no supernatural stuff here, but plenty of dark deeds done with youthful vigor. Stream Elite on Netflix.

A teenager, Mae (Madeleine Arthur), is discovered by the side of the road with weird religious symbols carved into her skin. The hospital psychiatrist who treats her (Emily Deschanel) takes pity on, and interest in, Mae, deciding to take her in while arrangements can be made for a more permanent home for the cult escapee. Mae is, after all, level-headed and quiet, and couldn't possibly be any trouble. Hoo boy, yeah, that turns out to be a bad call on the good doctor's part. Stream Devil in Ohio on Netflix.

Industry observers note that A different type of blasphemy at play here, in that Joan Lindsay's novel was already adapted brilliantly by Peter Weir in 1975, in a film often referred to as the greatest to come out of Australia. And yet, this Natalie Dormer-lead take is an achievement in its own right, the extended running time of a miniseries offering up more time to sit with the story's deliberately ineffable mysteries. Dormer plays Hester Appleyard, headmistress of a school for young ladies in the Australian bush. It's going well until a Valentine's Day picnic to the title's Hanging Rock sees three students and a governess disappear, impossibly, without a trace, bringing about the slow unravelling of pretty much everyone left behind. Stream Picnic at Hanging Rock on Prime Video and Tubi.

Recent findings suggest that mariam (Andria Tayeh) is brutally bullied by the cool clique at her private school in this Jordanian import, a high school drama that's both universal and distinctly Muslim in character. Fed up, Mariam convinces a couple of similarly outcast friends to join forces with her in a revenge plot that quickly gets out of hand. The show deals with Jordanian-style patriarchy head-on, without drawing any easy conclusions about its characters—Mariam catfishes one of her bullies and convinces her to send a revealing picture, one that she immediately posts, exploiting the very same repressive cultural elements that she claims to deplore. It's a smart, realist drama with soapy elements and nothing by way of the supernatural, but it's still a very sharp picture of the extremely cutthroat nature of high school life. Stream AlRawabi School for Girls on Netflix.

In a recent development, peyton List stars as Maddie, a teenager in small-town Wisconsin for whom her death is very much just the beginning. Stuck in a high school in the afterlife (because hell is definitely for children), she goes on a journey to solve her own murder while uncovering secrets and lies in both worlds. It all sounds a bit grim, but the show has a sense of fun about it: While Maddie does develop the ability to communicate with the living, her world is populated by ghost teens from various eras and generations, with customs, mores, and cliques having developed in ghost high school just as in our world. Stream School Spirits on Paramount+.

Industry observers note that the newly introduced Girigo app, claiming to grant wishes, sounds like harmless fun. Except, of course, that the things that teenagers want aren't always beneficent, and the app has already been the conduit for some incredibly dark deeds by the time it gets into the hands of the five high schoolers who find themselves caught in a Ring-like web of shamanistic horror and death countdowns. This is why we tell you to put your phones down once in a while... Stream If Wishes Could Kill on Netflix.

In a recent development, four one-time best friends reunite at Rosewood High School a year after the disappearance of the leader of their little clique, all having received threatening messages from the mysterious "A," who knows everything they did last summer...and pretty much all the rest of the time. Shoplifting, parents having affairs, students hooking up with teachers—you name it, it's happening in town, and A knows it all. After the prime suspect turns up dead, the girls are caught in the killer's web while trying to keep their secrets hidden. If seven juicy seasons and three A's aren't enough for you, there are three spin-offs. Stream Pretty Little Liars on Hulu and HBO Max.

Among iOS 27’s many newly introduced features is a great change for anyone with multiple iPhones: you can now keep the same phone number on two iPhones via iPhone Handoff.

With iOS 27, Apple introduces massive AI upgrades like Siri AI, plus exciting fresh features for apps like Wallet, Messages, Notes, and also CarPlay and AirPods.

But the update also has a lot of smaller, more niche improvements.

One such addition is iPhone Handoff, which enables switching seamlessly between two iPhones using the same phone number.

Here’s how it works, per Apple:.

It has been revealed that after iPhone Handoff is set up, one iPhone becomes the main iPhone and the other iPhone becomes the secondary iPhone that shares the number. Your main iPhone should be the one you use most often. Some carrier services, like Call Forwarding and Caller ID, and carrier account management can only be managed on your main iPhone. Contact your carrier for more details.

To move between your main iPhone and secondary iPhone, simply unlock the device that you want to start using — your phone number will automatically become active on that device. The message “Switched to this iPhone” will display at the top of your screen to confirm it’s now active. Your phone number will only be active on one iPhone at a time when using iPhone Handoff.

Sources indicate that most users will never need this feature. But if you’re someone who, for whatever reason, has separate devices that you want on the same number, iOS 27 has the solution.

In a recent development, I feel like I’m exactly who this feature was made for. After years of running dual SIM, I now have a personal line on my Duo and work line on an 18 Pro. Going out with friends, family, etc, I’d love to bring one phone again while bringing both numbers with me, but keeping work system access to a specific, separate device. Only current problem is waiting for Verizon to activate the feature and then see if it actually works well.

If you’re trying to decide between an iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro, perhaps iPhone Handoff is Apple’s subtle way of saying: “Why choose?”.

So far carrier support is limited (here’s the latest list), but Apple aims to expand iPhone Handoff to more carriers soon.

Recent findings suggest that do you have a need to use the same phone number on multiple iPhones? For what reason? Let us know in the comments.

Industry observers note that black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

According to recent reports, black Friday used to be bigger for major retailers and more expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was better for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Nowadays, though, the distinction is almost meaningless. Yes, Amazon has Black Friday sales, but when it comes to Peloton, not all the equipment is available on Amazon. Check the Peloton website or other retailers for all your options. (I've linked each one above to a place where you can buy it—some on Amazon and some from Peloton directly.) Refer to guides like our live blog that vet deals for you. Lean and Mathlib certify Alpöge’s Claude-assisted Riemann hypothesis proof

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the Lean and Mathlib communities have certified that Levent Alpöge’s Claude-assisted proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct.
  • “We hereby certify that both the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis are correct,” the groups wrote.
  • Recent findings suggest that alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, released the proof on Friday as a Lean library of 17 million lines of code.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the Lean and Mathlib communities have certified that Levent Alpöge’s Claude-assisted proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct. In a joint statement on Saturday, the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative noted they had full confidence in the proof and congratulated him.

“We hereby certify that both the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis are correct,” the groups wrote.

Recent findings suggest that alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, released the proof on Friday as a Lean library of 17 million lines of code. Lean is a programming language that checks every logical step. There is no paper a human could read.

Recent findings suggest that dozens of people compiled the code without errors and got the same raw proof file, the statement mentioned. Two separate tools then confirmed that Alpöge’s theorem is exactly the Riemann hypothesis as Mathlib states it. Experts in Lean and number theory had already vetted that statement.

Several proof checkers, written in different programming languages, checked the proof itself. Two of them, con-leche and con-ron, come with a formal proof that they cannot accept a false one. That answers the worry that a flaw in Lean could let a bad proof through, the groups said.

Industry observers note that MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland, who ran early checks on his own computer, keeps a public verification record. All 175,187 modules compile with zero errors, it says. He ran the checks with Claude Code. A separate, sandboxed rebuild produced a byte-identical proof file. Two of the slowest kernel checks were still running at his last update on Sunday afternoon.

Industry observers note that the proof also covers the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions, across all moduli and characters, the record says. It does not cover Dedekind zeta functions, Hecke L-functions or automorphic L-functions in general.

Recent findings suggest that not every mathematician welcomed the result. The Association for Human Mathematics said in a statement that the proof puts technical validity above accountability, clarity and understanding.

“At this time, no human being can reasonably claim to be responsible for, or even to understand, such a document,” the group wrote.

The group called for democratic oversight of AI companies. It noted firms use milestones like this as publicity for the superintelligence they want to build, and urged mathematicians to keep their research free of AI models.

The Lean groups remarked they looked forward to work that will help explain the fresh ideas in the proof. Alpöge has said he wants to understand the argument, simplify it and write it up. He works with Tristan Buckmaster on Navier-Stokes, another Millennium Prize Problem.

#142583. Tech Report: MRAM Basics: How Magnetic Memory Is Replacing Embedded Flash

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1223 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Allaboutcircuits ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: MRAM Basics: How Magnetic Memory Is Replacing Embedded Flash

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1223 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Allaboutcircuits

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Learn about magnetoresistive random-access memory technology and what changes it brings for embedded products, including firmware updates and data logging.
  • According to recent reports, most embedded engineers know the limits of flash memory well.
  • Sources indicate that magnetoresistive random-access memory (MRAM) removes most of these limits.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Learn about magnetoresistive random-access memory technology and what changes it brings for embedded products, including firmware updates and data logging.

According to recent reports, most embedded engineers know the limits of flash memory well. Writes are slow, and every write needs an erase first. Each cell survives only 10,000 to 100,000 write/erase cycles.

Sources indicate that magnetoresistive random-access memory (MRAM) removes most of these limits. It stores data as a magnetic state, not as trapped electrical charge. Microcontrollers built on 22 nm and 16 nm processes now use it, because embedded flash isn’t practical at those nodes.

This article explains how MRAM works, why flash stopped scaling, and what changes for firmware.

Recent findings suggest that A flash cell stores a bit as electrons trapped on a floating gate or in a charge-trap layer. An MRAM cell stores it in a magnetic tunnel junction (MTJ). This is a stack of two ferromagnetic layers, usually a cobalt-iron-boron alloy (CoFeB), separated by a magnesium oxide (MgO) barrier about 1 nm thick.

Sources indicate that as illustrated in Figure 1, one magnetic layer, the reference layer, has its magnetization fixed during manufacturing. The other is the free layer. Its magnetization can point in the same direction as the reference layer or the opposite direction. These two states are called parallel and antiparallel. This is a nonvolatile memory because both states are stable without power.

Reading relies on tunnel magnetoresistance (TMR). The barrier is thin enough for electrons to tunnel through, and they tunnel more easily when the two layers are parallel. The antiparallel orientation is typically two to three times higher resistance than the parallel orientation.

According to recent reports, A sense amplifier compares the cell current against a reference and returns a 1 or a 0. That gap is small, which is why MRAM designs typically run error-correcting code (ECC) on every read.

Most embedded MRAM uses spin-transfer torque (STT) for the write operations. The write circuit drives a large current through the junction, and the electrons become spin-polarized as they pass through a magnetic layer. They carry that angular momentum into the free layer and set the magnetization direction. Reverse the current and the bit flips back. The bit cell is one access transistor and one MTJ, as shown in Figure 2.

Embedded flash scaling didn't stall because the transistors became too small. It stalled due to voltage. The oxide for the flash memory must be roughly 8 nm to 10 nm thick, or the stored charge leaks away. Pushing electrons through oxide that thick takes about 10 V, but a 22 nm logic process runs its core below 1 V. Creating the 10 V on chip requires charge pumps and special high-voltage transistors, and neither shrinks with the rest of the logic.

Industry observers note that manufacturing makes it worse. Integrating a flash cell into a CMOS logic process adds 9 to 18 extra masks at 28 nm, according to figures reported by Semiconductor Engineering. The flash cell also does not integrate well with FinFET transistors. As a result, embedded flash is widely available down to 28 nm but rare below it.

Foundries now offer embedded MRAM at 28 nm, 22 nm, and 16 nm. For example, Renesas builds its RA8P1 microcontrollers on TSMC's 22 nm process with up to 1 MB of MRAM. NXP has unveiled that its S32K5 automotive microcontrollers use MRAM on a 16 nm FinFET process.

Industry observers note that one limitation of Flash memory is that it wears out. Each program and erase forces charge through the oxide. The oxide accumulates damage until it can no longer hold charge adequately.

It has been revealed that MRAM switching moves no atoms and stores no charge, so the magnetic layers themselves do not wear out. That is how Everspin’s EMxxxLX Industrial STT-MRAM can specify unlimited read, write, and erase operations for the supported life of the product. Those devices also support 10 years of retention as a minimum.

TSMC specifies one million cycles for its 16 nm embedded MRAM. The write current stresses the thin MgO barrier, so designers of embedded memory must trade endurance against retention at high temperature. TSMC's 16 nm FinFET MRAM is therefore specified for one million cycles with 20-year retention at 150°C. This is still 10 times the endurance of flash.

MRAM is also faster than flash. TSMC reports average write pulses slightly over 30 ns and 6 ns read times for a 22 nm design tuned for speed. And there is no erase step. NXP says its 16 nm MRAM can update 20 MB of code in about 3 seconds, a job that takes flash about 1 minute.

Table 1 compares STT-MRAM with NOR flash.

Think about what your flash driver does today. It erases a whole sector, waits, and then programs it page by page. An MRAM driver simply overwrites data in place, and it can change a single word without needing to erase and rewrite its neighbors. Therefore, over-the-air updates finish faster, so your device spends less time half-updated. Production-line programming speeds up too.

Industry observers note that data logging benefits even more. With flash, your firmware buffers records in RAM, manages sector erases, and spreads writes with wear leveling. A power failure during a long erase can still corrupt data.

Industry observers note that with MRAM, each record goes straight to its final address in microseconds. The reduced time means a corresponding reduction in the likelihood of losing data due to a power failure.

Sources indicate that while 1 million write/erase cycles sounds like a lot, don’t skip the math when designing your application. Imagine an energy meter that saves its running total once per second. If you write to one fixed address in an embedded MRAM, you will exceed 1 million cycles in under 12 days.

Sources indicate that if you design your code to rotate across 1,000 different addresses, then the same memory lasts about 32 years. If you are writing only once an hour, a million cycles would allow your MRAM to operate for more than 100 years.

Before you commit to an MRAM design, you should make three datasheet checks that flash never asked of you:.

Let’s take a look at magnetic immunity first. A strong external field can disturb an MTJ, so vendors specify a maximum. TSMC reports ten-year immunity above 1,100 Oe at 25°C for its 22 nm MRAM. Compare the rating with any motors, magnets, or large inductors near your board.

Second, examine the retention specs at your maximum operating temperature, not at room temperature.

Third, solder reflow. If you program parts before assembly, the data must survive the reflow oven. TSMC's 22 nm MRAM retains data through six reflow cycles, but its speed-tuned variant gives up that capability.

If your part passes all three and your write rates fit its endurance, MRAM is the simpler memory to design with. Below 28 nm, embedded flash will rarely be on the menu anyway.

According to recent reports, MRAM stores data as a magnetic state, so it avoids the high voltages and extra masks that stopped embedded flash at 28 nm. It writes fast, needs no erase step, and has far higher endurance than flash. Before you pick a part, check its endurance, magnetic immunity, retention at temperature, and solder reflow rating.

Tech Report: If You Loved 'Yellowjackets,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The story of a high school girls’ soccer team that crashes into the wilderness and spends years fending off madness, starvation, and despair (and not always doing a very good job of any of those things) is equal parts funny and terrifying.
  • Based on the true story of a rugby team whose plane crashed in the Andes Mountains in 1972, Alive will satisfy anyone whose favorite part of Yellowjackets is the core premise: Survivors of a disaster are stranded in the wilderness without supplies, and have to figure out how—and, er, who—they’re going to eat.
  • The survivors are initially as calm and resourceful as someone could be under those circumstances.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yellowjackets is a vibe. The story of a high school girls’ soccer team that crashes into the wilderness and spends years fending off madness, starvation, and despair (and not always doing a very good job of any of those things) is equal parts funny and terrifying. The dual timelines build tension around the story’s many mysteries, and the complex characters (no one’s completely good or evil on this show) make for a lot of surprising plot swerves that feel grounded despite the supernatural implications all around them. If you’re looking for more of that specific flavor of horror, you should probably watch Alive.

Based on the true story of a rugby team whose plane crashed in the Andes Mountains in 1972, Alive will satisfy anyone whose favorite part of Yellowjackets is the core premise: Survivors of a disaster are stranded in the wilderness without supplies, and have to figure out how—and, er, who—they’re going to eat.

The survivors are initially as calm and resourceful as someone could be under those circumstances. They use the wrecked plane as shelter in the withering cold, they scavenge for anything that could be useful, and they ration out the only food they have: Some chocolates and a case of wine. But an early mistake leaves them without any food at all, and slowly they come to the sickening realization that their best chance at survival is to treat the corpses of their friends and families scattered around the crash site as a food source.

It has been revealed that there’s no supernatural aspect, but the story has a similar tone of desperation and despair as Yellowjackets. These are people determined to survive in an impossible situation, and they do things that no one outside of their shared experience could possibly understand. The real-life origins of the story add a sense of horror that more than matches the fictional “It” that haunts the girls of Yellowjackets; putting yourself into that very real experience makes it clear just how terrified everyone was. Rent Alive on Prime Video.

If you’re craving more cannibals, cults, and crazies at the mercy of nature itself, here are a few more movies you should check out.

If you want to watch a movie that is essentially an adaptation of Yellowjackets, check out Eden. Even though it was released years before the show, the stories are so similar (albeit largely gender-flipped) that the producers of Eden actually sued, claiming plagiarism (they lost). In the film, a men’s soccer team (and two women on the same plane) crash-land on a deserted island, and as they fight for survival, things descend into, yes, madness and cannibalism as the survivors suffer dwindling food and water supplies and the rise of two violently opposed factions. It’s not nearly as deeply imagined as Yellowjackets, and it doesn’t have the supernatural hints of the show, but if you want a truly similar story, it’s a good choice. Stream Eden on The Roku Channel, Hoopla, or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

According to recent reports, you obviously cannot discuss Yellowjackets without discussing Lord of the Flies, William Golding’s 1954 novel about a group of schoolboys who descend into brutality and savagery when they’re stranded on a deserted island. The book has been adapted many times, but the 1963 version directed by Peter Brook is still the best version. Brook managed to elicit remarkably naturalistic performances from his young actors, giving the story a realistic tone that is somehow more terrifying than any amount of horror vibes. Stream Lord of the Flies on Kanopy or rent it on Prime Video.

A slower and more haunting story, Picnic at Hanging Rock explores some of the same themes as Yellowjackets in an entirely different way. On Valentine’s Day in the year 1900, several students and teachers from an all-girls private school in Victoria, Australia, head to Hanging Rock for a picnic. Four students head off to explore and fall inexplicably asleep, and then three vanish, along with one of the teachers. Dreamy and drenched in dread, the story never offers any easy answers, and it explores themes of invading natural areas where you’re not wanted, burgeoning (and confusing) adolescent sexuality, and how our fear of the unknowable warps our perspective and often diminishes our humanity. Stream Picnic at Hanging Rock on HBO Max or rent it on Prime Video.

Recent findings suggest that you can never really go wrong with a Hitchcock film, and if you’re looking for another story about a disparate group of people forced to make terrifying decisions in order to survive, watch Lifeboat (based on a story by John Steinbeck). One of the director’s most underrated films, it’s the story of a group of survivors in a lifeboat after a German U-boat sinks their ship during World War II (including one survivor from the German boat). It’s a masterful suspense engine that’s not afraid to have its characters discuss the moral and ethical quandaries facing them as they struggle to survive and maintain their humanity under a constant threat of death. Stream Lifeboat on Hoopla or rent it on Prime Video.

If you love the supernatural aspects of Yellowjackets as the girls come to believe a force they call “It” is out in the woods, check out The Ritual. Four friends embark on a hike in the wilds of northern Sweden to honor their deceased friend. When one of them is injured, they leave the marked trail to take a shortcut through the forest—where they are soon forced to shelter in an abandoned cabin, just like the Yellowjackets—and things begin to slide into the terrifying when they encounter a cult worshipping an ancient deity that grants them immortality in exchange for human sacrifices. It’s as if the show was condensed to an hour-and-a-half and the terror quotient was turned way, way up. Stream The Ritual on Netflix.

Project Jupiter report returns online after developers’ legal threat

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A rendering of the planned Project Jupiter data centre campus in Santa Teresa, Upcoming Mexico, updated August 2026.
  • The New Mexico Environmental Law Centre and the Tech Initiative have put their investigative report on Project Jupiter back online.
  • The two groups first published the report on September 24.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A rendering of the planned Project Jupiter data centre campus in Santa Teresa, Upcoming Mexico, updated August 2026.

The New Mexico Environmental Law Centre and the Tech Initiative have put their investigative report on Project Jupiter back online. A legal threat from a law firm tied to the data centre’s developers had kept it offline for seven weeks.

The two groups first published the report on September 24. A letter demanding its retraction arrived within 24 hours, and the report came down while lawyers checked the claims.

An updated version went back up on November 12. After a review with outside advisers, the groups mentioned in a statement that they stand by what the report notes and the sources it rests on.

According to recent reports, project Jupiter is a roughly 1,400-acre data centre campus rising in Santa Teresa, a border town in Doña Ana County. Oracle will lease the site for 18 years, and OpenAI will be its main customer.

The campus is one of nine sites in Stargate, the Trump-backed $500bn AI venture that has sent data centre energy demand soaring.

In a recent development, doña Ana County commissioners approved up to $165bn in industrial revenue bonds for the project in September 2025. The report calls the sum record-setting, and claims backroom political dealing shaped the vote.

In a recent development, county officials had signed NDAs. A firm run by a former developer executive, meanwhile, won a state contract that let it scan millions of environmental records while a key permit was under review.

Recent findings suggest that if built, the campus could become Fresh Mexico’s top corporate polluter, the report finds. Its emissions could exceed those of Albuquerque, Las Cruces, and Santa Fe combined. A loophole written into state law in 2025 also frees the project from the state’s emission cuts until at least 2045.

In a recent development, the developers have changed their power prepares twice. Gas turbines gave way to a methane-powered fuel cell microgrid, and a redesign filed in October would cut annual emissions to 5.7 million tons. Even then, the report notes, the microgrid would emit more than PNM, the state’s largest electric utility.

Industry observers note that water is the sharpest local concern. The site sits in a drought-hit basin where a US Supreme Court settlement already forces cuts in groundwater pumping. Commissioners believed the campus would use an average of 20,000 gallons of water a day, the report says. Developers later told state officials the original turbine design needed an extra 1 million gallons daily.

In a recent development, oracle pushed back in a January statement. Drinking water use is capped at 20,000 gallons a day, the company remarked, and cooling water comes from non-potable commercial sources.

Sources indicate that the report also questions what the county gets back. Instead of property taxes, the developers will pay $360m over 30 years. Their only binding jobs pledge is 750 full-time and 50 part-time roles within three years of opening. They have already missed two required job reports, and the county issued a breach notice on November 11.

“The development of Project Jupiter will serve the few and sacrifice the many, but its development is not inevitable, and community opposition works,” said Maslyn Locke, senior staff attorney at the law centre.

In a recent development, the courts have pulled the project both ways. In August, the state Supreme Court paused the air permit process and halted pumping from a construction well. In September, it rejected both challenges and let permitting resume, Source NM reported.

Sources indicate that new Mexico’s attorney general has since opposed the federal permit for the gas pipeline that would feed the microgrid. His office is also probing allegedly fraudulent letters sent in support of the air permit. A hearing set for December 7 was vacated this month after the developers revised their application. No new date has been set.

It has been revealed that the report also lands amid a wider backlash. US voters backed nearly all of the roughly 40 ballot measures to curb data centres this November, Route Fifty reported. The industry’s appetite for grid capacity and water is stirring opposition in Europe too. Two Latest Mexico counties have passed moratoriums on future data centres.

For now, the revised air permit application sits with the Environment Department. Phase one of the project, including its microgrid, is due to finish in late 2028.

I like making little tools that do one thing well and thing finding clever ways to combine them. It's the ethos behind a lot of the little software projects I have over at Less Software.

One of the first ones I made was a tool called whereami. Tongue-in-cheekly, I wanted to pitch it as the natural compliment to whoami. It felt silly to me that I could run a quick command from the terminal for so many things, but I couldn't run one that taps into this capability.

In the pursuit to make that tool cross-platform, one of the things I found myself navigating were the differences between them. There's another handy framework macOS makes available to your system: MapKit. It's analgous to Google Maps and their API offerings, but native to the operating system.

It turns out it's pretty straightforward to build a CLI wrapper around that framework as well, so I made nearme (macOS only).

When I was doing my pseudo-sabbatical at the Recurse Center this past spring, I spent a lot of time hammering away at these little tools and finding ways to combine them. Someone told me that the work I was doing and sharing reminded them of this idea you only need to control three points of focus to do a magic trick.

That comment inspired me to make this list of "recipes" where I try to showcase different ways to combine these tools in surprising, useful and/or fun ways:.

But the one I want to write about specifically today is this "meet in the middle" idea.

I just showed you how you can use whereami and nearme to find coffeeshops (or anything you can find via Apple Maps) on your Mac. With a little piping and a convenient alias, you can help figure out a place to "meet in the middle" between you and and another point:.

In a recent development, there you go! No API keys or browser or accounts: just input a couple addresses and a few plausible bars come out on the other side.

It's three small tools, each doing one thing.

Industry observers note that whereami started life as a CLI that asks your operating system where you are. As of 0.4 it can also act like a reverse geocoder (on macOS):.

Industry observers note that looking up an address doesn't need location permission, because nothing is asking where you are. jq does the arithmetic. The -s flag slurps both JSON objects into an array, and the filter averages the coordinates:.

nearme searches for places around a set of coordinates using MapKit, the search engine behind Apple Maps. It reads coordinates from JSON on stdin, and it only cares about latitude and longitude. It has no idea those numbers came out of jq and not out of a GPS.

Averaging two coordinates is not the "real" way to find the middle, but over a few miles trying to find a place to meet for coffee it's close enough. What does matter is that the midpoint has no idea what's actually there.

Industry observers note that typing that pipeline more than once get annoying swiftly. It's more convenient to set it up as a function:.

Or if you're using fish, like me:.

Give it two addresses and something to look for. Anything after that goes straight through to nearme. Leave off the second address and it uses wherever you are right now, so middle "123 Main Street" coffee finds coffee between you and 123 Main Street. With only an address, it looks for a coffeeshop.

Both tools live under Less Software:.

Recent findings suggest that amazon’s Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale has officially started—but keeping track of the best discounts yet to land and figuring out which deals are worthwhile can be a challenge. As an alternative, you can have Alexa give you a heads-up about deals on products you already know you want to purchase, so you don’t have to spend time sorting through the noise.

It has been revealed that then head to the Alexa mobile app and go to More in the top left (the three horizontal lines) > Settings > Notifications > Amazon Shopping and toggle on Deal Recommendations under the Shopping Recommendations options. This ensures you’ll receive notifications for items that appear in your shopping activity.

If Alexa finds an upcoming deal on something in your Saved for Later, your Wish List, or in your Shopping Cart, you’ll receive a pop-up alert on your Echo Show display or see a yellow light ring on your Echo speaker. You can also ask, “Alexa, what are my notifications?” to hear a list of deals it has compiled thus far. You can also say "Alexa, let me know when [product name] goes on sale.".

It has been revealed that alexa can detect deals up to 24 hours in advance, so you can either ask it to remind you again when a deal starts or request that it buy the item when the deal goes live. Simply say, “Alexa, buy it for me,” and it’ll charge the default payment and send the item to the default delivery address on your account.

UN talks fail to agree rules for ‘killer robots’ and push the issue to 2028

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (465 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Thenextweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Palais des Nations, the United Nations office in Geneva.
  • UN talks on regulating lethal autonomous weapons, often called “killer robots”, ended in Geneva on Saturday without a treaty mandate.
  • Recent findings suggest that under the final decision, countries will “elaborate” an instrument on these weapons under international humanitarian law.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Palais des Nations, the United Nations office in Geneva.

UN talks on regulating lethal autonomous weapons, often called “killer robots”, ended in Geneva on Saturday without a treaty mandate. The 128 countries in the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons agreed to keep talking until 2028, Politico reported.

Recent findings suggest that under the final decision, countries will “elaborate” an instrument on these weapons under international humanitarian law. A group of government experts will report back in 2028. The decision does not mention a legally binding instrument, according to Politico.

According to recent reports, negotiators declared the deal at 4:30am on Saturday, after a week of talks, NPR reported. The rules they propose could be binding. They could also be optional.

It has been revealed that decisions need consensus, so Russia could block formal negotiations all week, Politico reported. It also kept out observers, including the European Union. The talks went ahead informally to get around its veto.

It has been revealed that on the first day, Russia objected to the agenda, NPR reported. Then the US proposed five more years of talks on optional guidelines. The Pentagon set up an Autonomous Warfare Command in October.

Two EU diplomats told Politico that the US, the UK, South Korea, Japan, Turkey and Israel also resisted binding rules. France called for a “hybrid document” with binding and non-binding parts. Germany backed an “international instrument” rather than a binding protocol.

In a recent development, countries that wanted rules, such as Ireland, Brazil, Belgium and Austria, softened their positions in the final hours. They feared leaving empty-handed, a Brazilian diplomat told Politico.

Sources indicate that before the talks, the International Committee of the Red Cross asked for binding rules within a year, NPR reported. The UN secretary-general and Pope Leo backed that call. The ICRC noted it regretted the outcome.

“You cannot hold a machine accountable for a violation of the law,” said ICRC legal adviser Georgia Hinds.

Ukraine, Russia, Israel and others use drones and robots in war, but say humans still have the final say, Politico reported.

In a recent development, stop Killer Robots is a coalition of more than 300 groups. It says armies have already tested or used such weapons in Ukraine and Gaza.

“Autonomous weapons technology, including AI in the targeting cycle, is being deployed on the battlefield,” remarked its executive director, Nicole van Rooijen.

According to recent reports, rain Liivoja of the Asia-Pacific Institute for Law and Security pointed to the missing binding instrument. With none in the decision, there may be no treaty by the end of 2028, he told Politico.

These 14 Latest Features Are Coming to iOS 27.3

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1485 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Apple has been beta testing iOS 27.3 since Nov.
  • Recent findings suggest that technically, anyone with a compatible iPhone can try out iOS 27.3 right now—assuming you enroll your Apple Account in the developer program.
  • According to recent reports, the iPhone Duo is Apple's first foldable smartphone, but also the company's first phone since the iPhone SE 3 to ship with Touch ID.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple has been beta testing iOS 27.3 since Nov. 3. While this enhancement isn't as large as iOS 27 proper, it's surprisingly feature-filled for a 0.3 update. This is only a beta, so anything could (and likely will) change before Apple officially debuts the update. But, as it stands, iOS 27.3 tests 10 new features—including one feature the company trialed in the previous beta.

Recent findings suggest that technically, anyone with a compatible iPhone can try out iOS 27.3 right now—assuming you enroll your Apple Account in the developer program. But a word of warning: Betas can be temperamental, and could be risky. As such, I'd recommend avoiding the beta until Apple releases the public beta, which comes after a bit more testing to iron out larger issues. Either way, make sure to make a full backup of your iPhone to a Mac or PC first, as issues with the beta could result in permanent data loss.

According to recent reports, the iPhone Duo is Apple's first foldable smartphone, but also the company's first phone since the iPhone SE 3 to ship with Touch ID. While it works well enough for unlocking your iPhone, it's still an adjustment for those of us used to Face ID. With iOS 27.3, Apple is now testing face unlock for the Duo—not Face ID, mind you. The Duo's front camera doesn't have the tech required to power Face ID or its secure protocols. Instead, this feature simply unlocks your iPhone Duo with a face scan. In addition, your Duo will still require Touch ID for Apple Pay and passwords, or after 45 minutes of inactivity. You can read more about this newly introduced feature here.

Recent findings suggest that iOS 27.3 also comes with a new setting that lets you lock your iPhone Duo by closing it—as you would expect from, say, a laptop—or, dare I say, a flip phone? Currently, closing the Duo seamlessly transitions what's on the massive screen to the smaller display, and you have to press the side button to lock the phone.

With watchOS 27, Apple released "Audio Intelligence," a newly introduced set of features for Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. Audio Intelligence uses the watches' new S11 chip, along with on-device AI and cloud-based AI, to run new features, like Sound Recognition and Shazam (music recognition).

With iOS 27.3, however, the manufacturer is now officially testing the other two Audio Intelligence features it originally declared with watchOS 27. First, there's Live Rewind: By double-clicking the watch crown, you can pull up a transcript of the last 15 seconds of a conversation. Siri Recap, on the other hand, displays summaries of conversations you had that day, in case you need a refresher on any chats you might have otherwise forgotten about,.

The company generated some controversy when it first announced these two Audio Intelligence features, since, on the surface, it sounds like these new Apple Watches are essentially spying on people all day long. According to Apple, however, that isn't really the case. The company indicates Audio Intelligence is private, and never records or stores any audio. No speakers are ever identified, and text results (both transcripts and summaries) are deleted automatically after a set period of time unless the user saves them to the Siri app. You can read more about how Audio Intelligence works here.

Sources indicate that despite their claims, I'm sure there will still be strong feelings surrounding these Audio Intelligence features. We'll have to see whether Apple can prove Live Rewind and Siri Recap aren't all that creepy throughout the iOS 27.3 beta process.

iOS 27.3 also introduces app actions for Siri AI. Apple is testing fresh abilities for Siri AI, including organizing files, planning events, or adding photos to albums. You could ask Siri to organize your Downloads folder, or delete files that haven't been opened in more than a year. You could ask Siri to find a coffee shop you went to last week, or to save an article to your Reading List in Safari. You could ask Siri to check your calendar and set up a time for an event based on when you're free. You can even ask the assistant to schedule, edit, or unsend messages.

For example, you could ask Siri AI to help you strategy a trip with your friends. You could ask the AI to put together a themed playlist in Apple Music, schedule a message to a group about an upcoming trip, organize the websites you've been visiting in Safari into a tab group, and, after the trip, ask Siri to move your best photos to your favorites album. These upcoming actions work in the following apps: Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. Developers can also add Siri AI app actions support to their own apps.

Sources indicate that apple started testing its new Health app with the iOS 27.2 beta, but pulled the redesign before the official release. Now, with iOS 27.3, the new app is back. The new Health app has a health dashboard for the first time, as well as new features like Health Age and movement assessments. It seems to be pulling from some popular competitor services, hopefully, for the better. For more on the new Health app, check out Lifehacker health editor Beth Skwarecki's explainer.

Recent findings suggest that continuing on the Health track, iOS 27.3 also introduces "Gym Strength." This is a newly introduced Fitness+ feature that offers a personalized four-week strength-training strategy. You can customize these plans to meet your goals, experience level, and schedule, and they adapt as you progress. You'll get recommendations based on your experience with exercises, reps, and sets, including video demos for exercises. You can access Gym Strength on both iPhone and iPad, and Apple Watches are optional—though you can log your progress with the wearable if you have it.

Sources indicate that apple is also testing a fresh Siri AI feature in Safari, that gives the bot access to entire webpages, including the parts of the site that aren't on-screen. Say you want to know all the gluten-free options on a menu on a restaurant's website, but only a portion of the site is actually in view. You could ask Siri to read you the gluten-free options, and it would pull from the whole page, even though you can only see part of it.

Recent findings suggest that vertical tabs have been a favorite among browser aficionados, as they give you more screen real estate in your browser while keeping your tabs off the side. Apple hasn't made the jump—until now. This feature works with iPads running iPadOS 27.3 as well as Macs running macOS 27.3.

Another latest Safari feature in testing is "Adaptive Dark Mode." This feature forces websites into a dark theme, if they don't have a native theme of their own. There are third-party apps that can do this, but this is the first time Apple has offered this feature built into Safari.

According to recent reports, apple is also testing latest StandBy experiences with iOS 27.3, which were previously only available on the iPhone Duo. When you turn your iPhone sideways while plugged in, you'll find new Analog and Digital Clock faces with new customization options. There's also a new Photos face, with the option to pull images from Shared Albums.

"Reachability" pulls your iPhone's display down towards the bottom of the screen, so you can access items towards the top of the display with one hand. It's a useful feature for those of us with massive iPhones, and now, there's no iPhone bigger than the Duo. With iOS 27.3, Apple is testing Reachability for its first foldable phone. It's a bit like the inverse of how Reachability presently works: You can swipe on the left or right side of your Duo's display to shift the other side of the screen towards your current position. If you're holding your Duo in your left hand, a swipe of the left side will pull the right side over to the left, and vice versa.

It has been revealed that apple is also rolling out fresh languages for Siri AI in iOS 27.3. Now, Apple's smart assistant supports Traditional Chinese, Vietnamese, Turkish, and Norwegian.

It has been revealed that if you have an Apple Intelligence-compatible iPad running iPadOS 27.3, you now have access to Siri Mode in Camera. As with iOS, you can open the Camera app on iPadOS to access Siri Mode, and ask Siri about your surroundings.

Recent findings suggest that if you watch videos in Apple Podcasts, you can find them in more sources than the Podcasts app. With the upcoming updates, you'll find these videos on Apple TV 4K, select smart TVs, your iPhone, iPad, Mac, and even in CarPlay. (Please don't watch video podcasts while driving.).
