#142571. AI Is Giving Optical Computing Another Shot

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 26m • 📚 Deep Dive (5183 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ieee ↗ Open Full Page

AI Is Giving Optical Computing Another Shot

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 26 min read (5183 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~26 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The push to cut AI inference’s energy use could pay off in unexpected ways.
  • In a recent development, data centers already use light in networking.
  • The idea of computing with light has been around for over 70 years, but until recently it’s remained largely in the realm of research.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The push to cut AI inference’s energy use could pay off in unexpected ways.

In a recent development, data centers already use light in networking. Startup Optalysis aims to use specially engineered waveguides to add computational capacity to the networking path, doing math while data is in transit.

The idea of computing with light has been around for over 70 years, but until recently it’s remained largely in the realm of research. Over the past few years, though, optical computing has emerged as a fast-growing industry: Market valuation of companies in this sector now totals US $2.22 billion, up from $0.4 billion in 2022. One projection suggests that the market will continue to grow exponentially in the coming years.

Recent findings suggest that the reason for this sudden surge will surprise no one: AI. In particular, AI inference—the process of using AI models to respond to user queries—has driven much of the construction of huge, power-hungry data centers, and relatively energy-efficient optical systems are seen as a potential way forward.

“Most of the interest in [photonics] is driven by the fact that AI inference has literally become limited by power, and in a rather striking manner,” notes Peter McMahon, associate professor of applied and engineering physics at Cornell University, in Ithaca, N.Y., who has researched optical computing for over a decade.

Recent findings suggest that optics, at least on paper, carries the promise of doing the same math as today’s GPUs at a drastically lower level of power. Switching from electronics to optics would be a pretty radical solution. Nevertheless, like mushrooms after a rainstorm, optical-computing startups are popping up in the United States, China, Germany, and Israel. And while competing against such GPU makers as Nvidia is an ambitious goal, the investment in optical computing has spurred development of complementary approaches, such as designing alternative AI algorithms, taking on scientific computing, and enhancing in-network computing.

Optalysys, based in England, is inserting optical-computing elements into the networking path, where data centers already use light. The company’s basic on-chip optical element, shown in the inset, is a Fourier transform calculator.Optalysys.

According to recent reports, “I think it would be good for the technology if many of these companies made a good run at it,” indicates Logan Wright, assistant professor of applied physics at Yale University, in New Haven, Conn., and a former postdoc in McMahon’s lab. “I think that the technology that will be developed through this would be really, really useful, and enable photonic systems that maybe don’t get on this wave of AI but would be capable of doing really quite special things.”.

Inference makes up the bulk of AI energy use. The industry is already spending billions of dollars designing advanced GPUs and other chips to run inference as efficiently as possible. At the heart of the inference computation is one operation, done countless times a second: matrix-vector multiplication.

It has been revealed that back in 1978, optical-computing pioneer Joseph W. Goodman and his coworkers proposed a method for doing matrix-vector multiplication with light. The setup was relatively simple. Let’s say a vector of length N needs to be multiplied by a matrix of size N by N. N light-emitting diodes, all in a row, encode the elements of the vector into the intensity of light—the brighter the light from an individual diode, the greater the value that diode encodes. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads out the light vertically, essentially copying the vector N times. The light then passes through an attenuator of N by N pixels. At each pixel, the light is attenuated according to the corresponding value at that location in the matrix. Passing the light through the attenuator performs the multiplication. Finally, a cylindrical lens oriented perpendicular to the first lens re-collects the light from each row, summing it up. The final vector is measured by a row of detectors.

VECTOR-MATRIX MULTIPLICATION The most computationally expensive part of common AI today is vector-matrix (or matrix-matrix) multiplication. For a vector of length N (here, N = 3), it takes N2 (here, 9) multiplication steps and three accumulation steps—multiple additions at once. The argument for why optics might be advantageous over electronics goes something like this: Multiplying a matrix of size N by N by a vector of length N takes N2 multiplication steps. In electronics, each multiplication takes some energy, so the total energy used scales as N2. In optics, however, the multiplication step is passive: As long as the matrix stays the same, passing light through the attenuator costs almost no energy. The only cost is encoding the vector into light and reading out the answer, but the vector is of length N, not N2. So the energy used will scale as N, not N2, as bigger vectors and matrices are multiplied.Since Goodman’s 1978 proposal, the quality of the available optical elements has improved dramatically. Indeed, in 2022, a team of researchers at Cornell led by McMahon demonstrated an optical neural network that consumed less than one photon of energy—approximately 2.5 x 10-19 joules—per multiplication operation. In a standard computer, a single multiply operation can take between 10-14 and 10-12 joules, which suggests that optics could possibly reduce energy use by a factor of 100,000.But McMahon cautions against such extrapolation. First, the cost of encoding data into optics was not included in the calculation. Even if the scaling is favorable with light, in practice it’s not just the scaling that matters, it’s also the coefficients. Let’s say the energy cost of doing one multiplication with electronics is 1 picojoule, and the cost to encode one vector element with optics is 1,000 picojoules. The electronic approach still wins if the length N of the vector is fewer than 1,000 elements.McMahon claims this example is not far off from reality: “One of the key questions is, How major do you have to make the system before you start winning? Lots of people have done this calculation for various kinds of neural networks. The very rough answer is somewhere between N equals 1,000 and N equals 10,000.”It’s also notable to keep in mind a computing principle known as Amdahl’s law.“Amdahl’s law shouldn’t even be called a law. It’s a simple piece of common sense,” McMahon says. “If you have something that’s going to accelerate a computation, and it can accelerate 90 percent of the code, but there’s 10 percent of the code that it can’t accelerate, then the maximum possible speedup you can get is 10x.”With AI inferencing, the point is to save energy, not time. But Amdahl’s observation still applies. What fraction of today’s AI inferencing code can be better handled with optics is a complicated question that varies by approach. But it’s not 100 percent. Matrix-vector multiplication, or matrix-matrix multiplication, is only part of the inference workload—there are other, nonlinear operations that need to be performed on the data.Taking all of these caveats into account, optical-computing companies today are aiming for a 10- to 80-fold improvement in energy efficiency over today’s GPUs. The question is whether they can deliver on that promise at scale before traditional electronics catches up to those gains.Bridging the gap in free spaceThe startup Lumai, based in Oxford, England, has taken perhaps the most direct inspiration from Goodman and his team. Lumai’s head of product, Phillip Burr, declares that a free-space approach, where the light travels through air rather than on-chip waveguides, is what will enable the firm’s tech to beat GPUs.Instead of the fixed attenuator used in Goodman’s proposal, Lumai is using a modern programmable device called a spatial light modulator—a pixelated membrane akin to a fancy liquid-crystal display that can modulate both the intensity and phase of light. The rest of the design is more sophisticated in practice but similar in principle to Goodman’s design: A vector is encoded into light, copied N times via a lens, passed through the spatial light modulator, collected with another lens, and the result is converted back to digital electronics. The electronics then handle the nonlinear functions. “A full vector-matrix multiply completes in a single optical cycle,” Burr says.To accurately compare the energy expenditures of the optical and GPU approaches, you must first specify which part of the workload you’re considering. Modern inference is often split into two phases: prefill, where the input query is processed and propagated through the model, and decode, where the output is generated one word (or token) at a time. Prefill is the more computationally intensive of the two. It basically involves doing vector-matrix multiplications for the same matrix over and over. Decode also involves vector-matrix multiplies, but not as intensively—the time-consuming part of decode is reading the necessary matrices in and out of memory. Vector-matrix multiplication with free-space optics Chris PhilpotThe Goodman optical computer is the simplest version of a photonic vector-matrix multiplier. Here, the vector elements are encoded into the intensity of light from three light sources, such as LEDs. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads the light vertically. The matrix elements are encoded into the opacity of an attenuator, such that when light passes through each pixel it is multiplied (attenuated) by that matrix value. Finally, another cylindrical lens collects the light horizontally, performing the accumulation step, and a photodetector measures the output vector. Lumai, and other companies in the space, are focusing on the compute-intensive prefill phase of inference. Lumai claims that its Iris Nova optical server, made available for evaluation in April 2026, is a proof of concept, and its next-generation Iris Aura server will do prefill using roughly one-tenth of the energy a GPU would use.The startup Neurophos, based in Austin, Texas, is putting a different spin on the Goodman computer design. To pack more punch into a small device, the company is leveraging its expertise in metamaterials—complex structures that can manipulate light at scales smaller than a single wavelength. The structures it has designed are bigger than a wavelength but still quite small—just several micrometers per side.“The equivalent of the optical transistor that you can get from standard silicon photonics today is like 2 millimeters long,” says Patrick Bowen, CEO of Neurophos. “You just can’t fit enough [of] them on-chip to get a compute density that remotely competes with the latest and greatest [that] TSMC [Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.] does.”Based in Austin, Texas, Neurophos is using tiny metamaterials packed onto a chip to manipulate incoming light for efficient vector-matrix multiplication.NeurophosBowen’s team designed metamaterial-based modulators that can be programmed to manipulate the phase and intensity of light at the micrometer scale, resulting in an array of 1,000 by 1,000 modulators in a square chip with 5-mm sides. According to Bowen, Neurophos’s modulators switch over 10,000 times as fast as a standard liquid-crystal spatial light modulators do.Bowen also claims a performance advantage over Nvidia’s Blackwell GPU: “We’re targeting 50 times Blackwell B200’s speed and 35 times its energy efficiency, and have a road map to reach 250 times the speed and roughly 90 times the energy efficiency in subsequent generations.”The approach is CMOS-compatible, Bowen says, which should allow Neurophos to manufacture its chips on the semiconductor industry’s existing high-volume production lines. The company is currently choosing a site for a production facility ahead of its rack deliveries to customers in 2028.Both Lumai and Neurophos are betting they’ll get their products to market before traditional CMOS can catch up to their energy savings. “Silicon will keep improving, but digital efficiency gains now come slowly and at rising cost,” Burr says. “Optics offers a different scaling relationship, in which efficiency improves as matrices grow. Larger models, longer context windows, and agentic workloads are all pushing prefill in that direction.”Bridging the gap on-chipFree-space optics carries the promise of almost energy-free multiplication, as in Goodman’s design. But another big advance in optics since Goodman’s work in the 1970s is integrated photonics, which allows you to guide and manipulate light on-chip.“The name of the game is to do as large a vector size as possible to maximize the benefit of using optics, and for that reason the free-space approaches are promising,” says Yale’s Logan Wright. “But it’s still fundamentally harder” to use the free-space approach, “because there’s just so much less infrastructure than in silicon photonics.”Other companies—like Shanghai-based Lightelligence and Q.ANT, based in Stuttgart, Germany—are trading the 3D advantage of free-space optics for the manufacturability of photonics integrated directly onto a silicon chip.“There is a good reason that free-space optics are usually limited to 1,000 units a year,” says Q.ANT’s CEO and founder, Michael Förtsch. “The reason for this is lens inspection, assembly strategy, and so on. Semiconductor-manufacturable integrated photonic circuits are at this point way more promising to reach volume production.” Vector-matrix multiplication with integrated photonics Chris PhilpotOne way to do vector-matrix multiplication with light on-chip involves encoding vector elements into the amplitudes of pulses of light, traveling sequentially through a waveguide. The multiplication is performed by Mach-Zehnder interferometers: A waveguide splits in two, and the phase of light traveling through one of the paths is shifted by a controlled voltage. When the two paths reunite, the resulting light intensity depends on that phase shift, performing a multiplication. Encoding the matrix elements into the phase shifts turns this into vector-matrix multiplication. A photodetector then collects the light from all three pulses, performing the accumulation step.

According to recent reports, the most computationally expensive part of common AI today is vector-matrix (or matrix-matrix) multiplication. For a vector of length N (here, N = 3), it takes N2 (here, 9) multiplication steps and three accumulation steps—multiple additions at once.

The argument for why optics might be advantageous over electronics goes something like this: Multiplying a matrix of size N by N by a vector of length N takes N2 multiplication steps. In electronics, each multiplication takes some energy, so the total energy used scales as N2. In optics, however, the multiplication step is passive: As long as the matrix stays the same, passing light through the attenuator costs almost no energy. The only cost is encoding the vector into light and reading out the answer, but the vector is of length N, not N2. So the energy used will scale as N, not N2, as bigger vectors and matrices are multiplied.

In a recent development, since Goodman’s 1978 proposal, the quality of the available optical elements has improved dramatically. Indeed, in 2022, a team of researchers at Cornell led by McMahon demonstrated an optical neural network that consumed less than one photon of energy—approximately 2.5 x 10-19 joules—per multiplication operation. In a standard computer, a single multiply operation can take between 10-14 and 10-12 joules, which suggests that optics could possibly reduce energy use by a factor of 100,000.

But McMahon cautions against such extrapolation. First, the cost of encoding data into optics was not included in the calculation. Even if the scaling is favorable with light, in practice it’s not just the scaling that matters, it’s also the coefficients. Let’s say the energy cost of doing one multiplication with electronics is 1 picojoule, and the cost to encode one vector element with optics is 1,000 picojoules. The electronic approach still wins if the length N of the vector is fewer than 1,000 elements.

McMahon says this example is not far off from reality: “One of the key questions is, How big do you have to make the system before you start winning? Lots of people have done this calculation for various kinds of neural networks. The very rough answer is somewhere between N equals 1,000 and N equals 10,000.”.

It’s also notable to keep in mind a computing principle known as Amdahl’s law.

According to recent reports, “Amdahl’s law shouldn’t even be called a law. It’s a simple piece of common sense,” McMahon notes. “If you have something that’s going to accelerate a computation, and it can accelerate 90 percent of the code, but there’s 10 percent of the code that it can’t accelerate, then the maximum possible speedup you can get is 10x.”.

It has been revealed that with AI inferencing, the point is to save energy, not time. But Amdahl’s observation still applies. What fraction of today’s AI inferencing code can be better handled with optics is a complicated question that varies by approach. But it’s not 100 percent. Matrix-vector multiplication, or matrix-matrix multiplication, is only part of the inference workload—there are other, nonlinear operations that need to be performed on the data.

It has been revealed that taking all of these caveats into account, optical-computing companies today are aiming for a 10- to 80-fold improvement in energy efficiency over today’s GPUs. The question is whether they can deliver on that promise at scale before traditional electronics catches up to those gains.

Sources indicate that the startup Lumai, based in Oxford, England, has taken perhaps the most direct inspiration from Goodman and his team. Lumai’s head of product, Phillip Burr, declares that a free-space approach, where the light travels through air rather than on-chip waveguides, is what will enable the organization’s tech to beat GPUs.

Industry observers note that instead of the fixed attenuator used in Goodman’s proposal, Lumai is using a modern programmable device called a spatial light modulator—a pixelated membrane akin to a fancy liquid-crystal display that can modulate both the intensity and phase of light. The rest of the design is more sophisticated in practice but similar in principle to Goodman’s design: A vector is encoded into light, copied N times via a lens, passed through the spatial light modulator, collected with another lens, and the result is converted back to digital electronics. The electronics then handle the nonlinear functions. “A full vector-matrix multiply completes in a single optical cycle,” Burr says.

To accurately compare the energy expenditures of the optical and GPU approaches, you must first specify which part of the workload you’re considering. Modern inference is often split into two phases: prefill, where the input query is processed and propagated through the model, and decode, where the output is generated one word (or token) at a time. Prefill is the more computationally intensive of the two. It basically involves doing vector-matrix multiplications for the same matrix over and over. Decode also involves vector-matrix multiplies, but not as intensively—the time-consuming part of decode is reading the necessary matrices in and out of memory.

The Goodman optical computer is the simplest version of a photonic vector-matrix multiplier. Here, the vector elements are encoded into the intensity of light from three light sources, such as LEDs. Then, a cylindrical lens spreads the light vertically. The matrix elements are encoded into the opacity of an attenuator, such that when light passes through each pixel it is multiplied (attenuated) by that matrix value. Finally, another cylindrical lens collects the light horizontally, performing the accumulation step, and a photodetector measures the output vector.

Lumai, and other companies in the space, are focusing on the compute-intensive prefill phase of inference. Lumai claims that its Iris Nova optical server, made available for evaluation in April 2026, is a proof of concept, and its next-generation Iris Aura server will do prefill using roughly one-tenth of the energy a GPU would use.

The startup Neurophos, based in Austin, Texas, is putting a different spin on the Goodman computer design. To pack more punch into a small device, the company is leveraging its expertise in metamaterials—complex structures that can manipulate light at scales smaller than a single wavelength. The structures it has designed are bigger than a wavelength but still quite small—just several micrometers per side.

“The equivalent of the optical transistor that you can get from standard silicon photonics today is like 2 millimeters long,” claims Patrick Bowen, CEO of Neurophos. “You just can’t fit enough [of] them on-chip to get a compute density that remotely competes with the latest and greatest [that] TSMC [Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.] does.”.

Based in Austin, Texas, Neurophos is using tiny metamaterials packed onto a chip to manipulate incoming light for efficient vector-matrix multiplication.

Bowen’s team designed metamaterial-based modulators that can be programmed to manipulate the phase and intensity of light at the micrometer scale, resulting in an array of 1,000 by 1,000 modulators in a square chip with 5-mm sides. According to Bowen, Neurophos’s modulators switch over 10,000 times as fast as a standard liquid-crystal spatial light modulators do.

Bowen also claims a performance advantage over Nvidia’s Blackwell GPU: “We’re targeting 50 times Blackwell B200’s speed and 35 times its energy efficiency, and have a road map to reach 250 times the speed and roughly 90 times the energy efficiency in subsequent generations.”.

The approach is CMOS-compatible, Bowen says, which should allow Neurophos to manufacture its chips on the semiconductor industry’s existing high-volume production lines. The organization is right now choosing a site for a production facility ahead of its rack deliveries to customers in 2028.

Recent findings suggest that both Lumai and Neurophos are betting they’ll get their products to market before traditional CMOS can catch up to their energy savings. “Silicon will keep improving, but digital efficiency gains now come slowly and at rising cost,” Burr notes. “Optics offers a different scaling relationship, in which efficiency improves as matrices grow. Larger models, longer context windows, and agentic workloads are all pushing prefill in that direction.”.

Free-space optics carries the promise of almost energy-free multiplication, as in Goodman’s design. But another significant advance in optics since Goodman’s work in the 1970s is integrated photonics, which allows you to guide and manipulate light on-chip.

It has been revealed that “The name of the game is to do as large a vector size as possible to maximize the benefit of using optics, and for that reason the free-space approaches are promising,” indicates Yale’s Logan Wright. “But it’s still fundamentally harder” to use the free-space approach, “because there’s just so much less infrastructure than in silicon photonics.”.

Other companies—like Shanghai-based Lightelligence and Q.ANT, based in Stuttgart, Germany—are trading the 3D advantage of free-space optics for the manufacturability of photonics integrated directly onto a silicon chip.

Industry observers note that “There is a good reason that free-space optics are usually limited to 1,000 units a year,” notes Q.ANT’s CEO and founder, Michael Förtsch. “The reason for this is lens inspection, assembly strategy, and so on. Semiconductor-manufacturable integrated photonic circuits are at this point way more promising to reach volume production.”.

One way to do vector-matrix multiplication with light on-chip involves encoding vector elements into the amplitudes of pulses of light, traveling sequentially through a waveguide. The multiplication is performed by Mach-Zehnder interferometers: A waveguide splits in two, and the phase of light traveling through one of the paths is shifted by a controlled voltage. When the two paths reunite, the resulting light intensity depends on that phase shift, performing a multiplication. Encoding the matrix elements into the phase shifts turns this into vector-matrix multiplication. A photodetector then collects the light from all three pulses, performing the accumulation step.

In Q.ANT’s approach, the input data is encoded into the phase and amplitude of light pulses via on-chip modulators. A vector in this scheme is represented as a sequence of such pulses, each representing one vector element. The light is guided around the chip with waveguides. The basic computational element is an interferometer: A waveguide splits into two paths, and the light beam traveling down one path is subjected to a phase shift, controlled by a set voltage. When the two paths recombine, the resulting interference performs a computation. Then, photodetectors and analog-to-digital converters turn the result back into digital data. The serialized vector-matrix multiplication approach is slower than Goodman’s computer, where the whole calculation happens at once. However, the slower speed can be mitigated by using multiple wavelengths at once, effectively encoding multiple vectors into light simultaneously.

Recent findings suggest that Q.ANT’s Native Processing Server is already being used in research institutions like the Leibniz Supercomputing Centre in Munich and the Jülich Supercomputing Centre in Jülich, both in Germany. Earlier this year, the organization revealed a commercial sale to the cloud provider Ionos. Similarly, Lightelligence’s PACE2 processor is capable of multiplying 128-by-128-element matrices. In a paper released in 2025, the company described vector-matrix multiplication at a 1-gigahertz frequency and 3-nanosecond latency, claiming two orders of magnitude lower latency than with traditional GPUs.

The energy advantage is yet to be conclusively demonstrated, however, and Q.ANT’s Förtsch admits there is still a ways to go. The main glitch is the energy cost of analog-to-digital conversion and back. As long as a fast, low-energy converter does not exist, Förtsch notes, “we don’t see realistic chances that…a general vector-matrix multiplication machine in optics makes sense.”.

Not everyone in the field is focused on matrix-vector multiplication, despite it being all the rage in the AI inference world. In fact, while the optical vector-matrix multiply idea goes back to the 1970s, other computations with optics have been investigated as far back as the 1950s. For example, a Fourier transform—a common operation that decomposes a complex wave or signal into its constituent frequencies—can be done in optics with a single lens.

Industry observers note that “A digital chip has to approximate [Fourier transforms] in many small steps, using hundreds to thousands of transistors and more compute cycles,” states Q.ANT’s Förtsch. “Models that use such nonlinear functions can reach the same or better accuracy with fewer parameters and fewer operations.”.

Even though Q.ANT’s optical processor has been used for traditional vector-matrix multiplication, the company believes its greatest advantages lie in alternative AI architectures that leverage more complex functions. “Tasks such as image classification and segmentation rely heavily on operations like Fourier series, transformations, and other nonlinear functions, which photonics handles natively. We see similar potential in generative AI, especially image and video generation,” Förtsch indicates.

In a recent development, the Israel-based startup LightSolver is also targeting algorithms that are a more natural fit for its device. “If you look at propagating electromagnetic waves, essentially, they are running differential equations in their nature,” claims Ruti Ben-Shlomi, CEO and cofounder of LightSolver. She says differential equations can be solved much faster and with higher energy efficiency on the firm’s laser processing unit (LPU) than on a traditional computer.

LightSolver’s LPU is an interesting twist on the Goodman optical-computer design. It has input light, a programmable membrane in the form of a spatial light modulator, and output light, but the whole thing is placed in a cavity, where light bounces back and forth many times before reaching a steady state. In addition, the team places a gain medium inside the cavity. This gain medium functions much like those found inside a laser, causing the bouncing light to build up in intensity.

LightSolver, a startup based in Israel, is using free-space optics to promptly solve differential equations by harnessing the natural properties of light. LightSolver.

Sources indicate that lightSolver’s team is currently working on AI applications for its LPU as well, using the organization’s own algorithm to do image generation from text. “We’re not doing vector-matrix multiplication very fast. We are doing something different. We need to assume that the way you train the model, and you then do inference, is completely different. But if you do it differently, you’ll be able to do image generation with dramatic energy-consumption decrease and speedup,” Ben-Shlomi says. LightSolver has a working prototype of its LPU, and the team is working on a larger, rack-mountable box.

In a recent development, yet another way to leverage light’s particular strengths is being pursued by Optalysys, a startup based in Leeds, England. Nick New, founder and chief product officer, has a background in free-space optics, and so he understood that taking a Fourier transform is very easy to do with light.

The key idea behind Optalysys’s technology is taking that Fourier capability of optics in free space and making it work on-chip. “Rather than using a lens these days, we have our own component, which is a passive component in the plane of the silicon that does that same job,” Fresh states. And by cleverly designing that component with multiple outputs, the team figured out how to perform different operations as well. “Because of how the Fourier transform response is generated, you can actually pull out different mathematical operations from it,” New says. “We can produce very large, high-precision digital functions at superhigh efficiencies, using our analog photonics approach.”.

“We’re effectively adding processing to where there is none right now.” —Nick Latest, Optalysis.

According to recent reports, instead of redesigning an accelerator from scratch, Optalysys is targeting a piece of the AI workload that’s often already in the optical domain: networking. In the data center, racks of computers are connected to each other with fiber optics, and the optical connections are increasingly getting closer and closer to the GPUs and CPUs themselves.

Recent findings suggest that some computations already happen while the data is en route. These computations, which include combining results from multiple GPUs, are executed inside network switch cards. But the cards naturally use power to do that math. With passive optical components, these computations could be done essentially for free.

Sources indicate that new says that in addition to communication between GPUs, Optalysys’s technology could be used to facilitate a GPU’s communication with memory, doing things like compression and format conversion on the fly. Going back to AI inference, this approach could improve the decode part of the workload. Unlike prefill, decode is memory bound: The most costly part is shuffling model data in and out of memory. “We’re more focused on the memory-bound applications, which fits very well with this principle of adding processing into the communication path,” New says. “We’re effectively adding processing to where there is none right now.”.

Recent findings suggest that how likely are optical computers to replace GPUs in the data center? Yale’s Wright is not too optimistic. “The direction of algorithm development is not going to be a direction that is automatically favorable for optics,” he states. “In fact, it’s most likely to go in the opposite direction, because [AI model developers] want it to work better on GPUs.”.

It has been revealed that however, even if our AI queries aren’t going to be computed in light in the next few years, that investment in the technology won’t be in vain. Says Wright, “The reason that I and many other people in the field are at least somewhat optimistic is that there’s real investment from companies like Nvidia and TSMC in developing co-packaged silicon photonics—not for computing, but for circuit switching and interconnects, and that just kind of opens the door to do a little bit more in the future.”.

Whether that technology ends up crunching vector-matrix multiplication, doing bespoke simulations, or performing in-network computations, the computing ecosystem seems ripe for a variety of approaches. “We see the data center of the future as heterogeneous: CPUs, GPUs and photonic NPUs [native processing units] each take on the tasks they are best suited for,” states Q.ANT’s Förtsch. “Running each task on the most efficient hardware can significantly reduce energy use and operating costs.”.

Marlowe raises a $277M seed to run AI on chips that aren’t Nvidia’s

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that marlowe, a startup founded in May by former Convoy and Microsoft executives, has raised $277M in seed funding led by Accel at a $1.15B valuation.
  • In a recent development, marlowe, a startup that builds AI data centres around chips from companies other than Nvidia, has raised $277M in seed funding, it unveiled on Monday.
  • Bessemer, Altimeter, Atreides and Eclipse also invested, along with angels including Box CEO Aaron Levie and Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that marlowe, a startup founded in May by former Convoy and Microsoft executives, has raised $277M in seed funding led by Accel at a $1.15B valuation. It builds AI data centres for inference using a mix of chips from companies such as Etched and AMD, rather than Nvidia alone.

In a recent development, marlowe, a startup that builds AI data centres around chips from companies other than Nvidia, has raised $277M in seed funding, it unveiled on Monday. Accel led the round, which values the six-month-old company at $1.15B, GeekWire reported.

Bessemer, Altimeter, Atreides and Eclipse also invested, along with angels including Box CEO Aaron Levie and Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi.

Marlowe focuses on inference, the work of running AI models for customers. It argues that demand is outgrowing supply, and that relying on one chipmaker creates a bottleneck for the whole industry. It intends to match each type of AI task, such as coding agents or voice assistants, with the chips and data centre design that suit it best.

Recent findings suggest that its first site, built around chips from Etched, goes live in December and will mainly serve a large AI coding firm. A second site using AMD’s Helios racks is due in the second quarter of 2027. AMD has also backed TensorWave’s AI cloud, which runs only on its chips.

“Marlowe is a true partner that optimizes across our full stack,” noted Vamsi Boppana, AMD’s senior vice president of AI.

CEO Dan Lewis co-founded freight startup Convoy, and CTO Kutta Srinivasan led AI infrastructure at Microsoft. Marlowe says tuning every layer of its stack can deliver a two- to three-fold edge in performance and cost. Investors are betting big on cheaper inference: chipmaker SambaNova reached an $11B valuation in July, and Nebius paid $643M for 20-person Eigen AI.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo have been out for quite some time now, and despite that, it’s still incredibly challenging to order an iPhone Duo in a timely manner. If for whatever reason you’re considering skipping out on this year’s iPhones, here’s what you have to look forward to next year.

2027 is going to be a relatively big iPhone release year for Apple. First, the tech giant will be continuing the iPhone 18 lineup after it introduced a split release schedule. Then, in the fall, the company will debut a newly introduced round of flagships in celebration of the 20th anniversary of the iPhone. Here’s what to expect.

Industry observers note that for the first time, Apple will be introducing its base iPhone in the spring. Upgrades for the iPhone 18 aren’t quite clear, though more RAM is one of the key rumors. Thermal upgrades will likely happen as well, as well as the new Apple C2 modem.

It’s possible Apple will revision the design to fall more in line with the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro, though we don’t yet know.

This phone will of course equip the A20 chip, and it’ll probably start at the same $899 price point that iPhone 17 at the moment sits at – after it was increased from $799 in September.

It has been revealed that this phone will most likely just end up being a chip bump from the A19 to A20 chip, and debut in the Spring alongside the iPhone 18. Earlier this year, reports indicated that Apple would share many components between the iPhone 18 and iPhone 18e, though it isn’t quite clear what that could mean for the devices.

Out of all of the spring iPhone releases, this one is the one to look forward to. After receiving a lukewarm reception with the initial iPhone Air model, Apple went back to the drawing board and decided to modify the design to fit an ultrawide camera into the device.

Personally, I don’t think an ultrawide camera is too vital – though many people will see one camera on the back of the phone and immediately assume it’s less premium, so it’ll probably end up being an important upgrade for the sake of sales. Plus, ultrawide photos can be fun at times.

It should also have a larger battery, reportedly as large as 3500mAh. That’s a roughly 10% improvement from the original iPhone Air. iPhone Air 2 will likely also jump from Apples C1X modem to the C2.

In a recent development, for the 20th anniversary of the iPhone, Apple is expected to debut a fully redesigned iPhone to celebrate. It’ll reportedly be much more glassy, feature significantly slimmer bezels, a quad curved display, and ditch the flat edge design of the iPhone 12 and later.

According to recent reports, personally, I’m slightly skeptical that this’ll truly be a replacement to the “Pro” phone for thermal reasons, but time will tell. iPhone Duo seemingly has strong thermals while not featuring an aluminum unibody, so my concern might not be relevant. It’ll offer two, larger display sizes: 6.4-inch and 7-inch. This largely comes from the bezel reduction.

It has been revealed that I wish they prioritized the Telephoto camera more. I need that (whether it be on an Air or a Duo) way more than an Ultrawide.

If you’re holding out for iPhone 18 Pro, this “iPhone 20” is definitely the phone to wait out for.

Lastly, Apple will release a successor to its just-announced iPhone Duo next fall. Of course, you can expect next-generation Apple Silicon with the A21 Pro chip next year, but there aren’t many other substantial changes expected. Apple may bring proper Face ID to the outer display, an improvement from the recently-announced face unlock, but it’s unclear whether this feature will make the engineering cutoff date.

#142563. The next circle of security hell

📅 27 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (720 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Gentoo ↗ Open Full Page

The next circle of security hell

📅 27 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (720 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gentoo

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A few years back I wrote “The modern packager’s security nightmare”.
  • The point is that nowadays everyone and their chatbot became security researchers.
  • It has been revealed that in the end, security is tricky.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A few years back I wrote “The modern packager’s security nightmare”. Have things improved since? On the contrary, I feel like we’re slipping down a well-oiled slope with no end in sight. Vulnerabilities are reported at unprecedented rates. A lot of people are doing everything they can to patch them up, which doesn’t necessarily mean they’re not making things even worse. Complex software involves complex trees of dependencies, and every branch on that tree needs tending to. When they stop being reliable, people further down the tree start taking more weight. And there’s a limit of how much a single person can do, so what started as an effort to resolve an glitch upstream may rapidly become a weakness. Is software less secure these days? It’s tempting to say yes. I’d love to blame the corporate sector for egotistically dumping low quality software on us. I’d love to blame marketing-oriented people developing stuff with the sole goal of making a profit. I’d love to blame Rust for getting people obsessed about memory safety, and ignoring the kinds of vulnerabilities that aren’t caught by the compiler. Finally, I’d really love to blame slop. But the truth is, I don’t know. That’s really beside the point.

The point is that nowadays everyone and their chatbot became security researchers. Projects are being flooded with vulnerability reports. Even though pretty much every bug bounty was discontinued because of slop, people aren’t stopping. And even if we disregard truly invalid junk reports, there’s a lot left, and you have to deal with them somehow. You have to figure out how important they are, and how to fix them (or more likely, whether the fixes submitted are truly valid and don’t introduce regressions), or if you should reject them and why.

It has been revealed that in the end, security is tricky. We’re seeing lots of bugs like REDoS, or other kinds of “performance bugs”. Are they really vulnerabilities? Well, it depends on the attack vector. And that in turn depends on how the software is used. Some scenarios are really contrived, and feel like “shell can execute dangerous commands if you type them in”. But then, you also have really serious issues such as “timing attack can be used to guess user’s secret”. You need to know a lot to make that kind of judgment, and sometimes your judgment doesn’t really match customers’ expectations.

Sources indicate that in the end, what can project maintainers do? Even if they have the expertise and the energy to judge, if they can “know better”, there’s likely a CVE assigned already. It may have absurdly high score. All security scanners will complain unless you fix it, and people will come asking or complaining, or attacking, or forking. I mean, technology can’t handle nuances. More than once I’ve been doing unnecessary security stabilizations over vulnerabilities that didn’t affect Gentoo (for example, because we already unbundled the vulnerable dependencies), to avoid false positives from security scanners. I’ve been also doing meaningless version bumps (with no real changes or no changes that applied to Gentoo) so that our packages don’t get reported as being “outdated”. It’s a hassle and it sucks, but it saves people from worrying.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve said this before and I’ll say it again: most projects aren’t really prepared to handle security issues. And it’s not just about triage. It’s about having LTS or security branches, it’s about making proper security releases with minimal changes. Unfortunately, it’s quite common for security fixes to be combined with new features, deprecations, API changes. In extreme cases, people are caught with their metaphorical pants down, and suddenly need to make a security release in the middle of a major rewrite, or along with barely tested new code. And then, people downstream discover that they need to quickly deal with major API changes to upgrade past a vulnerable version. These things keep piling up.

According to recent reports, what happens next? The community reaches a breaking point. People can’t keep up. You discover you can’t rely on others, so you work around them. You start bundling more stuff. Soon enough your workload goes beyond your ability. Software development becomes “every chatbot for itself”. The nightmare becomes worse, and the wheel keeps turning.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla Reality View in FSD v15, crossing the Golden Gate Bridge.

Recent findings suggest that tesla has started rolling out version 15 of its Full Self-Driving (Supervised) software, which it indicates upgrades every part of its end-to-end driving network. The company unveiled the update in a post on X on Saturday. It says v15 handles safety-critical cases 25 times better.

FSD v15 now starting to roll out – upgrading every part of the end-to-end driving network.

Safety 25x better handling of safety critical cases.

Tesla Reality View Adds a live visualization of the drive that lets you see & control what FSD is planning to do.

Navigation for start & end of the trip now learns end-to-end from fleet route preferences. Later v15 releases will expand this to the entire route.

You also should notice better detection of signs, animals, debris, potholes and standing water, plus more natural speed handling in school zones and inclement weather.

Lastly, FSD can now slow for speed cameras & Bike Rack Mode lets you enable FSD w/ bike racks or similar hitch accessories.

— Tesla (@Tesla) November 21, 2026.

The full release notes, posted by Tesla’s Super Intelligence account, tie the 25x figure to the critical intervention rate. They credit an upgraded vision encoder that FSD shares with Tesla’s Robotaxi and Optimus robot. Tesla trained it on millions of internet videos.

Industry observers note that the headline feature is Tesla Reality View. It streams a real-time generated view of the drive from a virtual camera above the car. Drivers can see and control what FSD plans to do, and upcoming turns appear in the view, the notes say. It replaces all the separate model signals with one visualisation that uses less total compute.

“This is real-time AI video generation (no gaming engine!) using just half of one AI4 TRIP accelerator,” Elon Musk wrote on X.

Industry observers note that the view runs about a second behind the road, TechRadar reported. Musk noted it combines a shrunken version of one of Tesla’s world models with a diffusion model, and that Tesla will soon cut the lag by 35%, according to TechRadar. Only cars with Tesla’s latest hardware get it.

Drivers have compared the view to GTA VI, which launched days earlier, TechRadar reported.

Sources indicate that navigation now learns from fleet route preferences at the start and end of a trip, and later v15 releases will extend that to the whole route. Parking draws on each driver’s history, and the map can show several spots. Tesla also lists better detection of road signs, small animals, debris, chains, potholes and deep standing water.

Recent findings suggest that FSD can now slow down for speed cameras. If a driver cancels twice at the same camera, the car saves it and stops slowing there. Bike Rack Mode lets drivers use FSD with a hitch accessory, with reversing, Autopark and Summon switched off. Attention monitoring works more often with hats and sunglasses, and is less strict in faster driver profiles.

Recent findings suggest that the software is still Full Self-Driving (Supervised), so drivers must keep watching the road. Tesla has also started carrying riders in Cybercabs and plans to build them in Berlin.

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • My sleep really took a toll when the clocks fell back this year.
  • According to recent reports, I spend a lot of time on my phone both socially and for work and those hours of screen time can have a negative impact on my sleep.
  • In a recent development, I've found that by amending the color of my screen I can mitigate some of the ill-effects that phone use can have — like waking up at night.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

My sleep really took a toll when the clocks fell back this year. I was feeling agitated at bedtime, waking up at 3 a.m., and feeling groggy when my alarm clock went off. That was until I looked at how I was spending my evenings — bathing in the blue glow of my phone as I scrolled into the night.

According to recent reports, I spend a lot of time on my phone both socially and for work and those hours of screen time can have a negative impact on my sleep. However, I have stumbled upon a free iPhone setting that has helped me sleep through the night.

In a recent development, I've found that by amending the color of my screen I can mitigate some of the ill-effects that phone use can have — like waking up at night. I caught up with board-certified physician Dr. John La Puma whose work delves into modern exhaustion and how food, light and outdoor protocols impact it.

As a sleep writer I'm precious about my bedtime routine. I begin with a dark shower, make a herbal tea, and get into bed by 9 p.m. without fail most nights. But, as the evenings got darker and I began spending more time indoors, I found it harder to shut off to sleep and experienced more fragmented sleep through the night, no matter how well I thought I was preparing to rest.

I'd be tossing and turning and then wide awake at 3 a.m. which made for some pretty grumpy mornings. So I was determined to find the cause (and solution) to save my rest this winter.

Eventually, I pinpointed the change in my routine: increased screen time in the evenings. Whereas in the summer I tend to spend the evenings outdoors, as the nights got darker and longer, I was passing more time glued to emails, chatting in the group chat, or hooked on Instagram reels.

Sources indicate that surrendering to the fact I'm not going to eliminate all evening screen time, I've made it my mission to minimise the affect my iPhone has on my sleep. Alongside Wind Down and Sleep Schedule, I recently found the Apple's Night Shift mode.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

In a recent development, this setting automatically adjusts the colors of your display to the warmer end of the spectrum. Instead of bright white light, it indicates a warmer tone, making the display easier on your eyes.

Dr. La Puma explains bright, blue-rich light has the biggest impact on tricking your brain into staying awake and alert. So, swapping this for a dimmer, warmer light should make you feel sleepier in the evenings, prevent cortisol spikes, and improve overall sleep outcomes.

"Your brain reads evening light as daytime".

But he states, it's vital to dim your screen in the evening as well as putting on Night Shift mode (the mode only changes the tone of the light; it doesn't tamper with the actual brightness level.).

This isn't my first brush with Apple's sleep features. I've already set up my Sleep Schedule, turned on Sleep Focus, and made sure I get a reminder to prioritise sleep at 9:45 p.m. every night (15 minutes prior to my desired sleep time). However, the Night Shift mode is super useful now the evenings are darker and longer. It helps mitigates the effect of that bright white light I'd get from my phone between sundown and bedtime.

Activating Apple Night Shift is simple. Head to your iPhone settings app. Locate 'Display & Brightness' tab. Click into 'Night Shift' and toggle on 'Scheduled'.

Industry observers note that you can then choose to set a custom schedule – so it turns on between 7 p.m. and 7 a.m., for example – or automate the schedule to the actual sunset and sunrise. This way your screen will change as soon as the sunsets and return to white light when the sunrises.

Recent findings suggest that there's also options to manually enable Night Shift, and you can adjust your color temperature. Switch it one manually and you'll immediately see the difference it makes to your screen.

But there are two precautions from Dr. La Puma. First, "Night Shift warms the color of the screen. It does not dim it, and brightness matters as much as color.".

Switch on Night Shift, then also "turn brightness all the way down" and "put the phone in another room an hour before bed," advises the Californian sleep doctor. "That is what helps.".

Second, he claims, "What you are reading or watching keeps you alert too." Whether it's fast paced TikToks or overwhelming news feeds, the content you consume around bedtime can keep your mind ticking when it should be winding down.

Therefore, it's worth considering that late night stimulation for relaxing sleep sounds (our sleep writer, Frances Daniels, has been enjoying Apple's free sleep sounds feature lately) or guided meditations.

In a recent development, it's just light, how harmful can it be to your sleep? Well, light is actually a key in your circadian rhythm. It has the power to reset your body clock in the mornings and delay sleep onset in the evenings.

This is all down to the hormone cycles it controls. Bright light suppresses melatonin (the hormone that makes you feel sleepy) and increases cortisol (the hormone that makes you feel alert.) Therefore, too much bright light exposure around bedtime can cause 3 a.m. cortisol spikes, forcing you awake.

Spending too much time exposed to bright artificial light in the evenings can cause sleep problems because, as Dr. La Puma explains, "Your brain reads evening light as daytime." As such, it will suppress sleep-inducing hormones.

"Light reaches melanopsin cells in the retina, which signal the master clock to hold back melatonin. Bright, blue-rich light from overhead LEDs and screens does this most," he indicates.

It has been revealed that A 2011 study in the Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism found even ordinary room light before bed delayed melatonin and shortened its night by about 90 minutes. The result? "You feel wired at bedtime, fall asleep later and sleep more lightly," explains Dr. La Puma, who has written a whole book on how the 'indoor epidemic' can impact our sleep.

Great sleep doesn't always come naturally to everyone. Sometimes you need to tweak your habits and environment to help prepare your body for rest. Dr. La Puma has shared his top tips for giving yourself the best chance of getting quality slumber.

It has been revealed that if you want to take restricting your light consumption a step further, consider investing in some blue light blocking glasses from $15.99 now at Amazon. I've recently purchased some of these and am excited to test how effective they are. Early research in the Therapeutic Advances in Ophthalmology Journal shows promise in their ability to help protect sleep quality.

Sources indicate that the best sunrise alarm clock you can buy, the Hatch Sleep Clock is the ultimate gadget for regulating your circadian rhythm. By evening, a warm-toned sunset simulation sends you to sleep. By morning, gradually brightening light wakes you up. Now Black Friday sleep sales are here, you can grab $62.50 off the Hatch Sleep Clock. Just prepare to pay a $4.99/month subscription fee to access all features.

Industry observers note that I've spoken about swapping scrolling for reading around bedtime and the hooga red light clip will come in handier than you think. Easily clipping on your book, it helps promote melatonin production and means you needn't get up to turn off a lamp when you feel sleepy. Trust me, it's $12.99 wisely spent.

#142556. Why a Computer Scientist Thinks Superintelligence Won’t Happen

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 24m • 📚 Deep Dive (4709 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ieee ↗ Open Full Page

Why a Computer Scientist Thinks Superintelligence Won’t Happen

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 24 min read (4709 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~24 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction.
  • According to recent reports, these concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI).
  • These ideas have prompted varied reactions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yet trying for it may still be disastrous.

Industry observers note that many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction. It started when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon announced his resignation, warning that his employer and OpenAI were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s head of alignment science, replied, “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” And Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei subsequently told CNN, “I agree with Jacob much more than I disagree with him.”.

According to recent reports, these concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI). The result will be artificial superintelligence (ASI), a system with cognitive capabilities so vastly exceeding those of humans that it will easily evade our control and perhaps even wipe out our species. Artificial superintelligence is, it should be noted, a far more ambitious goal than artificial general intelligence (AGI), which generally refers to AI that can match human capabilities across a broad range of cognitive tasks.

These ideas have prompted varied reactions. Some argue that the concept of ASI is being used for marketing or to instigate regulation that will help the incumbent labs squash new competitors. Others focus on the plausibility of such systems killing us all, debating the finer points of specific scenarios such as AI-engineered superviruses. Still others claim that aligning ASI to human interests is feasible and so we should rush ahead to usher in this digital utopia.

Recent findings suggest that amid these conversations, one question has received comparatively little attention: From an engineering perspective, is superintelligence even possible? The answer is notable because it can help us calibrate our anxieties and develop the most effective possible responses to this emerging technology.

Sources indicate that I recently explored this topic in a computer science doctoral seminar that I taught at Georgetown University, in Washington, D.C., in which my students and I examined the technical and cultural roots of the superintelligence story. (For those who are interested, we published an annotated bibliography of our class readings.) I came away with several key objections to the feasibility of ASI, which I’ll detail below, as well as a deeper fear that even if the promised intelligence explosion never arrives, pursuing it can still create real harm.

RSI is an old concept. In a 1965 paper, statistician I.J. Good speculated that a rapid cycle of AI self-improvement could lead to an “intelligence explosion.” The idea gained traction in the 1990s among the Extropians, a Bay Area futurist group, where it offered a way to discuss ASI without having to address the engineering details of how one would build such a system. The concept was taken up by such notable figures as Eliezer Yudkowsky (who later founded the rationalism movement) and Nick Bostrom (who helped steer effective altruism to focus more on existential risks to humanity).

Recently, however, this topic has shifted from thought experiment to practical engineering within both Anthropic (makers of Claude) and OpenAI (makers of ChatGPT). In a June blog post titled “When AI Builds Itself,” Anthropic described how LLM-powered agents are speeding up the writing, debugging, and optimization of code, and also automating parts of research such as running experiments and logging results. The company’s internal data, the report concluded, “is showing that AI is already accelerating the development of AI systems.” OpenAI has been similarly explicit about its intentions; in a September report, the company announced a goal of developing an automated researcher by March 2028.

But do these efforts put the companies on a trajectory toward uncontrollable RSI? Several obstacles undermine this claim. Consider the availability of the data needed to improve AI systems. Through 2023, major advances in LLMs came from scaling up the size of the models. The original GPT-1 had 117 million parameters (values learned during training that shape how the neural network processes information). This quantity jumped to 1.5 billion for GPT-2, to 175 billion for GPT-3, to (likely) more than a trillion for GPT-4’s release three years ago. After GPT-4, however, continued scaling began yielding diminishing returns. This led engineers to increasingly turn their attention toward “post-training” phases, where techniques from reinforcement learning are applied to improve an already trained model’s performance on specific tasks. This approach rewards a model for producing successful responses, helping it better produce similar answers in the future. It requires, however, lots of examples of relevant inputs paired with correct outputs.

Such datasets are relatively easy to generate in highly structured fields such as computer programming and mathematics, which helps explain why we’ve seen rapid and impressive advances in these narrow domains. Progress in areas that lack easy access to this type of training data has been less dramatic. This might explain why AI can tackle advanced theorems but struggles to empty an email inbox. “What if the jagged frontier is mainly math + code (which you can push arbitrarily far with [reinforcement learning techniques]),” the French AI researcher François Chollet recently hypothesized, “and everything else starts to plateau because it is still bottlenecked by human generated data?” The deployment of automated coding agents and LLM-powered researchers won’t overcome this fundamental limitation.

Powerful, specialized AI tools bring major benefits, with constraints that make their behavior easier to predict and control.

Claims that RSI is imminent also understate the massive scientific efforts required for major AI advances. Consider the critical role of backpropagation, an algorithm that enables very large neural networks to learn by tuning internal parameters, layer by layer, to reduce errors in their predictions. This algorithm enabled the deep learning revolution, but it didn’t emerge ex nihilo in the minds of its creators. The influential 1986 paper on backpropagation by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams built on decades of critical breakthroughs in mathematics and computer science.

An intelligence explosion leading to ASI would similarly depend on a long sequence of innovations of comparable importance, which would build on many significant science and engineering advances that haven’t yet happened. This would require AI agents to somehow simulate, organize, and evaluate decades of worldwide scientific effort across numerous fields—an impossibly ambitious task. Indeed, recent research led by computer scientists at Princeton found that current AI tools had difficulty making autonomous progress even on highly constrained research questions. “Our results provide early evidence that today’s agents can do the engineering of AI research,” the researchers conclude, “but struggle with critical parts of the research life cycle.” The leap from this current reality to a future in which these same types of tools are automating science is almost too massive to imagine.

Industry observers note that finally, the RSI narrative downplays resource limitations. Tens of thousands of human brains have worked for decades, aided by increasingly powerful computers, to develop today’s AI systems, which can match human intelligence in some domains. That represents a massive investment in computation of both the biological and digital variety. What if the next intelligence level requires double the resources, and then the next level requires double again? Soon there would be no number of chips or data centers that we could build to provide the necessary compute and keep advancing toward ASI.

Industry observers note that pulling together these threads, I believe that the idea of RSI leading to an intelligence explosion is highly speculative and based on many unproven assumptions. While RSI isn’t definitively impossible, the idea demands more technical skepticism than it’s right now receiving. Carl Sagan’s adage that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence certainly applies here.

There’s an implicit claim in the superintelligence discourse that computers are theoretically capable of any calculation that can be imagined, so long as you can find a sufficiently smart algorithm, running on sufficiently powerful digital processors. In this context, RSI is merely a process for rapidly uncovering the special algorithms that can implement unimaginable smarts.

We cannot simply assume that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve.

But this is not how computer scientists think about computation. In his canonical 1937 paper, “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. His elegant proof established the space of possible problems to be uncountably infinite (like infinite precision decimal numbers), while the space of possible algorithms is only countably infinite (like whole numbers). Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. Theoretical computer scientists, in other words, don’t assume that computers will solve everything; we’re instead excited whenever we find something that these machines happen to be able to efficiently handle.

In a recent development, we cannot simply assume, as the futurists often do, that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. There might be some capabilities in which machines can obtain seemingly magical levels of performance, but there will also be many others that no machine, whether computer or human, will ever make much progress.

A relevant counterargument here emphasizes the speed of silicon chips compared to human neurons: Perhaps the sheer speed of digital computation can yield machines that run cognitive circles around our clunky brains, even if they’re not solving vastly more complicated problems than we’re already capable of tackling. But as the computer scientist and science fiction author Vernor Vinge pointed out, rapidity in cognition is not the same as intelligence. Speeding up the mind of a dog, he argued, wouldn’t enable the animal to play chess. Implementing roughly human-level intelligence on a faster machine might be impressive, but it’s not necessarily alarming.

At the moment, there’s a growing list of tasks that AI systems can perform better than humans, including winning complex games, identifying software bugs, and proving certain types of math theorems. It’s tempting to extrapolate from this specific progress to general mastery of every ability you might imagine. But it’s notable to remember that the frontier of AI capabilities has always been jagged, with some research directions yielding impressive results and many others proving to be dead ends—a reality that would not have surprised Turing. More likely than a future dominated by an all-powerful superintelligence system is one in which we continue to painstakingly explore the space of problems well suited to AI, creating useful tools but falling well short of the digital deity predicted by the futurists.

Cal Newport, a computer science professor at Georgetown University, is skeptical that AI can achieve superintelligence through recursive self-improvement.

Recent findings suggest that last fall, the prominent AI doomsday theorist Yudkowsky appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show” to talk about superintelligence. The episode was ominously titled “How Afraid of the A.I. Apocalypse Should We Be?” Klein and Yudkowsky promptly got into the difficulty of “alignment”—training an AI system to act in a manner that aligns with human interests. Yudkowsky argued that we are struggling to control our existing systems, which implies that we’ll have no chance of controlling the much smarter variations of this technology that are soon to follow.

Recent findings suggest that to underscore his point, he referred to a disturbing incident described in the system card for OpenAI’s GPT-o1 model. OpenAI had set up a security challenge that instructed an LLM-powered coding system to break into a server to retrieve the contents of a protected file. But a configuration mistake prevented the server from launching, rendering the task impossible. Instead of giving up, the system exploited a security flaw to start a upcoming instance of the server, adding a command that directly revealed the protected file’s contents. “It jumped out of the system,” explained Yudkowsky, adding: “This is not something that any human particularly programmed into it.”.

In a Georgetown University doctoral seminar, Cal Newport and his students examined the intellectual history and technical plausibility of superintelligence. Explore their annotated bibliography of key papers.

Recent findings suggest that though this 2024 incident flew largely under the radar at the time, a more troubling episode made a bigger splash this summer. OpenAI revealed that one of the company’s models circumvented its restricted internet access to hack into Hugging Face servers, seeking information that would help it pass a cybersecurity evaluation—all without the knowledge of its human creators. OpenAI soon admitted that the Hugging Face attack was just one of many examples of its systems going rogue. An opinion article published in The Hill articulated a widely held reaction when it described this behavior as “something straight out of sci-fi.”.

These examples seem to support Yudkowsky’s fear that AI will inevitably develop a mind of its own, a key step on the route to uncontrollable ASI. But a closer look reveals a less frightening picture. The systems involved in these hacking incidents were AI agents: programs that continually prompt an LLM to ask what actions to take next in pursuit of a goal. In the hacking incidents, this basic ask/act pattern was repeated in a long-running loop with minimal human supervision.

Recent findings suggest that using LLMs to suggest actions over long time horizons is a risky proposition. As any frequent chatbot user can attest, LLM outputs can be plausible and logical while still veering off in unexpected directions that violate commonsense human norms about what’s appropriate.

In the GPT-o1 incident, for example, it’s likely that the agent reported the error message caused by the server misconfiguration to the LLM. During its training, the LLM had probably encountered reports of similar error messages accompanied by instructions for how to restart the server in question, so it passed along similar instructions to the agent. This is a perfectly plausible response when considered in isolation, even if it led to actions that a human would immediately reject as violating the spirit of the experiment. Something similar helps explain the hacking attacks over the summer. The LLM suggesting a hack to succeed at a cybersecurity challenge is a perfectly plausible response, even if it’s not what the experimenters had in mind.

I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

The misaligned behavior that troubles commentators like Yudkowsky, therefore, doesn’t necessarily reveal something fundamental about advanced AI. It’s instead an expected side effect of the particular strategy of letting LLM outputs determine the actions of an autonomous agent without sufficient constraints. An obvious way to address these risks is to consider alternative architectures. Fortunately, there are many examples of AI systems that can complete tasks at human or superhuman levels without relying solely on LLM output to determine their actions.

Consider Tesla’s rapidly improving autonomous driving systems, or DeepMind’s AlphaFold, which helped win its developers a Nobel Prize in Chemistry for its ability to predict protein structures, or the AI game engines that can now beat humans in many popular pastimes, including chess, poker, Go, and the strategy game Diplomacy. None of these systems, impressive as they are, create concerns about going rogue. Their construction prevents such an outcome: Instead of prompting an LLM to generate an open-ended strategy for pursuing a general goal, these AIs consider much more limited spaces of possible actions. AlphaFold never surprises its users because its architecture does only one thing: It maps amino acid sequences to 3D protein structures. Tesla’s cars never unexpectedly form vehicle swarms because they’re asked only to avoid immediate obstacles, not to craft convoluted plans for achieving long-term objectives.

The implication of recent AI hacking attacks, therefore, is not a reflection of the difficulties of alignment. It is instead evidence that autonomous systems powered primarily by LLM prompts are unpredictable and possibly unsafe. More task-specific architectures can produce impressive performance much more safely, if we’re willing to put in the effort to develop them.

Recent findings suggest that even if I’m correct that superintelligence is not a realistic engineering goal, this doesn’t mean we’re safe from harm. Merely pursuing ASI, as both OpenAI and Anthropic seem intent on doing, can create problems. Why, for example, did OpenAI persist in running its problematic hacking experiments over the summer, even after multiple warnings that the agents were likely to act unpredictably? Perhaps the firm judged these risks acceptable collateral damage in the race to be the first to bring ASI into the world.

This fascination with superintelligence might also explain why OpenAI and Anthropic have both described RSI as a critical goal. As argued earlier, RSI is a concept from futurism and not computer science, and it isn’t necessary to build useful AI products. But if you believe achieving ASI is your destiny, pursuing recursive self-improvement becomes a primary objective. This matters because even if RSI never produces an intelligence explosion, it will almost certainly lead to systems that are harder for humans to understand and control. Which is why I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

What’s needed now is for engineers and scientists with no financial or ideological skin in the game to participate in the AI discourse. We cannot let a few AI companies with mixed motives dictate the terms for how we discuss this technology. If superintelligence is a shaky concept, experts need to say so. If agents powered by prompting LLMs aren’t the best path toward safe and productive AI, experts should argue that as well. For the past few years, we’ve let a small group of individuals from the Bay Area who have quirky beliefs and astonishing sums of money tell us how to think about their products. It’s time for those of us able to think for ourselves on these matters to stand up and declare, “We’ve heard what you had to say. Now it’s our turn.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, dell, HPE, Lenovo and Supermicro are raising prices for Nvidia-powered AI servers months after buyers signed their contracts.
  • “It is disconcerting when you get a 25, 30, 45 per cent [price increase],” one of the people told the FT.
  • According to recent reports, GPU servers cost at least 20% to 30% more, one person said.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, dell, HPE, Lenovo and Supermicro are raising prices for Nvidia-powered AI servers months after buyers signed their contracts. Nikou Asgari reported the price rises for the Financial Times. The higher prices come when the equipment is ready to ship, according to people familiar with the matter.

“It is disconcerting when you get a 25, 30, 45 per cent [price increase],” one of the people told the FT.

According to recent reports, GPU servers cost at least 20% to 30% more, one person said. CPU nodes, where memory makes up much of the cost, have tripled in price or more.

Sources indicate that large trading firms are among the buyers hit, including Jane Street, Optiver and Hudson River Trading, the FT reported. After the massive cloud providers, they are some of the largest buyers of computing equipment, and they are building their own data centres for trading research. Jane Street has also signed with CoreWeave for cloud computing.

Recent findings suggest that most are agreeing to the new prices because they need the equipment. Contracts now carry an indicative price that can rise sharply by delivery, another person told the FT.

In a recent development, “We’ve never mentioned no,” the person said. “At the end of the day, the compute is valuable to us and we’ll pay for it.”.

Industry observers note that suppliers are largely passing on memory costs, the FT reported. Memory prices have risen more than 400% since the start of 2024, according to JPMorgan research cited by the paper. SK Hynix has said the memory shortage could last until 2030.

Recent findings suggest that one fight has reached court. In June, British trading firm XTX Markets sued Dell in Ireland, according to court filings seen by the FT. The two had agreed a fixed price of $549m for servers, and XTX paid an extra $5m for price certainty.

In a recent development, dell later told XTX it would have to pay at least $62m to $70m more, the filings say. Dell noted it could not absorb the rising memory costs, according to XTX. The case is ongoing.

HPE and Supermicro declined to comment to the FT. Dell and Lenovo did not respond. Supermicro raised its revenue forecast by $4bn in October on AI demand.
