But if you want that extra bit of assistance, I think the De'Longhi La Specialista Touch is the best espresso machine for most people.

Black Friday events are in full swing, which means there are plenty of deals on our favorite machines. We're keeping tabs on all the latest discounts in our best Black Friday deals roundup (and on plenty of other great tech we've tested). Or if you're holiday shopping, these are the best gifts for coffee lovers we recommend right now.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

If I was starting from scratch in my small kitchen, this is the machine I'd buy. The De'Longhi La Specialista Touch is strikingly compact and well-priced, but it doesn't skip out on smart features. Striking an ideal balance between user-friendly design and elevated touches, the La Specialista Touch walks you through every part of the brewing process with its responsive 3.5-inch touchscreen.

In a recent development, you can steam milk manually or use automatic features which this machine, which is a welcome feature that brings it into line with much more expensive options from the likes of Breville. In terms of cost, while it's an investment, I think the La Specialista Touch offers outstanding value.

It's fun to make espresso from scratch, but grinding, tamping and brewing can be a messy business. The La Specialista Touch doesn't have an in-built tamping arm, but it does include a tamping kit which allows you to check the volume of your grind and evenly compress it into a puck. The screw-on funnel helps keep things mess-free.

The La Specialista Touch is super interactive, starting at the bean grinding settings. It uses De'Longhi's "Bean Adapt" tech, which walks you through the grinding process by asking you about the type of beans you're grinding and the color, which can indicate the roast level. Based on that, it asks you to set your grinder to a specific number, and then asks you to use the smart tamper to tell the machine the amount of coffee it needs to grind to get the perfect level.

Following all of that, the machine then tells you to increase of decrease grind size depending on how long the extraction takes. Combine all those factors, and it tackles the cause of most bad espressos right from the start.

You can choose from 15 coarseness settings, which is pretty average for machines of this spec and price. It was capable of finely grinding light-roast beans, and there's plenty of scope to increase the grind size for darker roasts.

In a recent development, I made some yummy espresso with the La Specialista Touch. It allows you to save bean settings to shortcut the Bean Adapt process, and I was able to flip between my go-to Lost Sheep Get To The Hopper beans and some cheap Aldi beans with ease.

Industry observers note that when using great beans, the machine delivered a rich brew with notes of toffee and chocolate. It was the ultimate base for a latte or cappuccino, and if I was making an americano, I could leave my cup in place for the machine to top it up with hot water using a dispenser located right next to the group head.

It has been revealed that I should also note that this machine makes cold brew, which is an increasingly popular feature in more modern machines. My brew was light, fruity, and balanced, but you should note that it doesn't brew cold espresso.

In a recent development, you can steam milk both manually and automatically with this machine, but I have a preference for manual steaming. Its included (useful) temperature gauge prevents your milk from burning, but it also gets in the way a little when hand-steaming. I got used to it, but it was a minor annoyance at first.

In a recent development, as for the automatic milk steaming, this was among some of the best I've tried. If I'm being picky, this is a feature I think Breville machines dominae, but the La Specialista Touch did make some fantastic latte milk which poured well with some swirling. My cappuccino foam was light and a little dry, which made a great topper to a shot of rich espresso.

We don't give out five-star reviews often, but Breville's cheapest coffee maker is hard to fault. Featuring the stainless steel exterior and quality construction we expect from Breville, it features a cost-conscious price tag that those familiar with the brand may not expect.

Sources indicate that espresso machines can be chunky, so this is a rare compact option that will sit streamlined in just about any space. It's one of the few options in this guide that doesn't include a grinder, so you'll have to use pre-ground coffee or purchase your own grinder (check out our reviews of the best coffee grinders for some options, but they don't have to be expensive!) to use it.

Reviewer Erin said "Damn, this is such a good machine. This machine’s functionality vs. cost is darn near unbelievable" when she tested it, and called the espresso she made in the Bambino "delectable".

Industry observers note that this machine doesn't have a grinder, but it's worth digging into why that's not a bad thing. For a start, some enthusiasts prefer to buy separate grinders and espresso machines as it allows them to switch up their setup more easily, and if something breaks, you won't have to replace your entire coffee setup.

The machine comes with single-walled and double-walled baskets. If you proposal on using pre-ground coffee, I'd suggest starting with double-walled, as they can bring back some of the fresh and lively flavor you'll be missing from fresh-ground coffee.

The Breville Bambino produces very high-quality espresso without taking up too much counter space. Breville (or Sage, for European readers) is famed for making market-leading machines, and while this is one of the brand's entry-level options, it doesn't miss out on premium-feeling features or the powerful extraction you'll need to get a great shot.

There's pre-infusion, which will soak your puck to allow flavors to develop before extracting your shot, and there's also volumetric dispensing to pour either a single or double completely hands-free.

While you can get your barista on with this machine, it also comes with pressurized baskets, which will allow less finicky owners to get a decent brew out of pre-ground beans.

It has been revealed that unlike the Breville Bambino Plus, there's no automatic steaming with the Bambino. Reviewer Erin was sceptical of its one-hole steam wand — typically you'll be better off with a four-hole as it creates a higher level of pressure — but in testing, the Bambino had no trouble creating velvety-smooth milk.

The machine also comes with a milk jug, which is a nice bonus for an affordable machine, and its wand is more flexible than comparable machines from the likes of De'Longhi.

Sources indicate that if you're on a budget, the De'Longhi Stilosa will be a good starting point. Admittedly, you'll need some skill to get great espresso out of this machine. This is because it's manual, meaning there are very few assisted features to make life easier. However, if you're willing to put in the work, the good news is that this machine is more than capable of extracting quality espresso, especially if you pair it with a quality grinder.

In a recent development, considering the very reasonable price point, it's not surprising that this machine is mostly made of cheap-feeling plastic. But the good news is that under the hood, there's a decent brewer that performs as well as much more expensive machines.

Most impressive was its quality milk wand, which was capable of achieving a fine micro-foam that made delicious lattes and flat whites.

According to recent reports, this machine doesn't have a grinder. It's not too hard to make a decent manual espresso machine on a budget, but including a quality grinder (which is absolutely a non-negotiable if you care about great coffee) is expensive. Market-leading grinders can easily cost $300+, so if your machine offers both grinding and brewing capabilities for less than that, it's likely that the grinder is poor quality.

Sources indicate that so if you're on a budget and don't mind getting hands-on, the De'Longhi Stilosa is a good work around. Especially if you combine it with a quality hand-grinder like the sub-$100 1Zpresso Q Air.

Tested by our reviews writer (and former barista) Erin, the De'Longhi Stilosa competed with some of the much more premium machines she's reviewed.

Industry observers note that with a bit of experimentation and dedication, she found that there’s no reason why you can’t pull consistently delicious shots on the Stilosa. It does require a little know-how, but that's a classic trade-off for the price.

It has been revealed that because the machine doesn't brew to single or double shots, you need to monitor and switch it off yourself. For this, you'll be better off buying a coffee scale so you can tailor your ratios.

You might expect the steam wand on a cheap machine to be flimsy, but if anything, Erin found that the Stilosa’s steam wand can be a touch overzealous.

A former barista, Erin knows her way around a steam wand, and she found that this one needed full concentration during steaming to prevent the milk from becoming over-textured.

However, she did make some awesome lattes in the Stilosa. And for the price, it's one of the top steam wands she's tested.

Sources indicate that the Ninja Luxe Cafe Mini Plus is designed around automation, handling weighing, dosing, and grind adjustment for you, so if you're upcoming to home espresso, it removes much of the guesswork. We found its auto-grind-size calibration especially helpful, letting us lock in consistent results with barely any trial and error. This built-in guidance helps streamline the process for beginners, and it's often the number one reason friends and family tell me their machine doesn't work properly. It does, dad, you've just got the wrong grind size. With the Mini Plus, auto-grind-size calibration makes dialing in much easier for new people, so you can reliably pull good shots without trial-and-error adjustments.

With both automatic and manual milk options, the Mini Plus lets you choose how hands-on you want to be. This is especially helpful for beginners learning to texture milk at their own pace.

In a recent development, compared to the more advanced De'Longhi La Specialista Touch, which provides guided tamping and more complex brewing modes, the Ninja Luxe Cafe Mini Plus stands out for its simplicity and compact footprint. While it lacks in-built tamping and step-by-step drink guidance, it offers a straightforward way to start making espresso at home without requiring a lot of counter space or a steep learning curve.

In a recent development, something that really sets Ninja coffee makers apart is that their grinder works on an unusual weight-based system. That's the best way, in theory, to ensure you're getting your espresso ratio right every time, and it's why some coffee fanatics will pre-weigh their beans before feeding them into a coffee machine.

The Mini Plus does lack in-built tamping, which is something you'll find in more premium models from Ninja, but it does have a dosing funnel which allows you to catch every drop from the grinder and minimize countertop mess.

Sources indicate that reviewer Erin enjoyed the coffee she made with this machine, but it didn't blow her socks off. She described it as akin to chain coffee shop coffee, which is no bad thing, because the average coffee machine buyer simply wants to replicate their favorite to-go drink at home. But if you know your arabica from your robusta, it might not hit the mark.

Sources indicate that there are some pros and cons to the milk steaming with the Ninja Luxe Café line. The milk jug has an in-built spinner to create a vortex in the jug when you're using the automated steaming mode, but you can use the wand manually if you want to learn how to steam by hand.

A big bonus for those who drink a range of milk types is that if you opt for pre-set milk steaming, you can switch between plant and dairy milk settings to prevent oat or soy milk from burning.

Industry observers note that this is a halfway house between traditional milk steaming and using a handheld frother to create artificial bubbles in your coffee. Personally, I prefer the automated steam wands you'll find on Breville machines like the Bambino Plus.

But the in-built spinner does have one massive bonus in allowing you to create cold foam to pair with your cold coffee. This is something I've not seen in any of the other espresso machines on the market.

According to recent reports, if you want a hands-off espresso machine that delivers consistently excellent shots, the Terra Kaffe Demi is a confident pick. The main advantage of superautomatic machines is that they make your coffee from scratch with the touch of a button, but when testing these machines, we frequently find that the finished cup just tastes... bad. That's not an issue reviewer Dan had with the Demi, which allowed him to dial in his perferred settings for espresso and long black coffee, and delivered a consistently delicious brew, cup after cup.

Recent findings suggest that under the hood, the Demi automates the entire espresso process, from grinding with its conical burr grinder to dosing, tamping, and brewing. In testing, the shots came out reliably rich every single time. Plus, it looks fantastic, and packs in a lot of smarts without being too in-your-face about it.

The main downside is that there's no in-built milk frother. But we tend not to rate the milk frothers which come with superautomatic machines, anyway. You can buy Terra Kaffe's standalone milk frother separately, and use it to make everything from cappuccino to cold foam. The other main issue Dan encountered was that the water tank was on the small side at 47 fluid ounces.

It has been revealed that the Demi comes with conical burr grinders, which are typically a better pick than flat burr grinders due to their quieter operation and more consistent results. Because it's hidden away, we tend to find that manufacturers can cut corners when making the grinders for automatic espresso machines, so it's immediately a positive sign that the Demi features conical burrs.

What's less promising is the limited range of grind settings: from one through to five, which is significantly less than the 30+ settings you'll find from alternatives like the Breville Oracle Dual Builer.

According to recent reports, the Demi can make five drinks: Espresso, Lungo, Americano, Drip, and Hot Water. So, make that four coffee drinks. It's not the most versatile pick, but in testing we found that our espresso was lively and, most importantly, consistently good.

Dan, a noted coffee snob, noted "I was genuinely surprised at how consistent the shots are. Once I had my temperature, strength, and volume dialed in, the shots were as close to perfect as you could expect every time I hit the button.".

There's no milk frother here. Instead, you'll have to buy the newly-released Aero Milk Frother if you want a companion to turn your espresso into a cappuccino.

The latest premium contender from Fellow, the Espresso Series 1, is engineered for buyers who want café-level control at home—offering deep shot profile customization and a steam wand that could make a barista blush. If you’re the kind of person who tweaks pre-infusion, flow rate, or pressure profiles for each roast, you’ll be right at home here; the steam wand with its versatile ball joint is a standout for microfoam and serious cappuccino work.

In our testing, dialing in shots with the Series 1 felt more like sculpting than brewing. The results spoke for themselves: the espresso came through with a distinct sweetness and bright acidity that made it hard not to drink the entire shot at once. This isn’t just theoretical control—it’s the real, tangible difference you can taste in the cup, shot after shot.

Sources indicate that but there’s a trade-off. Compared to something like the De’Longhi La Specialista Touch, which is more compact and user-friendly, the Series 1 leans into complexity and countertop presence. It’s best for buyers who want to experiment, customize every variable, and don’t mind a learning curve (or a bigger footprint). If that’s you, there’s no better playground—but if you want guided simplicity or a tidier setup, look elsewhere.

There's no built-in grinder with the Fellow Espresso - you'll have to provide your own. Enthusiasts willing to spend the $1.5k to buy this machine likely have a grinder they're happy with already, but if you're building your set-up from scratch, be aware that your budget will have to allow for a grinder as well as brewing device, unless you buy an all-in-one coffee maker.

According to recent reports, you can let the Fellow do the heavy lifting when brewing, giving you automatic profiles and step-by-step instructions for brewing that you select with the built-in LCD screen. Or you can dive into the exhaustive settings menu and sort things yourself. Whichever way you want to do it, you'll end up with some awesome brews.

In a recent development, one small complaint we have is the machine's tendency to leave you with wet pucks of coffee grounds once you're finished making your drink. It's not a massive problem, but in theory the Fellow has the technology to produce dry, easily disposable pucks like most other espresso machines of this price.

Sources indicate that the steam wand on the Fellow Espresso is one of the best in the business. In fact it produced the single best result we've ever seen for non-dairy milk. It's the kind of milk results that no other machine we know of can match.

In a recent development, just watch out for the auto-purge function though. It can get in the way of cleaning if you know what you're doing.

It has been revealed that most of this guide is geared towards the average home brewer, but if you want to take it to the next level, the Gaggia Classic E24 is our recommendation. It was tested by our Reviews Editor Peter, a former chef and serious coffee-lover who doesn't mind taking the time to craft coffee the old-fashioned way. His main gripe was that it came with poor-quality tools, but these are easily replaced.

This machine lacks a lot of the assists you'll find with Breville and De'Longhi machines. There's no PID, no thermoblock, and you'll have to start and stop the extraction yourself.

Sources indicate that the plus side of this is that you get complete control over your shot of coffee. Some machines try and steer you because they assume they know better, but if you've got the know-how, this machine will leave you to it and not intervene.

Recent findings suggest that there's no grinder to be seen here. You'll want to pair this compact espresso machine with a quality home grinder such as the Eureka Mignon Specialita, which just so happens to be the grinder we used during testing.

Sources indicate that as I noted, this machine leaves all the hard work to you. It's a single-boiler without a PID. What does this mean? Well, it heats up the entire tank instead of the amount of water needed for a specific dose, and it won't monitor and adjust the temperature of your coffee during extraction. You can add a PID if you choose to modify this machine, but if you go as is, you're temperature-surfing to hit the optimum extraction.

Recent findings suggest that due to its larger brass boiler and brass group head, the Gaggia now offers higher levels of temperature stability (a common problem in machines without PID). Peter found that it was more than capable of extracting complex, punchy espresso. "I tested the Gaggia with a range of beans, including light-medium, medium and dark roasts, using washed, wet-hulled, honey-processed and natural processing. The E24 did justice to the lot.".

According to recent reports, peter made some brilliant lattes in this machine. Its steam wand is more powerful than any other in this guide (aside perhaps from the Meraki), because (like a commercial machine) it works with a boiler to hit high pressure on demand.

Sources indicate that this means you'll be able to create glossy microfoam for a flat white or cappuccino in a matter of seconds. Peter found that it could make a flat white in ten seconds flat. However, as you're working with one boiler, you'll need to 'purge' your machine to get rid of the overheated water after milk steaming is finished. The temperature will be too high to go back to brewing espresso.

In a recent development, I'm pretty cagey with who I let review espresso machines for Tom's Guide. When I bought my first espresso machine, I couldn't tell if my failure to get a good espresso out of my fancy fresh gadget was the machine's fault, or human error. If I'd written a review of that machine, it wouldn't have been very fair on the reader, or the machine!

According to recent reports, but now I've got five years of testing, well over 30 coffee machine reviews, and a Specialty Coffee Association qualification under my belt. My friends are always asking me questions about coffee, why their machine isn't working for them, or which they should buy, so I'd like to think I can be that person to our readers, too.

In a recent development, fortunately, at Tom's Guide, I'm not alone. We've got a brilliant team of experienced testers with almost 20 years of coffee expertise between us.

As a former barista (and current product tester), I've spent a lot of time getting hands-on with espresso machines.

After a combined three years at two of the biggest coffee chains and a year at an artisan independent coffee shop, I can detect a well-balanced shot when I taste it, and can also interpret the culprit behind a poor extraction, be it low pressure, grind size, or poor temperature controls.

Spending three years making hundreds of coffees a day might make a person gag at the sight of lattes, but coffee still holds a special place in my heart.

My favorite drink is an oat milk flat white, made with Kenyan or Ethiopian beans.

I’m Tom’s Guide's Reviews Editor and I’ve been an espresso enthusiast for almost a decade now.

Recent findings suggest that as a former chef, I started using commercial espresso machines to make tiramisu while working in an Italian restaurant, and that’s where my fascination with 9-bar pressure began. And it hasn’t stopped since.

Fun fact: every job I’ve held since has given me access to espresso machines — oddly enough, that includes when I worked at an energy company, where we had a commercial Expobar machine plumbed into the office kitchen!

These days, I spend large chunks of my day testing out the latest and greatest coffee gear, from coffee grinders and weighing scales through to pour-over drippers and, of course, espresso machines.

I’ve used home espresso machines from Breville/Sage, Rancilio, Gaggia, De’Longhi, Diletta and more. Through my years of testing (and tasting), I have the experience to know when a machine performs as it should and whether or not it’s worth your hard-earned cash.

We test a ton of coffee gear at Tom's Guide, and not everything can make it to the final guide. If I don't include something, that doesn't necessarily mean we don't recommend it, so if none of the machines listed above take your fancy, you might get along better with one of these tried-and-tested options.

KitchenAid KF8 Coffee Machine (★★★★☆).

According to recent reports, we don't tend to rate superautomatic espresso machines, but the KF8 surprised us. In fact, it used to feature in this guide until we tested the Terra Kaffe Demi.

Read the full KitchenAid KF8 Coffee Machine review.

Casabrews Ultra Coffee Machine (★★★★☆).

According to recent reports, if you're on a budget, Casabrews machines are worth a look. The trade-off is in the built quality, but in our tests, we did find that they're capable of making a tasty espresso.

Read the full Casabrews Ultra Coffee Machine review.

Meraki Espresso Machine (★★★★☆).

According to recent reports, newcomer to the espresso game Meraki is offering a stunning range of features for the price. The downside? It's still in development, with some tweaks having now been made to the model we first tested, which means we can't recommend it until we've tested the fresh and improved model.

Read the full Meraki Espresso Machine review.

The De’Longhi Dedica Duo is neat and compact, but it's quite expensive for what it is, especially when the Stilosa is cheaper and just as capable. However, you can't deny that it's a looker, which could make it a contender if you're setting up a coffee nook.

Read the full De’Longhi Dedica Duo review.

Our love of the Breville Bambino Plus is very well documented, but when we added its cheaper counterpart, the Bambino, to this guide, we felt that we didn't need both here. The Plus is incredible, with automated steaming and powerful extraction, but it's slightly less good value for money.

Read the full Breville Bambino Plus review.

De’Longhi La Specialista Arte Evo (★★★★☆).

In a recent development, looking for a budget-friendly espresso machine with character and an in-built grinder? The De’Longhi La Specialista Arte Evo is practically in a league of its own, offering specs that punch well above its weight. The only reason it's not in this guide is that we love the Specialista Touch more.

KitchenAid Semi Automatic Espresso Machine (★★★★☆).

The KitchenAid Semi Automatic Espresso Machine with Burr Grinder is the entry-level option in KitchenAid's line of coffee makers. It's a mid-price, high-quality option, but it lacks a lot of the automated features you'll see from options like Breville and De'Longhi.

Read the full KitchenAid Semi Automatic Espresso Machine review.

Recent findings suggest that with some trial and error though, Reviews Editor Peter hit his stride with the Silvia. After some experimentation he said he was "actually a little taken aback at how nice espresso shots tasted." If you've got a refined palate and espresso known-how, this could be a good option.

Read the full Rancilio Silvia (V6) Espresso Machine review.

De’Longhi Dedica Duo Espresso Machine (★★★☆☆).

The De'Longhi Dedica Duo is a good espresso machine capable of making pleasant cold brew for just $299. Even so, it's the same price as the fantastic Breville Bambino and $150 pricier than our favorite budget machine, the De’Longhi Stilosa.

Read the full De’Longhi Dedica Duo Espresso Machine review.

Philips Barista Brew Espresso Machine (★★★☆☆).

In a recent development, the Philips Barista Brew is Philips' first attempt at an automatic coffee machine. The rest of the line is superautomatic, and start at quite affordable prices. When we tested the Barista Brew, we didn't have an concern with the quality of its extraction or construction, it just struggles to break through the very crowded market of machines that look, cost, and perform almost exactly the same.

Read the full Philips Barista Brew Espresso Machine review.

You probably didn't come to this guide looking for a wireless coffee maker, but this non-electric option is very affordable, super portable, and ideal for travel. It uses a valve to create the pressure needed to extract espresso, and we were really impressed by how well it worked.

Read the full Wacaco Minipresso review.

It has been revealed that the Terra Kaffe is super smart. It claims to feature AI tech that will personalize your brew to your specific preferences, and it certainly looks space-age. The price will rule it out of contention for most people though, and it's also a very large option.

Read the full Terra Kaffe TK-02 review.

Philips 3200 Series LatteGo (★★★☆☆).

According to recent reports, the Philips 3200 Series LatteGo is one of the most affordable superautomatic espresso machines on the market. It feels plasticky in use and the milk dispenser will struggle to compete with more expensive options, but if you want a one-and-done option that doesn't cost the earth, it's a good choice.

Read the full Philips 3200 Series LatteGo review.

You can make any kind of coffee drink you like with this automatic machine from Ninja, but the mixed quality of the outputs prevented us from awarding a higher rating.

Read our full Ninja AutoBarista Pro review.

Philips Café Aromis 8000 Series (★★☆☆☆).

It has been revealed that one to avoid this time around — it makes coffee, but there's not much to say about it. It costs far too much money for the quality of espresso that it spits out, even if the device itself does look pretty special.

Read the full Philips Café Aromis 8000 Series review.

It has been revealed that we review a lot of espresso machines at Tom's Guide. Very few of them make it into our buying guides, but you can see a comprehensive list of other models we've tested at the bottom of this guide.

According to recent reports, when it comes to testing espresso machines, there's a lot of room for human error. In order to minimize this, I work closely with a team of true coffee experts, from former baristas to serious home baristas. Every review you'll read on Tom's Guide will be from a true espresso enthusiast who can tell their flat whites from their cappuccinos and their arabica from their robusta.

Sources indicate that we consider a huge range of factors when evaluating espresso machines. Here's a non-exhaustive list of the things we test for:.

According to recent reports, ease of use: You shouldn't have to be a pro to work an espresso machine. These appliances are designed to make life easier, so while it's fair to expect a learning curve if you opt for a manual machine with lots of hands-on features, we mark machines down for any quirks or fiddly features that will make day-to-day use harder for the average buyer.

In a recent development, ease of cleaning: Some machines are splashy, messy, and get greasy from the touch of a button. These are workhorses, sure, but they're also meant to look nice, so we evaluate whether they spill grounds, splatter milk, or will require any major upkeep with each review.

Value for money: Even a budget espresso machine can be expensive, so we always consider whether a machine is priced competitively when putting it to the test. If we wouldn't recommend our friends spend their money on a machine, we wouldn't recommend it to you, either.

According to recent reports, grinding: If a machine has an in-built grinder, we put it through the same testing that we use when evaluating the best coffee grinders. After all, the quality of your grinder plays a massive part in achieving a good extraction. It's the single most key part of any espresso-brewing process. We evaluate the range of grind sizes on offer with every machine (you'll want a very fine consistency, but this will vary depending on the bean you use), as well as how much coffee a machine grinds automatically. A lot of enthusiasts brew using ratios, so we like to weigh the grounds before we brew for good measure.

Brewing: Albeit an crucial step, this is also the simplest to test. Whether a machine can brew well is dependent on the performance of the grinder, but we know we've got a quality coffee if it brews at that sweet spot between 190 to 200°F (88 and 93°C) and we get between 25-30ml of espresso. We use a coffee scale to test this, just to be extra thorough.

According to recent reports, taste test: Metrics aside, it's all in the taste-test. We buy high-quality coffee (presently, we're using a subscription to Hard Lines' specialty coffee) that's freshly-roasted to give our machines the best possible chance of brewing a brilliant espresso. And if it tastes too bitter or too tart, we know it's not the beans' fault! If the coffee tastes too grassy, it suggests the machine doesn't brew hot enough, and if it's burnt-tasting, that's a sign that it's not got good temperature regulation and is scorching our grounds.

Milk steaming: Steam wands need to be powerful, ergonomic and responsive. A great wand will not only heat your milk but also help to create a powerful vortex, which will add texture and incorporate air into your milk jug. I'll get more into how to use a steam wand below, but you best believe that if former barista Erin can't get a good texture from a steam wand, there's no hope for a home user.

According to recent reports, super-automatic espresso machines will often feature milk dispensers that automatically froth your milk and pour it into your mug. This is really convenient if you don't like the idea of learning to steam milk by hand, but just so we're clear, these machines don't steam your milk. They simply heat it and inject some bubbles as they pour into your cup. It gets the job done, but it's not going to compete with a coffee shop-quality flat white.

Longevity: You need to be prepared to look after an espresso machine. They block easily if you don't descale regularly, and your group head and steam wand will need to be flushed out periodically. This aside, we've also tried machines that simply don't feel like they're built to last. Where possible, we like to hang onto a top pick for prolonged home use and testing. That way, we can update our guide if it doesn't seem built to last. Our number one, the De'Longhi La Specialista Opera, is currently living with Erin as her home machine, allowing us to continue to evaluate its position in this guide.

Recent findings suggest that this question used to be a lot more simple to answer: there's manual, and there's super-automatic! However, things have changed a lot in the last few years, and now there's an increasing number of machines that sit somewhere in between.

In truth, it would be easier to characterize types of espresso machine as a spectrum, all the way from lever pump machines like La Pavoni to one-touch super-automatics like Jura.

But to make life easier, I've divided the domestic machines in this guide into three categories:.

It has been revealed that espresso machines are pretty complicated, which is why I did a dedicated Specialty Coffee Association course before compiling this guide. While I’ve tried to make it as accessible as possible, there is some terminology you might need to learn to understand the reviews below. Here are the ABC's of espresso machines.

If you’re completely new to espresso machines, the thing you have to ask yourself is: “how much time do I want to spend, how much skill do I have, and how much am I prepared to put into this?".

It has been revealed that I posed this question to Lucy Dunstan, Product Manager at SMEG and La Pavoni. “It’s quite simple really, it’s all about extracting the flavor from your coffee,” she told me.

In a recent development, “There’s a scientific process for making an espresso. It has to be between 88 and 93°C [190 to 200°F], you have to put about 9 bars of pressure on it, and you want to extract between 25 and 30ml of liquid. So what all these machines do is offer a way of controlling that process.”.

Sources indicate that there are so many variables that stand between your machine and a perfect espresso. This includes the beans you use, how you grind them, the volume of grounds in your portafilter, the pressure you use when tamping, the temperature stability of your machine, the water pressure exerted, the volume of water pushed into your puck… that’s a non-exhaustive list, and it’s before we even get into milk steaming!

There are so many variables that stand between your machine and a perfect espresso.

Industry observers note that here’s what I wish I’d known when I bought my first espresso machine: The more automated features you opt for, the fewer variables you’ll need to worry about. “Sometimes with espresso machines, an entry-level price will actually require more skill,” states Dunstan.

According to recent reports, “If you’re completely new to espresso machines, the thing you have to ask yourself is: how much time do I want to spend, how much skill do I have, and how much am I prepared to put into this? So you’re either someone who doesn’t have a lot of time to spend on making your coffee, or you want to delve into that world where you’re getting hands-on.".

There's an unfortunate irony with espresso machines. You can get good espresso with a cheaper machine, but to do so, you'll need to learn the ins and outs of how these machines work. For the entry-level buyer without much knowledge, you'll often have to spend a lot more on a super-capable machine that will take all the hard work out of the equation.

It doesn't make much sense, right? Coffee enthusiasts can get away with spending $200 on a basic espresso machine because they've got the skill to use it properly, but if you're just dipping your toes in the water? Well, prepare to spend at least $500. It's no wonder why so many people opt for a pod machine like a Keurig or a Nespresso!

It has been revealed that fortunately, the market is catching up. An increasing amount of espresso machines feature assisted settings that will remove some of the variables that can mess up your espresso. This includes automated grinding that controls the volume of coffee dispensed into your portafilter, automated tamping for an even pressure, and even hands-free steam wands that will texture your milk for you.

It has been revealed that the majority of the machines I've included in this machine fit into this automatic category in some sense. I think they're the best option for most people, allowing you to learn as you use the machine and get hands-on if you wish, but also taking the reins when you just want a low-effort espresso.

You'll see in the products included I've mentioned how many bars of pressure they each have, but what does this mean, and does it even matter? Well, the short answer is no. You won't necessarily see a better extraction from a machine with 20 bars over a machine with 15. This is because the ideal pressure needed for espresso is 9 bars.

I asked Luke Lane, Training & Events Manager for Sage Appliances, to explain the significance of pressure for espresso machines. "You want to hit 9 bars for optimal extraction," he told me.

According to recent reports, "If the pressure is too low, you'll bring out grassy flavors. The pressure won't bring out the sugars from your beans.

"Too high, and your coffee will have a bitter, burnt taste.".

If all you need to make a great espresso is 9 bars of pressure, so I asked Lane why so many espresso machines have more?

Sources indicate that "Think of it like a car," Lane told me. "You don't want to drive it at top speed all the time, but driving in a comfortable range of what your car is capable of will mean it's not constantly being run flat-out.".

He explained that despite the maximum pressure of any machine, they'll use OPVs (which stands for over pressure valves) to keep espresso extraction running at a consistent 9 bars of pressure.

So, while higher pressure doesn't necessarily mean a machine is any better, you might not want to buy a machine with a maximum output of 9 bars, or it could lead to a shorter lifespan for your machine.

Most espresso machines will come with four baskets: two single and two double, with a mix of double-walled and single-walled constructions. I'll explain the difference between single-walled and double-walled below, but what's the significance of your basket size and capacity?

Luke Lane, Training & Events Manager for Sage Appliances, explained it to me: "There are two main basket widths: 54mm, which features on Sage / Breville's Barista range, and 58mm, which features on our Jet range.".

"58mm is considered to be commercial-grade. The larger and shallower basket will give you marginally better results because you're more easily able to permeate all of the grounds inside your basket.".

In a recent development, after testing countless espresso machines, I don't think my palette is quite so attuned that I could turn my nose up at an espresso from a 54mm basket. But it's useful to know if you want to replace or upgrade any parts of your machine what size portafilter baskets the group head will fit.

Industry observers note that single-walled and double-walled baskets, also known respectively as unpressurized and pressurized, are included with your espresso machine to give you options. As a general rule of thumb, you'll get better results from a pressurized basket if you're using pre-ground coffee. It will help you overcome some of the shortcomings of a grind size that's too coarse, or coffee that's less fresh. But if you want to taste the authentic flavor of your fresh-ground beans, a single-walled basket is the way to go.

In our reviews, we always use fresh-ground coffee, so we stick to single-walled baskets for the majority of our testing.

Sources indicate that when I asked him to explain how pressurized baskets work, Luke Lane, Training & Events Manager for Sage Appliances, said "Think of a group of people running down a hall and having to go through a door." He explained, "That's what the double-walled basket does. It creates pressure by restricting the flow of your coffee, forcing it to build up more flavor and crema than you'd have been able to achieve with a less fresh coffee.".

According to recent reports, we've done a thorough explainer on this in our guide to pressurized coffee baskets — how do they work and when should you use them? The short answer? They can act as a cheat code to a better espresso if you're not working with the ideal gear, but a machine with an in-built grinder shouldn't need one.

Sources indicate that the vast majority of domestic espresso machines use thermoblock technology to heat water on demand. But how does it work, and what are the pros and cons?

There are very few single boiler machines on the market, but the Rancilio Silvia is one of them. Boiler machines will heat your water and keep it at temperature for as and when you decide to use it. A single-boiler uses one boiler for both the group head and the steam wand, which require different temperatures and therefore will need to you purge excess hot water as you use different elements of the machine.

Dual boilers have one boiler for the group head, and another for your steam wand. They're not super popular for domestic, and I've not included a dual-boiler in this guide. They have a higher energy consumption because they keep your water hot for more precision and stability.

Industry observers note that what about thermoblock? I asked Lucy Dunstan, Product Manager at SMEG and La Pavoni, to explain. “A thermoblock is a heated metal block with one or more pipes running through it that will rapidly heat water on demand," she explained.

"They’re usually very compact so they don’t take up much space, meaning they can be fitted in smaller machines, and they’re more energy efficient [than a dual boiler].”.

“So the advantage is that they’re fast, small, and energy-efficient. The disadvantage is that they offer less temperature consistency than a dual boiler machine.

Industry observers note that "And they can, over time, be susceptible to limescale, so they may not last as long. Whereas if you buy a dual boiler La Pavoni machine, and you look after it, I’d expect it to last you a lifetime.”.

The Fluance RT86 seems to have made improvements in the areas that matter most, including a upcoming nine-inch carbon fiber tonearm and better vibration isolation.

Firstly, the turntable is driven by a servo-controlled belt-drive motor, which uses an optical sensor to regulate speed. Next, the RT86 includes a nine-inch carbon fiber tonearm with adjustable VTA, which helps to level cartridges of varying heights, and a removable headshell which lets you install multiple cartridges more easily.

The Fluance includes a 4.1-pound antiresonant acrylic platter. The platter sits on a high-mass wood plinth with a motor isolation system and adjustable isolation feet.

In addition, buyers now have a choice of two different cartridges: the Audio-Technica AT-VM95ML Microlinear cartridge or the Ortofon 2M Blue. Having tested the 2M Blue as part of the RT85, I would suggest users opt for the Audio-Technica as I found the Ortofon too bright for that setup.

This Tech Wreck Looks Just Like 2018. Back Then, Here's What Happened Next.

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (914 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 10 stocks we like better than NASDAQ Composite Index ›.
  • Recent findings suggest that the last two months have been brutal for the technology sector, especially semiconductors.
  • Recent findings suggest that is the AI bubble popping, like the dot-com bubble in 2000?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Billy Duberstein – Nov 23, 2026 at 9:30AM EST.

10 stocks we like better than NASDAQ Composite Index ›.

Recent findings suggest that the last two months have been brutal for the technology sector, especially semiconductors. Today, everyone has an opinion on when the bottom might be in.

Recent findings suggest that is the AI bubble popping, like the dot-com bubble in 2000? Or is the current downturn like other difficult corrections that preceded big rallies, such as the COVID downturn or the post-COVID inflation scare?

Industry observers note that in this investor's eyes, the 2026 tech wreck looks almost exactly like a different year. Here's why today's decline looks so similar, and how the market reacted after that example.

The parallels between this sell-off and that of late 2018 are striking:.

Sources indicate that the parallels are very striking, though the composition of the decline has nuanced differences. In 2018, the Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC +6.13%) crashed about 23.6% peak-to-trough in late December, finishing the year down roughly 3.9% overall.

At the moment, the Nasdaq is down about 13.9% from its Oct. 6 high and is now down 2.7% for the year. While the current top-to-bottom downturn hasn't been as deep, the semiconductor index has seen a larger drawdown than in 2018, over 43% from its highs, versus roughly a 23% drawdown in late 2018. That's in line with the more severe drawdowns in the chip sector in 2022 and early 2025, likely due to concerns that the massive AI build-out will run out of steam.

So while the Nasdaq hasn't seen as big a top-to-bottom drawdown as in 2018, it is down similarly for the year, and certain components, such as the chip subsector, are actually down more.

There are, of course, no perfect parallels, even if history does rhyme, and today's drawdown has both positive and negative differences relative to 2018.

On the positive side, the AI build-out appears to be far larger and earlier in its life cycle than the "boom" of 2018, which was centered on traditional cloud computing. GPU rental prices remain resilient, and token consumption is growing rapidly.

According to OpenRouter, an API service that allows developers to consume tokens from multiple models, token consumption is still rising exponentially, up 25x since January. And the trajectory doesn't seem to be slowing down; October's consumption of 790 trillion tokens grew nearly 37% over September, in just the span of one month!

Of course, there is also the big elephant in the room that wasn't present in 2018: Nvidia (NVDA +30.77%) and the recent scandal surrounding CEO Jensen Huang's untimely resignation.

As of this writing, the SEC has launched an investigation into Nvidia's accounting practices and whether the company knowingly funneled its advanced GPUs to China. Nvidia had also provided financing or an implicit backstop for a web of customers, including start-ups that use all these tokens, as well as the "neoclouds" that provide computing for them.

In a recent development, whether Nvidia will continue down the path of aggressively funding start-ups and neoclouds remains unknown. If it doesn't, the ultimate impact on the AI trade, which is partly dependent on these start-ups and neoclouds, both of which consume and produce tokens, remains unclear.

The good thing is that the three massive hyperscale cloud providers have strong balance sheets to fund the build-out, so it isn't as if their continued investment will stop as long as token demand is there, which it appears to be. However, it remains to be seen whether Nvidia will continue being as aggressive in funding some of its customers and neoclouds as it was before.

In a recent development, the good news for investors is that after the 2018 decline, 2019 was a great year for the stock market. The Nasdaq Composite not only rebounded 35.2% but also grew over the two following years.

According to recent reports, of course, that rally was somewhat dependent on the U.S. not falling into a recession, combined with the Federal Reserve backing off its interest rate increases and then later returning to interest rate cuts. The Fed raised rates four times in 2018, weakening the economy. However, investors took comfort in the 2019 "dovish pivot," which included three rate cuts, and the market rallied over 35% despite S&P 500 (^GSPC +4.44%) earnings growth of only 5.4% that year.

In September, the Federal Reserve began raising interest rates again, with officials recently saying more hikes are likely. Therefore, all eyes will be on fresh Fed Chair Kevin Warsh at the next Fed meeting, scheduled for Dec. 9.

It has been revealed that it is often a fool's errand to try to time the market's ups and downs, especially amid this unprecedented AI boom. Still, the many parallels to the late-2018 downturn offer hope for next year.

Amid all the turmoil and uncertainty, investors should stick with their regular investing looks, allocating a portion of their savings to high-quality stocks each month, with an eye toward the long term -- not just next month or next year.

  • The new Google Wallet app lets you digitize physical cards, including payment, loyalty, and membership cards, as well as boarding passes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Google Wallet app is available for iPhone consumers in the US for the first time. iOS users who download the new Google Wallet app can manage online payments for faster checkout at places that support Google Pay. However, Apple restricts Google’s ability to offer tap-to-pay service on the iOS app, so users won’t be able to use Google Wallet for contactless checkout on iPhone.

Also: You can use Google’s Spark AI agent, renamed Tasks, for free now – with limits.

The new Google Wallet app lets you digitize physical cards, including payment, loyalty, and membership cards, as well as boarding passes. Google Wallet app users on iOS will also be able to view receipts and track orders pulled from Gmail in one app.

There used to be a Google Pay app for iOS, but it was discontinued in 2024. The old Google Pay app also didn’t support tap-to-pay on iPhone, but it offered limited functionality, including support for loyalty and gift cards, as well as purchase tracking.

The biggest difference between the old Google Pay app for iOS and the new Google Wallet is the AI component, which supports agentic shopping, likely as Google’s longer-term play.

According to recent reports, one of Google’s goals for the Wallet app on iOS is to make it a central place to manage purchases made by its AI agents. The Agents section in Google Wallet for iPhone lets you manage and monitor purchases made through Gemini.

Industry observers note that agentic commerce is on the rise, as evidenced by the growing use of Meta’s Muse. Gemini can make purchases and payments through the Tasks feature, which lets you give Gemini permission to buy the items you want and set your maximum budget.

Also: Google Wallet just turned your Android phone into a digital house key.

The Google Wallet app for iOS becomes the central hub for purchase management in agentic commerce through Gemini. In it, you can view active tasks to see which purchases Gemini is working on, as well as completed purchases and receipts.

Google has been working on two technologies to support its agentic commerce strategy: Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP) and Agent Payments Protocol (AP2).

UCP is a technical language that enables AI agents to communicate with retailers and make purchases, while AP2 is the payment framework that establishes rules and authorization for agents to make payments.

Google Wallet serves as both the AI-powered wallet and the consumer-facing record of transactions made by Gemini.

Also: Google Wallet has a lot of fresh tricks – these 5 are my favorites.

Sources indicate that along with Google, major retailers supported the development of UCP, including Shopify, Walmart, Target, and Etsy. When Google confirmed AP2, more than 60 organizations became involved, including PayPal, Salesforce, Mastercard, and American Express.

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1066 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Zdnet ↗ Open Full Page

90% of employers reject resumes that look like AI – yet half use AI to interview

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1066 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that hiring managers are more suspicious than ever of AI use in applications, and it’s impacting who they consider.
  • Latest data from hiring systems firm Greenhouse found that “nine in ten US employers (90%) believe they’ve turned away real candidates because those applications seemed fake or AI-generated.” Greenhouse clarified that it doesn’t know whether employers are putting applications through AI detection tools or not.
  • Also: How many jobs is your state losing to AI?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that hiring managers are more suspicious than ever of AI use in applications, and it’s impacting who they consider. At the same time, they’re turning to AI to help screen more candidates — meaning those videos you’ve seen on the internet of people pranking AI interviewers aren’t going away anytime soon.

Latest data from hiring systems firm Greenhouse found that “nine in ten US employers (90%) believe they’ve turned away real candidates because those applications seemed fake or AI-generated.” Greenhouse clarified that it doesn’t know whether employers are putting applications through AI detection tools or not.

Also: How many jobs is your state losing to AI? This dashboard tracks the cuts – and the cost.

“The survey data is self-reported, so it reflects what employers believe has happened, not a measured outcome,” Greenhouse’s Head of Voice AI Ophir Samson told ZDNET via email.

Employers are also reacting to AI by adjusting their hiring processes: 86% of those surveyed reported changes to account for AI’s impact. 57% of them did so by adding another human interview.

Recent findings suggest that “As jobseekers rely more on AI to polish and send out their job applications, employers are finding it harder to tell who’s actually right for the role,” the report stated, echoing an ongoing push-and-pull between applicants and hiring teams. AI resume screeners automatically toss a majority of applications they deem unfit, so applicants try not to get tossed by formatting their material for the screener, which then backfires anyway.

In a recent development, the report highlights how a tough economy and an influx of AI hiring tools are colliding, arguably to benefit employers over applicants. Greenhouse noted that, ironically, AI tools are helping hiring managers while also making resumes untrustworthy, and applicants would rather be interviewed by AI than not at all.

Also: How to beat the AI algorithm and get the job of your dreams.

“A growing number of employers are using AI not just to filter candidates out, but to have conversations with more candidates, earlier, through AI-powered voice technology,” Greenhouse remarked, adding that “half now use AI interviews to hear from more candidates, and 40% of those have found strong candidates they would have missed.”.

Industry observers note that greenhouse itself offers a voice AI screening interview tool. Samson told ZDNET that an HR professional ran 200 candidates she’d rejected through Greenhouse’s tool, and it suggested 19.

“All five of the finalists came from that group, and she ultimately hired one from the group,” Samson stated.

What we don’t, and maybe can’t, know is the inverse: whether AI screeners influence hiring managers to turn away candidates they actually should have considered. At least in Greenhouse’s case, Samson said Voice AI doesn’t make hiring decisions or “automatically advance, reject, or rank candidates.”.

“Recruiters review every output, and one recruiter owns the outcome and can explain how they reached it,” he noted.

Greenhouse’s report surveyed 1,347 hiring managers and recruiters across the US, UK, Germany, Australia, and Ireland from late September to mid-October, and found that half of employers using voice AI “say the early-stage candidate experience has improved.”.

Also: ‘So perfect, they are literally identical’ – Your AI-polished resumes are recruiters’ fresh top stressor.

It’s unclear what “improved” means there, though, and whether applicants themselves would agree with that. Still, when given the choice, only 7% of applicants in the US would turn down an AI interview, per an earlier Greenhouse report. Additionally, “70% of those who’ve had a live AI interview say it helped them show their skills,” that report stated.

But how swayed is that by the state of the US job market? October’s job report was better than expected, but it’s still been a tough year overall for job-seekers. Greenhouse’s findings could be as much a reflection of how desperate applicants are as an endorsement of or comfort with AI screenings.

“The job market could be a factor. Our Future of Hiring Candidate Report highlights 81% of job seekers were rejected from a job in the past year without speaking to anyone at the manufacturer, human or AI,” Samson said. “But I’d be careful about reading the data as desperation. Candidates are setting clear conditions: nearly half (49%) want to know if a human will review their responses and 40% want to know how they’ll be evaluated.”.

Also: Why replacing staff with AI backfires – and 5 ways smart leaders generate real value instead.

According to recent reports, samson noted that a software engineer named Ryan Quinlan, who was hired at Blissway, initially thought “talking to an AI” sounded stranger, but that it ultimately “felt like a conversation” that let him mention skills he’d forgotten to include on his resume. Samson said that Ryan has been “a ‘maybe’ on paper,” but that the AI interview helped him get over the line to be considered.

“For most applicants, a human conversation was never on the table,” Samson said. “The real choice is a resume lost in a pile, or 15 minutes to tell their story.”.

Greenhouse found that while employers are using AI to screen more candidates, most are maintaining human oversight over the most important decisions in the hiring process.

“Of all the tasks employers would hand to an AI agent, deciding which candidates to advance came last, at just 7%,” Greenhouse said.

A recent California law aims to protect employees from being fired by AI systems that make determinations about their performance without a human co-signing the assessment. As with many AI productivity tools in the workplace, proper adoption ideally equates to more time for human workers to handle more important tasks.

Also: 92% of HR say staff can train for AI jobs – but half of companies still hire outside.

“Of employers who’ve saved time with AI, 85% put it back into candidates, most often by spending more time with shortlisted candidates (45%) and interviewing more candidates earlier (40%),” Greenhouse mentioned.

The main question around AI interviewers remains whether they’re correctly capturing your interview the way you’d hope a human interviewer would (though that’s still deeply subjective and out of applicants’ control anyway).

According to recent reports, “When AI interviews are implemented thoughtfully and transparently, they pay off for both candidates and recruiters,” Samson remarked. “Every candidate who uses our Voice AI can opt out, and about 90% rate the experience as excellent.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s been over two months since Meta debuted its Muse AI agent, giving people new tools to automate tasks like handling email replies, booking travel or even shopping for you.
  • Sources indicate that muse has been highly controversial, the subject of several security warnings and privacy breaches.
  • Industry observers note that AI agents are marketed as providing convenience by acting on your behalf.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s been over two months since Meta debuted its Muse AI agent, giving people new tools to automate tasks like handling email replies, booking travel or even shopping for you.

Sources indicate that muse has been highly controversial, the subject of several security warnings and privacy breaches. Meta’s Muse AI agent quietly builds a profile on you the second you start using it, even if you explicitly tell it not to. That turns Jolly, its supposedly cute and cuddly mascot, into the friendly face of some serious security flaws.

Industry observers note that AI agents are marketed as providing convenience by acting on your behalf. But the trade-off is privacy and control. You’re handing over your personal information to a black box with little visibility into how it’s used. Multiple incidents are fueling a conversation about the dangers of agentic AI and whether they require higher security standards before being granted access to user data.

According to recent reports, that’s especially the case when it comes to handing over sensitive financial information. If you give an AI access to your digital wallets to shop for you, the risk extends beyond an authorized purchase. You could be exposing your bank accounts to a potential security breach or data exposure, with little recourse to fix it. If you were considering letting Muse make decisions and transactions with your money ahead of Black Friday and Cyber Monday, you should know it’s still raising red flags as a shopping companion.

In a recent development, given Meta’s track record of privacy fines, data sharing and security concerns, it’s worth proceeding with caution. A few months ago, a lifestyle blogger reported that the social media platform’s AI asked intrusive questions about her kids and pieced together private information about her life from her posts. Meta’s controversial smart glasses have received pushback on multiple fronts — from its facial recognition software to the way it captures and stores data.

Despite the risk, Muse has remained popular and now faces competition from Anthropic’s newly released Claude Duet, another AI business agent. Meta is also releasing a $300 portable device, Charm, in a virtual-toy style that will work with Muse.

A representative for Meta has not responded to CNET’s request for comment.

Muse asks for the keys to your digital life: passwords, full disk access, emails, calendar invites, contacts, Notes and WhatsApp chats. Meta also feeds your conversations into its AI training pipeline by default, leaving it on you to dig through the settings and opt out.

Within weeks of launch earlier this fall, a security researcher demonstrated that the assistant could be hijacked via a zero-day exploit that Meta’s own documentation acknowledged was easy to trigger. Then, an investigative journalist discovered Muse digging through his private Apple Messages without permission. Meta disputed the claim, but Apple took it seriously enough to roll out an emergency upgrade to MacOS privacy controls.

More recently, Meta employees themselves have flagged instances where Muse may have accessed encrypted messages from apps such as Signal or information from other Muse customers, which Meta has chalked up to “isolated incidents” and that permission to access apps and information from notifications has to be explicitly granted in a statement to news outlets.

If the previous incidents weren’t enough to give you pause, there’s also a widely publicized case in which Muse mistakenly shared the home address of a Toronto tech reviewer, Matt Robb, with a potential buyer on Facebook Marketplace. Muse invited the stranger to Robb’s home without his explicit consent or knowledge, then later apologized for doing so, as detailed in a Threads post. Robb hadn’t realized that he had inadvertently granted Muse blanket permission to automatically reply to Marketplace inquiries using the details he provided, including his address.

Before facing a potential security nightmare, here are a few other things to know about Muse.

According to recent reports, muse uploads iOS or Mac data even when you tell it not to: Meta’s Muse appears to blatantly ignore user permissions, according to a September report by AppleInsider. In one case, the AI agent synced roughly 187,000 lines of a user’s Apple Messages without their consent, even though “Full Disk Access” was turned off. The report highlights that Muse pinged a user’s messages database thousands of times despite disk access being disabled. Muse then successfully harvested texts from the user’s Mac — not from Meta’s Messenger, but from Apple Messages. Even people who refuse to use Muse may have their data collected by the AI if they text someone who does have it installed.

According to recent reports, muse could hand over data to human callers: Before Meta debuted the ability for its Muse to make outbound business calls on your behalf, internal Meta documents revealed that the organization planned to rely on human contractors at call centers to help make reservations and appointments. That means not only would the software have access to all your private data, but a total stranger might also be managing your personal commitments — all without your knowledge. The human concierge feature appears to have been rolled back for now, according to Reuters.

Muse has the most robust data collection: In September, the VPN organization Surfshark said it found that Meta Muse is collecting — or attempting to collect — 31 out of 35 types of data, putting it far ahead of other popular chatbots like Gemini, ChatGPT and DeepSeek. Muse also collects highly sensitive personal information like location data, sexual orientation, genetic information or biometric data. Muse (along with Meta AI and Gemini) also reserves the right to use collected audio data for other purposes, such as analytics or product personalization. Surfshark released a full dataset of what it uncovered.

Meta has tried hard with Muse to make the AI agent seem cute and approachable, but when it comes to your money and giving Muse access to it, it’s best to be very cautious for the time being.

Black Friday week has arrived and if you're looking to scoop a great deal on running shoes in the sales, you have some great options to pick from.

Amazon's Black Friday running shoe deals are already going strong, and most brands are running their own individual sales too, which contains some of the best running shoes I've tested over the past year or two.

I've picked out the biggest and best deals on some of my favorite running shoes below, with savings on everything from comfortable cushioned sneakers to plated speedsters.

The Aero Razor is a very underrated running shoe and competitive with popular options like the Adidas Evo SL. This is a wild price on such a good shoe, and if you're looking for a lightweight daily trainer that comes alive in interval workouts, it's worth checking out.

It has been revealed that the Puma Velocity Nitro 4 is always a great value option for runners looking for a cushioned shoe. Several colors are less than $100 at Amazon, with the lowest price I've found being $84. The Velocity Nitro 5 is out now, but I didn't find it a huge improvement on the 4 in my testing.

In a recent development, you can stack discounts in the Saucony sale by adding a reduced shoe to your cart and then using the code 'CHEER' at checkout for another 25% off. That means you can get the Saucony Endorphin Speed 5 for just $82, which is an amazing price for a plated trainer like this.

It has been revealed that the Nike Structure Plus is a very cushioned and comfortable stability shoe. This low price is achieved by picking the color reduced to $104 in the sale, then using the code 'BFRIDAY' to take 25% off that price at checkout.

The Nike Pegasus 42 is the latest version of Nike's reliable and popular workhorse trainer. It's good for walking and gym workouts alongside running, last forever, and looks good too. You can get this price, which is the cheapest I've seen the Pegasus 42, by picking the cheapest color of the shoe and using the code 'BFRIDAY' at checkout.

The Adidas Adizero Evo SL is a long term favorite of mine and many runners, partly because it's great value even at full price. It's a lightweight shoe that excels for faster training runs, but can be used for all your training. It's down to $105 at Amazon in the black color.

The Asics Gel-Kayano 32 is a comfortable stability shoe that's great for walking as well as running. With the Asics Gel-Kayano 33 launching recently, the previous model is available in a few sales, with this deal for $124 on Amazon being the price to beat.

Sources indicate that the Hoka Challenger 8 flies under the radar but is worthy of being just as popular as better know shoes like the Clifton and Bondi. It's a versatile all-terrain shoe that's worth looking at if you mix up the surfaces you run on. It's comfortable, lightweight and grips well on both the road and light trails.

The Asics Superblast 3 is one of the better running shoes I've tested this year, but the Superblast 2 is still worth considering if you're looking for a versatile max-cushioned sneaker that's $50 less than the latest model. It's great for all kinds of runs, and I often used the Superblast 2 for trips with a lot of walking as well.

Latest Update: The Flipper One is more than a Zero 2.0 – it’s a $399 Linux computer with a $13M Kickstarter

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (717 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Flipper One crowdfunding campaign has broken the $13-million mark, smashing the funding raised for previous Flipper devices and demonstrating strong interest in the successor to the Flipper Zero.
  • According to recent reports, the thing that made the Flipper Zero so popular was how easy it was to use.
  • Also: The Flipper One may be the ultimate Linux PC for hackers in 2026 – and I’m excited.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Flipper One crowdfunding campaign has broken the $13-million mark, smashing the funding raised for previous Flipper devices and demonstrating strong interest in the successor to the Flipper Zero. The $399 Flipper One is a pocket Linux computer focused on networking, with delivery estimated for July 2027. But it isn’t simply an updated version of the Flipper Zero. It’s a very different animal and a much more serious bit of kit.

According to recent reports, the thing that made the Flipper Zero so popular was how easy it was to use. You could fire it up and turn the volume down on the TV at your parents’ place, see the radio waves coming from your car’s key fob, and copy hotel room key cards.

Also: The Flipper One may be the ultimate Linux PC for hackers in 2026 – and I’m excited.

It could do a lot, there wasn’t a steep learning curve, and you didn’t need to buy anything else. Did the fake videos on TikTok from people claiming they could change the prices at gas stations (I wish!) or start cars remotely help make the Zero more popular?

Industry observers note that unfortunately, yes. But what made it successful was that it packed a lot of power into a package that was small, fun, affordable, and easy to use.

If the Flipper Zero, with its NFC, RFID, sub-GHz, and IR, was kindergarten, the Flipper One is a college degree: a pocket Linux computer focused on networking.

Industry observers note that this is reflected in the price. You can pick up a Zero for $169, while the Flipper One is $399.

What this buys you is the Flipper One base computer with a 256 × 144 grayscale LCD, Rockchip RK3576 8-core ARM SoC with NPU, a low-power MCU for handling the LCD and user interface, 8GB of LPDDR5 RAM, 64GB of UFS 2.2 storage, and a microSD slot.

If that $399 feels like a lot, it’s worth keeping in mind that, according to Flipper, the price only covers production costs and that the RAM and UFS storage account for at least half of the total hardware cost.

Sources indicate that if you think this is a lot, you could spend a lot more. Adding a LoRa, SDR, or 5G module will push the total up a lot higher. And if you want all three modules, you’re looking at $759 for the Flipper One Ultimate Bundle.

Also: The Flipper One is the Linux cyberdeck I wish my Raspberry Pi could be.

The reception has been strong enough that pledges have flown past the $300,000 goal that Flipper initially set, with over 24,000 backers pledging over $13 million. Close to 5,300 backers have gone for the Ultimate Bundle, compared to just over 4,300 choosing the bare Flipper One.

This suggests that backers really want the radio capabilities that this newly introduced platform offers.

If you want one, this crowdfunding run is a good time to get one because it’s a Kickstarter Special slashing 25% off an estimated retail price of $550.

The response over on Reddit has been a little more subdued, with some being taken aback by the price of the Zero’s bigger sibling.

Also: 7 useful things I can do with my Flipper Zero – as someone who’s used it for years.

As someone who homebrews a lot of electronics, I’m going to say that the price is justified, and this project goes far beyond something you could put together with a Raspberry Pi and some code.

The Flipper One campaign runs until Dec. 17, 2026, with delivery estimated for July 2027.

It has been revealed that keep in mind that this is a Kickstarter pledge, not a purchase, and that rewards aren’t guaranteed. Flipper also states on the Kickstarter page that component shortages are the biggest risk to the project and that they “could cause significant delays to production and delivery.” It also says that if RAM prices continue to rise, it cannot “rule out adjusting some product specifications, including reducing the amount of RAM.”.

Also: Is the Flipper Zero the best multi-tool for hacking?

And the good news here is that I’ve seen several analysts predicting that RAM prices will begin to go down in 2027 as demand eases off.
